problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Clusters of tiny insects feeding on tender new growth and on the underside of leaves.
prevention: Check leaf undersides regularly
Natural predators such as ladybugs often keep aphids down

problems.name: Corn earworm and other caterpillars
problems.signs: Caterpillars ('worms') found in the pods. Usually a minor problem, unless you plan to save seed.
prevention: Inspect plants frequently

problems.name: Root-knot nematodes
problems.signs: Stunted, yellow or poorly producing plants; roots show galls and swellings when pulled up.
prevention: Do not follow nematode-susceptible crops such as tomato or sweet potato
Rotate crops
Use soil solarization
Cover crops can help suppress nematodes

problems.name: Fusarium and Verticillium wilt
problems.signs: Plants turn yellow, wilt and die.
prevention: Rotate crops
Use disease-free seed

problems.name: Stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs
problems.signs: Pods grow bent, twisted or misshapen where the bugs have fed on them, though the pods can still be eaten.

problems.name: Damping off and root rot
problems.signs: Young seedlings rot and die; root decay is more common when okra is planted in cold, wet soil.
prevention: Wait until the soil is warm before sowing

problems.name: Southern blight
problems.signs: Damage at the base of the plant that destroys the tissue there; the fungus lives in the soil and returns the next season.
prevention: Pull out any plant you think is infected
Rotate crops

problems.name: Tough, fibrous pods
problems.signs: Pods turn tough, stringy and woody when left on the plant too long, and cropping slows.
prevention: Pick every day or two while pods are small and tender

text.summary: Okra is a tall, upright, warm-season vegetable grown for its tender green or red pods. It wants full sun, warm soil and frost-free weather, and it grows fast once settled. Pods must be picked young and often to keep the plant cropping. It suits garden beds and, with a compact variety, a pot.
text.how_to_plant: Sow okra only once frost has gone and the soil about 10 cm down has warmed to at least 18.3 degrees C (65 F); cooler soil risks seedlings rotting. Pick a sunny site with well-drained soil. Soak the seed overnight, then push it 1 to 2.5 cm into the soil. Thin seedlings so the plants stand 23 to 61 cm apart, with rows at least 91 cm apart. For an early start, raise seedlings indoors for four to five weeks first, and plant them out once the weather is warm.
text.how_to_care: Okra likes full sun and warm weather. It copes with dry spells fairly well but crops better if watered every week or so when rain is lacking. Keep water steady while pods set and grow, water at the base of the plants, and avoid soggy or poorly drained soil. Mulch 5 to 7.5 cm deep with organic material to hold moisture and hold weeds down. Feed with a balanced fertiliser at planting, following the label, and go easy on nitrogen, which grows leaves instead of pods. Avoid growing it after crops prone to nematodes, such as tomato or sweet potato.
text.harvest: Expect the first pods about 50 to 70 days after sowing; one guide gives up to 90. Cut pods while they are tender, around 5 to 10 cm long; bigger pods turn tough and fibrous. Pick every day or two and remove any old pods you missed, because they slow further cropping. The plant keeps bearing until frost. Cover your hands and arms when picking, since its fine hairs irritate bare skin. Fresh pods keep about 2 to 7 days in the fridge.
common_mistakes: Sowing into cold soil, which leaves seed slow to come up and seedlings liable to rot.
Leaving pods on the plant until they are large; they turn tough and woody and slow further cropping.
Giving too much nitrogen, which makes leafy plants with poor yield.
Growing okra again where nematode-susceptible crops grew, without rotating.
Poor drainage in beds or pots, which damages the plants.

problems.name: Thrips
problems.signs: Tiny slender insects feed on the leaves, leaving silver or grey patches; leaves may twist and die.
prevention: Wash them off with a stiff spray of water
Spread an organic mulch around the plants
Encourage predatory mites and lacewings in the garden

problems.name: Onion maggot
problems.signs: White worms feed on seedlings, roots or bulbs.
prevention: Rotate crops and plant in a different part of the garden each year
Cover the crop with floating row covers
Destroy affected plants
Keep the bed clean and avoid excess decomposing organic matter

problems.name: Bolting
problems.signs: The plant sends up a flower stalk instead of swelling a bulb.
prevention: Do not plant too early, before a cold spell has passed
Avoid oversized sets and transplants, which bolt more readily

problems.name: Rust
problems.signs: Brown to orange raised spots or patches appear on the foliage.
prevention: Space plants so they are not crowded

problems.name: Pink root
problems.signs: The roots turn pink.
prevention: Use a long crop rotation
Solarize the soil where onions were grown

problems.name: Neck rot
problems.signs: Watery decay appears inside the bulb while it is in storage.
prevention: Avoid excess moisture near harvest
Cure the bulbs well before storing them

problems.name: Basal rot
problems.signs: The base where roots meet the leaves rots, and the plant grows slowly and poorly.
prevention: Use a long crop rotation
Solarize the soil where onions are planted
Avoid over-watering

text.summary: Bulb onion is a sun-loving crop grown from seed or from transplants in fertile, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Bulbs form only when the day is long enough for the variety, so match the type to your latitude. Expect bulbs roughly 90 to 130 days after sowing, ready once the tops fall over.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a spot in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil and plenty of organic matter. Sow seed about 0.5 to 2 cm deep, or raise seedlings indoors for about 8 weeks and then plant them out. Seed germinates over a wide range of soil temperatures and usually comes up within 4 to 21 days. Thin seedlings to about 10 cm apart, in rows roughly 20 to 60 cm apart. Check the day-length type of the variety against your latitude, because a bulb forms only when days reach the length that type needs.
text.how_to_care: Onions have shallow roots, so keep the soil moist and the bed weeded. They are hungry plants: give a balanced fertiliser when planting. Mulch lightly while the plants are young. Do not draw soil up around the stems, which invites stem rot. Planting too early, or using oversized sets or transplants, can make plants flower instead of forming bulbs. Keep onions out of ground that grew onion-family crops in the past three to four years.
text.harvest: Lift bulbs once the tops have fallen over and turned brown and the outer skins have gone papery. Leave them to dry where they grew for a week or two, then finish curing in a shaded, well-ventilated spot until the skins are papery and the roots dry. Curing before storage helps avoid rots. Store cured bulbs somewhere cool and dry with good air movement.
common_mistakes: Planting sets or transplants too early, which makes them bolt.
Hilling soil up around the stems, which encourages stem rot.
Letting plants suffer drought stress, which cuts yield and bulb size.
Growing a variety whose day-length type does not suit the latitude, which may never form a bulb.
Storing bulbs that were not cured well first.

text.summary: Bunching onion is a leafy onion that forms no large bulb. It is grown for its green tops and white stem bases, in beds or pots, in sun or part shade. Seed sown in place gives a first pick about 50 to 75 days later, and the leaves can be cut again and again.
text.how_to_plant: Sow where the plants will stay, or raise seedlings in trays and move them out; one guide starts them 8 to 10 weeks ahead. Outdoors, sow once the soil is at least 10 degrees C, in fertile, well-drained soil with a pH of about 6 to 7. Sow seed 0.5 to 1.5 cm deep in rows 15 to 36 cm apart. Seedlings can take 7 to 10 days to appear. Space plants about 1.5 to 5 cm apart. Bought seedlings can also be planted. A pot needs to be at least 15 cm deep and have drainage holes.
text.how_to_care: Give plants full sun or part shade. Keep weeds away from the plants, and spread straw as mulch to keep weeds out and hold in moisture. Avoid crowding plants, which helps against rust. Watch for thrips, which leave silvery patches on the leaves. Rinse them off with a hose, mulch around the plants and welcome predatory insects. Rotating crops also helps.
text.harvest: Start cutting once the plants stand about 15 cm tall. Snip some leaves as needed and leave the rest to regrow, or lift whole plants after loosening the soil with a fork. Trim the roots, then rinse and dry the plants. They keep about a week in a plastic bag in the fridge, or you can chop and freeze them for cooked dishes.
common_mistakes: Planting too close together, which invites rust.
Letting weeds crowd the bed.

fields.note: s6: leeks develop edible white stems 6 to 10 inches long. One source. s6 prints leek as Allium cepa var. porrum, a wrong name; its leek lines still count (rule 136a).

s1: prefers full sun; s5: position the pot in full sun; s6: all onion relatives, which its introduction says include leeks, should be grown in full sun. s2 (same group as s1) says direct light for at least 6 hours a day. The Seed Collection's sun sentence is not used (see header).

s20 (UC Master Gardener Program; the page credits the table to the California Master Gardener Handbook, 2nd edition, Table 5.2): the 'Minimum (F)' column of its seed germination table gives 32 F for leeks = 0.0 C, exact. A multi-crop table counts for a plant that has its own row (leeks). One source: FLAGGED. 0 C sits far below the growth minimum (7.2 C, s19) and the start of the germination optimum (10 C, s7); those measure other things, so there is no clash, but the horticulturist should say whether 0 C is a usable lowest sowing temperature. Other figures, not counted: Kitchen Garden Seeds prints a germination range of 45 to 75 F (a seed company's range is an optimum, rules 27 and 102a); Wisconsin advises about 70 F until seeds sprout (a management cue).

Seed companies' germination temperatures (rule 27). s4: 18 to 23 C; s7: optimal soil temperature 10 to 25 C (50 to 75 F, stated in both units; 75 F is 23.9 C, so the units disagree and the metric figure counts, rule 70). Both ends rest on s7; only the 10 end is flagged (8 C below s4's 18).

Rule 140, the only source: Utah State Extension, Temperature Management in High Tunnels, Table 3 (credited to Knott's Handbook), row 'Chive, Garlic, Leek, Onion', minimum 45 F = 7.2 C (rounded to the nearest tenth, rule 100b; rule 209). No other allowed source states this field. Flagged.

Rule 140, the only source: Utah State Extension, Temperature Management in High Tunnels, Table 3 (credited to Knott's Handbook), row 'Chive, Garlic, Leek, Onion', maximum 85 F = 29.4 C (rounded to the nearest tenth, rule 100b; rule 209). No other allowed source states this field. Flagged.

s2 uses two frost words, 'Hardy (plants can withstand heavy frosts)' and 'Leeks are fairly hardy'; 'fairly hardy' maps to light and the less hardy class is the source's vote (rules 136c, 127d). One source: flagged (hardy against light). s1 calls leek a hardy cool-season biennial (life-cycle phrase, no vote, rule 121b).

s1: leeks grow in all soil types provided they are rich, well drained, moist and fertile (rules 53, 91d), which names every texture; s7: even in heavy soils leeks are easy to grow (heavy soils map to clay, rule 109c). Sandy and loam rest on s1 alone: flagged.
s1: fertile, well-drained soils; s5: quick-facts value well drained.
s5 gives pot instructions: position the pot in full sun and choose a pot at least 300 mm wide and deep. One source.
s5: a pot at least 300 mm wide and deep = 30 cm. The page says leeks can be spaced 10 to 20 cm apart in a pot, so the pot holds several plants and no volume is stored (rule 71). One source.

direct: s4 ('Sow seeds directly in the garden 5mm deep ...', set per crop), s1 and s6 (seed spacing in the row); dissent: s7 says 'Transplanting is required' (rule 136d), so direct wins three to one. indoors: s7 (sow in flats indoors), s1 (transplants need 6 to 8 weeks of growth). s4's 'sown directly ... OR seedlings can be raised' and 'Raise Seedlings' lines are template (on its asparagus, Brussels sprouts and celery pages) and give no vote. s2's indoor-start clause is template (word for word on UMD's kohlrabi and Brussels sprouts pages; rules 56 and 131h) and gives no vote. No source says transplants are bought.

s1: transplants need 6 to 8 weeks of growth before planting in the garden (seedling age at planting out, rule 31). Not counted: s7's '6-8 weeks before the last frost date' (counted back from a frost date, rule 31). One source: flagged.
s4: around 10 to 14 days at 18 to 23 C; s7: seeds should sprout in 10 to 16 days.

Days from sowing (maturity_from). s1: generally 100 to 120 days to mature (its 'may be harvested as early as 60 days after seeding' is a possibility and gives no figure, rule 133d; s2 is in the same group, rule 133b); s6: about 120 days from seed to maturity; s3: three to four months = 90 to 120 days (30 days per month, rule 17; the page describes only sowing, rule 33). Three groups state figures; the 90 end rests on s3 alone, 10 percent below 100: no flag. Not used (rules 47, 50): s2 'Days to maturity: 70 - 120, depending on the cultivar' (no start point); s4 about 120 to 150 days (its page offers direct sowing or raised seedlings, no start point). Counted from transplanting, not stored: s8 21 to 30 weeks = 147 to 210 days; s5 12 to 20 weeks after planting = 84 to 140 days (7 days per week, rule 48).

Sowing: s6 and s1 state it, s3's page describes only sowing (rule 33). Transplant (dissent, not in sources, rule 98d): s8 ('from transplants') and s5 (12 to 20 weeks after planting, on a page that raises seedlings then transplants them), so sowing wins three groups to two (rule 131b). s2 and s4 give no usable start point; s7 says days are counted from transplant date but gives no figure.
s4: leeks are best left in the ground until needed; s7: dig at any size, as needed (rule 113d).

Seed depth. s4: 5 mm = 0.5 cm; s7: in flats, 5 mm = 0.5 cm (s7 prints '5mm (¼”)', but ¼ inch is 6.35 mm, so its units disagree and the metric figure counts, rule 70); s1: 1/4 to 1/2 inch = 0.635 to 1.27 cm (the top; 1.27 is exact at two decimals). The top rests on s1 alone: flagged. Transplant planting depths are not stored (no field for them): s8 'up to 10 cm deep'; s1 a 6 inch (15.24 cm) dibble hole; s7 a 15 cm (6 inch) dibber hole; s5 'plant seedlings 15 cm deeper'.

Between plants. s8: 10 to 15 cm; s6: thin to 4 inches or set transplants 4 inches = 10.16; s1: thinned to 4 to 6 inches = 10.16 to 15.24 (its 3 to 4 inch sowing distance is left out because it thins, rule 122b); s2: 5 inches = 12.7; s4: 12 cm; s5: 20 cm in the garden and 10 to 20 cm in a pot; s7: 20 cm (8 inches = 20.32, the metric figure counts, rule 70).
s4: 45 cm; s1: 8 to 16 inches = 20.32 to 40.64; s8: 30 to 45 cm; s7: 45 cm (18 inches = 45.72) and rows can be as narrow as 20 cm (8 inches) in raised beds.

s1: thinned to 4 to 6 inches (the larger, safer end counts, rules 14 and 103b) = 15.24. s6 (not in sources, rule 98d) says thin to 4 inches = 10.16; s4 (not in sources) says thin so plants are spaced about 12 cm apart (optional thinning, counted, set per crop). Three single-source figures tie and the larger stands (rule 103b). Spread is 33 percent of the stored value, and one source: flagged.
s7: usual seed life 1 year (single figure, min = max). s4 says leek seed does not store well long term and to use fresh seed each year (no figure). One source.

s7: balanced organic fertiliser worked in along the row (the main feed). One source. Not mapped: s6's 5-10-10 formula (phosphorus and potassium tie, rule 82) and its calcium nitrate side dressing (supplement, rule 86b); s1's nitrogen side dressing (supplement).

s2: mulching is essential to keep the weeds out and the moisture in; s1's 'Organic mulches help conserve water ...' is template (word for word on USU's pea page) and not counted; s5: mulch with an organic mulch and water in; s7: mulch around the stems (and with straw to blanch).

straw: s5 (sugar cane or pea straw), s7 (straw), s2 (a heavy blanket of straw or leaves). compost: s1 (mulching with compost, grass clippings or leaves; s2 has the same sentence, same group); one group, flagged. Grass clippings and leaves are not mapped (rule 22).

s1: hilling gives a longer blanched stem; s3 and s6: start when the plants are as thick as a pencil; s7: hill soil up around the stem as the leek grows. Dissent in the same group as s1 (not in sources): s2 says blanching by hilling 'isn't absolutely necessary'. s5's 'you can also cover the lower stems ... or mound soil' is optional wording and is not counted.
Leeks are grown from seed (s4's line 'Sow seeds directly in the garden 5mm deep ...', s1, s6).

Rule 52: family name from IPNI (s9). Wikidata Q148995 (s11) and the seed-company pages print Amaryllidaceae; see the header. Synonyms: IPNI (s9) lists the names Allium ampeloprasum var. porrum and Allium ampeloprasum subsp. porrum but states no synonymy; Wikidata (s11) lists Allium porrum as a taxon synonym of Allium ampeloprasum, with no reference.

fields.value: Harvest once the stems are about 2.5 cm across; smaller leeks can be taken earlier, and plants can wait in the ground until needed.
fields.note: s1 and s2: ready when the stalks are 1 inch (2.54 cm) across; s6: ready when an inch or more across; s8: harvest when the base is around 2 to 3 cm across; s7: dig at any size, as needed.
s2: dig or pull; s7: dig at any size, as needed.

fields.value: fridge, cool dark, freeze, pickle, dry
fields.note: fridge: s2 and s6 (stored in a refrigerator), s8 (coldest part of the refrigerator); listed first, so it carries the storage-life figure. s1 (one source for each of the rest, none disputed, flagged): cool_dark (in very cold areas, store in cold 32-40 F, humid conditions in wet sand, rule 136f); freeze, pickle and dry ('can be frozen, pickled, canned or dehydrated'; dehydrated maps to dry, rule 136f; canned has no value in the list).
Method: fridge. s2: 7 to 10 days. s6 says several weeks (no figure, not counted). One source.

Toxic to dogs and cats (s18, a peer-reviewed review, rule 126k). s18 names leek (Allium porrum) with onion, garlic and chives, says dogs and cats are highly susceptible to Allium toxicosis and that cooking and drying do not remove the toxic effect. No plant part is named; the plant is named as a food. Leek and Allium are absent from the UGA C1245 list (s16) and the Illinois Plants and Pet Safety list (s17, not all inclusive); absence does not outweigh a stated harm (rule 124a).

Leek, Allium, onion, garlic, chive and wild garlic are absent from the Utah Poison Control web list (s14) and from both lists of the Utah brochure (s15, read as PDF text; it says its toxic list is not necessarily comprehensive). That leeks are eaten as food is not a safety finding (rule 36).

text.summary: Leek is a vegetable grown for its thick white stem. It wants full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and it also grows in a deep pot. Start it from seed, sown in place or raised in trays, then draw soil up around the stems as they grow so more of the stem stays white.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed about 0.5 to 1.3 cm deep where it will grow, or raise seedlings in trays indoors for six to eight weeks and move them out. Seed usually sprouts in 10 to 16 days. Space plants 10 to 20 cm apart in rows 20 to 45 cm apart, thinning to about 15 cm if sown thickly. Set transplants deep, in a hole made with a dibber, so more of the stem is buried and blanches. Leeks grow in any soil that is rich, drained and fertile. In a pot, use one at least 30 cm wide and deep.
text.how_to_care: Give leeks full sun. Keep the soil from drying out, and lay mulch around the plants to hold moisture and hold weeds back. As the stems thicken, draw soil up around their bases a little at a time, starting once the plants are about as thick as a pencil; starting too early is a mistake. Work a balanced fertiliser into the row, following the product label. Rotate crops to avoid onion maggot, and rinse thrips and aphids off with a hose.
text.harvest: Leeks are ready once the stems are roughly 2.5 cm across, though smaller ones can be pulled earlier. Expect a first harvest in about 90 to 120 days from sowing. Plants can stay in the ground until needed, so pick them as you go. Dig or pull them, then wash well before use. In the fridge they keep about a week to ten days.
common_mistakes: Hilling soil round the stems too early, before the plants are about as thick as a pencil.
Sowing old seed, which germinates poorly; leek seed lasts only about a year.

text.summary: Garlic is a bulb crop grown from separated cloves, not seed. It wants full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and it needs a spell of cold before it will form bulbs. Harvest comes roughly 200 to 300 days after planting. Hardneck types suit cooler climates, softneck types warmer ones.
text.how_to_plant: Break a bulb into single cloves and plant the biggest ones, pointed end up. Skip very small cloves, and skip garlic from a grocery store, which can carry disease. Set each clove about 2 to 7.6 cm deep and 7 to 20 cm apart, in rows about 15 to 60 cm apart. Choose a sunny site with deep soil that drains well and holds plenty of organic matter. Cloves need a spell of cold or they may fail to form bulbs, so plant early enough for them to get it before bulbing. A pot at least 20 cm deep can also work.
text.how_to_care: Give garlic full sun and soil that drains freely, because bulbs can rot in heavy, wet ground. It has a high appetite for nutrients, so work in plenty of organic matter and keep it fed. After planting, spread a layer of straw or compost to keep weeds down and hold in moisture. On hardneck types, pinch off the flower stalk when it curls so the bulb grows larger. Keep garlic and other onion-family crops out of the same bed for three years. Watch the leaves for thrips and rust.
text.harvest: Lift the bulbs when the tops start to yellow and flop over, before they dry out completely; some guides wait until about half the leaves are brown. Loosen the soil and lift gently with a fork. Dry the whole plants with tops attached in a shady, airy place for a week or two, or longer, until the skins turn papery. Then trim the roots and tops and keep the bulbs cool and dry. Stored this way they last roughly two to ten months.
common_mistakes: Planting garlic from a grocery store, which can carry disease.
Planting in heavy, wet or poorly drained ground, which can rot the bulbs.
Missing the cold spell cloves need, which gives small bulbs or none.
Leaving the bulbs until the tops are completely dry before lifting them.
Planting garlic where onion-family crops grew in the last three years.

problems.name: Onion thrips
problems.signs: Leaves turn silver or grey and may twist and die; the insects are tiny, slender and pale yellow to light brown.
prevention: Wash thrips off affected plants with a garden hose.
Spread an organic mulch around plants.
Encourage predatory mites and lacewings by companion planting.

problems.name: Rust
problems.signs: Brown to orange raised spots or patches appear on the leaves.
prevention: Space plants so they are not overcrowded.
Give the recommended amount of light.
Avoid over-feeding.
Remove dead plants.
Rotate crops.

problems.name: Pink root
problems.signs: A fungal disease that turns the roots pink.
prevention: Rotate crops on a five-year cycle.
Solarise the soil before planting chives.

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.signs: A fungal disease that turns leaves light tan to brown.
prevention: Practices that improve air movement and let the leaves dry reduce its severity.

text.summary: Chives are a clump-forming perennial herb grown for mild onion-flavoured leaves and edible purple flowers. They like sun and well-drained, organic-rich soil, cope with dry spells, and suit pots. Start them from seed or divide an existing clump.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil enriched with compost or other organic matter. Plant divisions of an established clump, or sow seed where it will grow. Seed can take one to three weeks to sprout; keep the soil moist meanwhile. Transplants need six to eight weeks of growth before they are planted out. Thin or space plants about 15 centimetres apart. Seed-raised plants vary in leaf texture and size. In a pot, allow at least 10 litres.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moist but well drained; established clumps tolerate dry spells. Chives need little extra feeding, though plants that are cut often can use a balanced feed. Mulch around them to hold moisture. Cut plants back every few weeks, and remove flowers before they fade so plants do not self-sow and overrun the bed. Divide clumps every two to three years to stop them crowding, and rotate the bed rather than replanting alliums in the same spot.
text.harvest: Start cutting once plants reach about 15 centimetres. Snip leaves with scissors or a knife near the base, leaving a stub of a few centimetres, or take the outer leaves and leave the rest to regrow. Cut regularly through the season so leaves stay tender. Use fresh where you can. Chives can be frozen for later use; dried leaves lose colour and quickly take up moisture. For a short wait, keep them loosely wrapped in damp paper in a bag with holes in the fridge. The flowers make an edible garnish.
common_mistakes: Letting flowers fade and set seed, so chives self-sow and crowd the garden.
Leaving clumps undivided for years, so plantings become overcrowded and lose vigour.
Cutting too seldom, which lets the leaves turn tough.
Planting in soil that does not drain well.

The NC State Toolbox page (s8, saved copy) has no poison field for dill (rule 141); its tag list includes '#non-toxic for cats', '#non-toxic for dogs' (tags, not a poison field; one source, and non_toxic needs two, rule 36). Absence is not evidence of safety.

Dill, Anethum, Anethum graveolens and Apiaceae are absent from the Utah Poison Control web list (s12, 35 entries; its Poison Hemlock and Water Hemlock entries are other species) and from both the toxic and the non-toxic lists of the Utah brochure (s13; it says its toxic list is not necessarily comprehensive). That dill is eaten as a herb is not a safety finding (rule 36). The NC State Toolbox page (s8, saved copy) has no poison field for dill (rule 141). The skin reaction in s16 is recorded under skin_irritant (rule 37). The Utah brochure (s13) and Illinois pet sheet (s15) are password-protected PDFs read from saved copies of other plants' pages (rule 142j); s12 and s14 were fetched live.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.signs: The plant sends up a flower stalk and heads for seed early, and the leaves decline soon after.
prevention: Thin seedlings so plants are not crowded
Sow a little at a time, so younger plants are always coming along
Grow a variety that resists bolting

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Small, soft insects gather on new shoots and on the undersides of leaves, sucking sap; they can be a problem when the plant starts to flower and the seeds ripen.
prevention: Hose the insects off the plant with water
Encourage natural predators of aphids

problems.name: Damping off
problems.signs: Seeds fail to come up, or young seedlings go soft and mushy at the base and collapse.
prevention: Sow in fresh potting mix when raising seedlings in containers
Keep the leaves dry
Avoid waterlogged soil

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.signs: Yellow to grey-brown patches show on the leaves, especially on the undersides.
prevention: Water at soil level
Remove affected leaves
Avoid overcrowding

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: White spots appear on the leaves and can spread across them.
prevention: Water at soil level
Improve air movement around the plants
Remove affected leaves

text.summary: Dill is a tall, feathery herb grown for its aromatic leaves and its seeds. It does best sown straight into the ground in full sun and well-drained soil, because it dislikes being moved. Leaves can be cut from roughly six to fourteen weeks after sowing, and repeat sowings keep a supply coming.
text.how_to_plant: Sow dill seed where it will grow, since the taproot resents disturbance and seedlings are best left unmoved. Choose a spot in full sun with well-drained soil that is slightly acidic, around pH 5.5 to 6.5. Cover the seed with only 2 to 7 mm of soil and leave rows about 30 cm apart. Seedlings can appear within 7 to 25 days; thin them to roughly 20 cm apart. Make a new sowing every two to six weeks for a steady supply of leaves. In a pot, use general potting mix and a container at least 20 litres and 30 cm deep.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moist but never saturated, and take care not to overwater once seedlings are up. Dill does not ask for very rich soil; a balanced fertiliser worked in at planting suits it. A light straw mulch helps hold moisture. Crowding and heat push the plant to flower early, so thin seedlings and sow in batches. Removing flowers prolongs leafy growth. Established plants tolerate light frost. Give tall plants shelter from strong wind.
text.harvest: Leaves can be cut as soon as the plant is big enough to use. Snip or cut them at the stem, taking the oldest stems first; early morning or late evening suits. For seed, let the flower heads mature, then cut them about two to three weeks after the flowers open, once the seed has turned brown. Hang the heads in a paper bag in a dry, airy place so the seed drops out. Leaves can be dried, frozen or pickled. Seed kept for the kitchen goes in a sealed container. Handling dill and then standing in strong sun can irritate skin.
common_mistakes: Starting seedlings elsewhere and moving them, when the taproot makes dill hard to transplant.
Sowing once only, when plants decline soon after they flower and repeat sowings keep leaves coming.
Letting the soil become saturated or overwatering.
Leaving seedlings crowded, which promotes bolting.

problems.name: Rust
problems.signs: Rust-coloured spots form on the leaves and stalks.
prevention: Rotate where snapdragons are grown from year to year.
Remove infected plants.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: Humid conditions bring a pale whitish or greyish film over the upper leaf surface, and the leaves can curl.
prevention: Space plants well and prune so air can move through them.

problems.name: Grey mould
problems.signs: A grey mould grows on flowers, leaves, stems and buds, mostly in cool, wet weather.
prevention: Remove affected plant parts.
Water at soil level and avoid watering late in the day.
Keep air moving between plants.

problems.name: Damping off
problems.signs: A seedling comes up looking healthy, then suddenly wilts and dies.
prevention: Do not overwater or overfeed seedlings.
Thin crowded seedlings and keep air moving over them.
Water seedlings from below.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Small sap-sucking insects gather on new shoots and under the leaves and leave a sticky residue.
prevention: Wash them off with a strong jet of water.
Encourage natural predators such as lady beetles.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.signs: Tender leaves and shoots are chewed, mostly at night, and slimy trails are left behind.
prevention: Remove their hiding places.
Collect them by torchlight or set traps.

text.summary: Snapdragon is a flowering plant grown as an annual for its spikes of blooms in many colours. Plants range from about 15 to 90 centimetres tall. It likes full sun and moist, well-drained soil, copes with light frost, and does well in pots as well as garden beds.
text.how_to_plant: Start seed indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the plants go out. The seed is tiny: press it onto the surface of seed-starting mix, or cover it with no more than about 3 millimetres. Sources give a germination soil temperature anywhere from about 12 to 24 degrees C, and seedlings should appear in roughly 1 to 3 weeks. The seed needs light to germinate. Choose a spot with full sun, where part shade is also acceptable, and soil that drains well. Space plants 15 to 30 centimetres apart. In a pot, allow at least about 10 litres for each plant.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moderately moist and avoid watering over the leaves, because wet foliage invites disease. Snapdragons have low drought tolerance, so do not let beds or pots dry out. Plants cope with light frost. Remove spent flower spikes to keep new blooms coming. Tall cultivars may need stakes. Give plants room for airflow, and watch for aphids, slugs and snails, rust and grey mould.
text.harvest: Snapdragon is grown mainly for its flowers. The flower spikes are good for cutting and for vases. The flowers are also edible, though bitter, so they suit use as a garnish. Removing finished spikes encourages the plant to keep producing new ones, and the blooms attract butterflies and hummingbirds to the garden. The sources give no fixed length for the flowering period, so judge cutting by how your own plants are performing.
common_mistakes: Watering over the leaves, because wet foliage invites disease.
Letting the plants dry out, because their drought tolerance is low.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.signs: The plant sends up a flower stalk early instead of making stalks, and the stalks turn pithy.
prevention: Do not sow or set seedlings out in very cool weather
Choose bolt-resistant varieties, especially for cooler climates
Harden seedlings by cutting back on water, not by chilling them

problems.name: Black heart
problems.signs: The leaves in the centre of the plant turn black, and the tissue dies. It shows late in the season.
prevention: Keep watering steady, because water stress makes it worse
Work lime into soil that is low in calcium

problems.name: Leaf spot
problems.signs: Small, round tan spots appear on the leaves, speckled with tiny black dots, and similar elongated spots form on the leaf stalks and stems. It is worst in cool, wet weather.
prevention: Sow clean seed
Do not replant celery in the same ground for at least three years
Remove infected plant remains from the bed
Give plants room for air to move between them in cool weather
Water at soil level, for example with drip lines, rather than over the leaves

problems.name: Stringy or bitter stalks
problems.signs: The stalks turn stringy, fibrous and bitter.
prevention: Keep the soil evenly moist through the season
Mulch to hold moisture

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Green or black soft-bodied insects feed on the underside of leaves, and the leaves become crinkled and curled.
prevention: Knock them off with a strong stream of water

text.summary: Celery is grown for its crisp leaf stalks and is usually raised from seed in trays, then transplanted. It needs rich soil, plenty of water and generous feeding, in full sun or part shade. A cold spell while the plants are young can make them run to seed, so do not set seedlings out in cold weather.
text.how_to_plant: Sow the tiny seed very shallowly, or barely cover it, because it needs light to germinate; an overnight soak can help it come up evenly. Keep the mix steadily moist, as seedlings may take one to three weeks to emerge. Raise them for about seven to nine weeks, or buy seedlings, then plant out about 15 to 40 cm apart in rows roughly 30 to 90 cm apart. Choose rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost. In a pot, use a container of at least 20 litres. Do not set seedlings out in cold weather.
text.how_to_care: Celery has shallow roots and a big appetite, so keep the soil evenly moist and feed about every two weeks. Mulch to hold moisture and cut weeds, and hoe only shallowly so roots are not harmed. Some shade in hot spells helps. Dry spells make stalks fibrous, stringy and bitter. Protect young plants from frost and from cold snaps that can trigger flowering. To get paler, milder stalks, wrap them for a couple of weeks before picking. Wait at least three years before replanting celery in the same ground.
text.harvest: Cut outer stalks once they reach about 30 cm long, leaving the centre to keep growing, or cut the whole plant at ground level. Picking a few stalks at a time can stretch the harvest over two to three months. Harvest before seed stems form and stalks turn pithy. Store celery in a perforated bag in the refrigerator and eat it soon after picking.
common_mistakes: Letting the soil dry out, which leaves the stalks stringy and bitter.
Setting seedlings out in cold weather, which can make them bolt.
Burying the seed, when it needs light to germinate.
Growing celery in poor, unfed soil; it needs rich soil and regular feeding.
Replanting celery in the same bed within three years.

text.summary: Asparagus is a long-lived perennial vegetable grown for its young spears. It is usually planted as one-year-old crowns in a permanent bed with full sun and well-drained soil. Let new plants build up before cutting much, then harvest for a few weeks each year, longer as the bed matures.
text.how_to_plant: Most gardeners start with healthy one-year-old crowns; plants can also be raised from seed, which takes longer. Choose a permanent site in full sun (some guides accept part shade) with well-drained soil, and keep the bed towards the rear of the garden, since the tall ferns shade neighbouring plants. Dig a trench and enrich it with compost or animal manure before planting. Set the crowns in the bottom of a trench roughly 10 to 30 cm deep, 20 to 50 cm apart, in rows about 100 to 150 cm apart. If sowing seed instead, sow about 1 cm deep once the soil has warmed to about 16 C, or raise seedlings in trays first. Finish by mulching the bed.
text.how_to_care: Weed the bed by hand and avoid tilling, which can damage the roots; pulling is kinder than hoeing. Add a fresh layer of compost or other organic mulch each year. Water stress while the roots are establishing can cut yields for years afterwards, so give new plantings special attention. Keep foliage dry where you can, for example with drip irrigation. Feed with a balanced fertiliser, following the product label. After the harvest ends, let the ferns grow and turn brown so they send energy back to the crowns, then cut them down. The red berries on female plants are poisonous; check with a vet or poison centre if anyone eats them.
text.harvest: Cut spears when they are about as thick as a pencil and roughly 13 to 23 cm tall, cutting or snapping them at or just below the soil surface. Harvest daily during the picking season, and go lightly at first while the bed is young. Stop when the new spears turn thin, and let the rest grow into ferns so the crowns can recover. Depending on the age of the bed, the harvest lasts from about one to about ten weeks each year. Refrigerate spears promptly, or blanch and freeze any surplus.
common_mistakes: Cutting heavily while the bed is young, which weakens the crowns.
Carrying on cutting after the spears have thinned to pencil size.
Cutting the ferns down while they are still green, before they have sent energy back to the crowns.
Hoeing weeds among the spears instead of pulling them by hand, which can break spears off.
Letting weeds and grasses take over the bed.

problems.name: Early flowering and bitter leaves
problems.signs: Plants run to flower and the leaves turn bitter, most often when the soil dries out; shorter days also trigger flowering.
prevention: Keep the soil consistently moist through the season

problems.name: Frost injury
problems.signs: Frost kills the plant; it dies with the first hard freeze.
prevention: Wait until frost danger is well behind you before planting out
In cool climates start seedlings indoors and transplant them after frost danger

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Tiny sap-sucking insects cluster on new shoots and under leaves; leaves wilt or discolour and honeydew attracts ants.
prevention: Wash them off with a strong jet of water
Encourage predatory insects

problems.name: Bacterial leaf spot
problems.signs: Irregular brown spots, wet at first and dry and scab-like later, on leaves and other parts; leaves and flowers can drop early.
prevention: Water at soil level, not over the leaves
Clear away fallen leaves
Rotate crops

problems.name: Fungal infection of the leaves (Cercospora)
problems.signs: A fungal infection damages the leaves.
prevention: Remove damaged leaves to stop the spread

text.summary: Malabar spinach is a fast-growing, frost-tender climbing vine grown for soft, spinach-like leaves and young shoots. It likes full sun and warm nights and needs a trellis or other support. It is grown as an annual, picking the young leaves and tips as the vine grows.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where the vine will grow, or raise seedlings indoors for about 5 to 6 weeks first. The seed coat is tough, so scarifying the seed or soaking it overnight speeds germination, which can take 6 to 21 days. Sow about 0.6 to 2.5 cm deep and leave 15 to 30 cm between plants. Choose a sunny spot with fertile, moist, well-drained soil, and give it a trellis to climb. Stem cuttings can also be used to start new plants.
text.how_to_care: Give the vine a sturdy trellis or similar support to climb. Keep the soil evenly moist, because dry spells and shortening days push plants into flower, and the leaves then turn bitter. Protect plants from frost; in cool climates the first hard frost ends the crop. Nights colder than about 15.6 degrees C can harm plants. In a pot, allow at least 40 litres per plant. Water at soil level, clear away fallen leaves and rotate crops to limit bacterial leaf spot.
text.harvest: Pick tender young leaves and growing tips once the plant is established, leaving some foliage so the vine keeps growing. Guides give roughly 50 to 85 days from sowing to a first harvest. Removing seedling tips at the 5 to 6 leaf stage encourages branching, and young stems can be eaten as well. Harvest before flowering begins, since the leaves turn bitter afterwards. Cut or pinch the leaves. Fresh leaves keep briefly in the fridge.
common_mistakes: Planting out before frost danger has passed.
Letting the soil dry out, which brings on flowers and bitter leaves.
Growing the vine without a trellis or other support.
Leaving tough-coated seed untreated, which slows germination.

Beet, beetroot, beets, sugar beet, Beta vulgaris, chard, Swiss chard, Amaranthaceae and Chenopodiaceae are absent from the Utah Poison Control web list (s12, about 35 entries) and from both lists of the Utah brochure (s13; its toxic list names rhubarb leaves and oxalis, not beet). problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.signs: Tender leaves and shoots are eaten, mostly at night, and slime trails are left behind.
prevention: Remove the places where they hide
Collect them by torchlight
Set traps
Keep free-range poultry where that is possible

problems.name: Bacterial leaf spot
problems.signs: Irregularly shaped brown spots on all the above-ground parts of the plant.
prevention: Water at soil level, not over the leaves
Clear away fallen leaves
Rotate crops

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.signs: Yellow to grey-brown patches on the leaves, mostly on the undersides.
prevention: Water at soil level, not over the leaves
Remove and destroy affected leaves
Do not overcrowd plants

problems.name: Root rots
problems.signs: The root decays and rots, and plant stands can thin out.
prevention: Rotate crops
Improve soil drainage

problems.name: Split roots
problems.signs: Roots crack or split open once they are mature, after the soil swings between wet and dry.
prevention: Water deeply and evenly so soil moisture stays steady
Allow for recent or expected rain when watering

problems.name: Bolting
problems.signs: The plant flowers and sets seed early, often after a spell of extreme weather or when planted too early.
prevention: Avoid sowing in very hot weather

problems.name: Overcrowded seedlings
problems.signs: Leafy tops grow but the roots stay small or fail to form.
prevention: Thin seedlings early so the roots have room

problems.name: Crusted soil and poor emergence
problems.signs: Seedlings come up poorly or unevenly, often where dry soil has formed a hard crust on the surface.
prevention: Apply a light layer of mulch after sowing
Water now and then in dry spells
Scratch the soil beside the plants to break the crust

text.summary: Beetroot is grown as an annual for its swollen root, and its young leaves can be picked as greens too. It tolerates light frost and wants a sunny spot with loose, well-drained soil. Seed is sown in the garden and the seedlings are thinned, because each seed gives several plants.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed 1.3 to 2.5 cm deep, using the deeper end in sandy soil, once the soil has warmed to at least 7.2 C. Each seed is really a cluster, so several seedlings can come up from one. Shoots usually show in 5 to 15 days. Thin them early to about 10 cm apart, in rows 30 to 76 cm apart, because crowded plants give leaves but few roots. Soaking the seed in warm water for a day before sowing can speed germination. Sow again every 2 to 4 weeks for a steady supply. Pick well-drained soil rich in organic matter.
text.how_to_care: Water deeply and evenly, because swings between dry and wet soil split the roots. Spread a light mulch right after sowing so rain does not wash the bed and the surface does not crust, and weed early and shallowly. Water the soil, not the leaves, to cut the risk of leaf spot and mildew. Thin on time, as crowded seedlings make tops but few roots. Light frost is tolerated; heavy frost is not. Sowing too early or in very hot weather can push plants to bolt. Watch for slugs and snails.
text.harvest: Pull roots from about 2.5 cm across and up to 7.6 cm; a 3.8 cm root is a common cooking size, and larger ones turn fibrous. Trim the tops to about 2.5 cm above the root. Young leaves can be cut for greens, taking up to a third of the foliage without harming the root. First roots are ready about 49 to 85 days after sowing. Roots keep one to two weeks in a bag in the fridge, and can also be frozen or pickled.
common_mistakes: Leaving seedlings crowded, which gives leafy tops but small or no roots.
Sowing too deep or letting the soil crust over, which gives a poor stand.
Letting the soil swing between dry and wet, which splits roots.
Watering over the leaves, which favours leaf diseases.
Leaving roots in the ground too long, so they turn tough.

problems.name: Leaf miners

problems.name: Aphids

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.signs: Holes chewed in leaves and shoots, mostly at night, with slimy trails left behind.

Collect them by torchlight or use traps

problems.name: Flea beetles

problems.name: Bolting
problems.signs: The plant flowers and sets seed too early, often after a spell of extreme weather.

problems.name: Bacterial leaf spot

Clear away fallen leaves
Rotate crops

text.summary: Swiss chard, also called silverbeet, is a leafy crop grown as an annual. Its leaves are picked from the outside of the plant while the centre keeps producing. It takes light frost, wants full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and suits a large pot as well as a bed.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where the plants will grow, 0.6 to 2.5 cm deep, in soil that is workable and not waterlogged. Seedlings usually appear in 5 to 14 days. For an earlier crop, raise seedlings indoors for 5 to 6 weeks and then transplant them. Space plants 10 to 35 cm apart in rows 20 to 60 cm apart; one guide thins to about 30 cm. Choose a sunny spot with fertile, well-drained soil, and avoid ground that stays waterlogged. A pot works too, at least 40 litres for each plant.
text.how_to_care: Mulch around the plants to hold moisture and hold down weeds, and keep the soil rich in organic matter. Light frost is tolerated, but heavy frost is not. Bolting is more likely after extreme weather: avoid sowing in very hot weather, and water deeply and regularly when it is hot. Water at soil level rather than over the leaves, which helps against leaf spot and mildew. Watch pots and beds for slugs, aphids and leaf miners, and cover plants with row cover if leaf miners are a problem.
text.harvest: Start picking when leaves are about 7.6 cm long, or let them grow to 20 to 25 cm. Cut or break off the outer leaves near the base and leave the centre to keep growing, so the plant keeps cropping through the season until frost or bolting ends it. A tired plant can be cut back to about 5 cm above the crown. First picks come about 40 to 70 days after sowing. Unwashed leaves keep one to two weeks in the fridge.
common_mistakes: Sowing in very hot weather, which can trigger bolting.
Growing in waterlogged soil.
Watering over the leaves, which favours leaf diseases.
Cutting the central crown instead of picking the outer leaves.

text.summary: Mustard greens is a fast-growing leaf crop with spicy leaves that are picked young or cut whole. Grow it in sunny, well-drained soil and keep it growing steadily. Leaves are usually ready within roughly 25 to 80 days of sowing. Hot weather makes the plants run to seed and the leaves turn bitter.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed straight into the ground in full sun, though part shade is tolerated. Pick well-drained soil with a pH of roughly 6 to 7. Press the seed in about 0.5 to 1.3 cm deep and keep the soil moist while seedlings establish. They usually emerge in 5 to 14 days. Thin to about 10 cm apart, or leave closer plants for baby leaves, with rows about 30 to 90 cm apart. For an earlier crop, raise transplants indoors for about 3 to 8 weeks first. Sow a short row every two to three weeks for steady picking.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist, because swings between wet and dry leave the leaves tough and bitter. Mulch with straw or grass clippings to hold moisture and keep weeds down. Use a balanced fertiliser, and a nitrogen side dressing helps quick growth. The plants tolerate light frost, and fabric covers protect seedlings on colder nights. Knock aphids off with a hose, and use netting or floating row cover against caterpillars and flea beetles. Change the planting spot from year to year to help limit disease.
text.harvest: Pick leaves once they reach full size, but take them young and tender for the best texture. Skip wilted or yellowed leaves. Strip the older outer leaves first so the centre keeps growing, or cut the whole plant. If the growing point is undamaged, plants can be cut to about 5 cm above the soil and can regrow. Harvest before flower stalks form. Leaves keep best in a plastic bag in the fridge for up to about a week, and they can also be blanched and frozen, dried or pickled.
common_mistakes: Letting plants stand into hot weather, when they run to seed and the leaves turn bitter.
Letting the soil swing between dry and wet, which makes the leaves tough and slows their growth.
Picking wilted or yellowed leaves.
Damaging the growing point when cutting, so the plant cannot regrow.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Colonies build up on new shoots and under the leaves; leaves crinkle, curl, wilt or lose colour, and sticky honeydew can draw ants.
prevention: Knock them off with a strong spray of water from a hose

problems.name: Cabbage moth, white butterfly and cabbageworm caterpillars
problems.signs: Caterpillars chew holes in the leaves and hide in the heads; the eggs are laid under the leaves.
prevention: Cover plants with netting to keep butterflies and moths off
Use decoys to deter them
Pick the caterpillars off by hand

problems.name: Flea beetles
problems.signs: Small black beetles chew tiny holes in the seed leaves and young leaves, which can thin out or kill seedlings.
prevention: Use row covers to protect young plants early on

problems.name: Cutworms
problems.signs: Caterpillars that feed at night chew through the stems of young seedlings at ground level.
prevention: Collect them by hand at night
Put a cardboard collar round each seedling stem

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: White spots on the leaves that can spread to cover the whole leaf; yields can fall.
prevention: Water at soil level, not over the leaves
Allow good air flow between plants
Remove affected leaves

problems.name: Alternaria leaf spot
problems.signs: Spots with concentric rings and a black, sooty look.
prevention: Avoid overhead irrigation
Practise good garden sanitation
Rotate crops

problems.name: Buttoning (tiny early heads)
problems.signs: Small, premature flower heads form instead of one full head, after cold weather, water or nutrient stress, or long delays in the seed tray.
prevention: Choose transplants with 4 to 6 leaves rather than large ones
Do not leave transplants in their trays too long

problems.name: Hollow stems
problems.signs: The stem is hollow; plants can still be eaten if the stems are not rotten.
prevention: Do not overfeed with high-nitrogen fertiliser
Grow so that heads mature outside the hottest weather

text.summary: Broccoli is a brassica grown for one large central head of tight flower buds, followed by smaller side shoots once that head is cut. It does best in full sun or part sun on fertile, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. It can be grown from seed or from transplants.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed about 0.5 to 1.3 cm deep, either where the plants will grow or in trays for planting out later. Sow outdoors only once the soil is at least about 7 degrees C; seedlings usually show within 3 to 7 days. Young plants are ready to go out after roughly 4 to 8 weeks; do not leave them waiting in the trays too long, because oversized transplants tend to form tiny heads early. Space plants about 30 to 60 cm apart, with rows roughly 40 to 90 cm apart. Pick a sunny site with soil that drains well, holds plenty of organic matter and sits around pH 6.0 to 7.5.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist and give plentiful water. A layer of straw or similar mulch holds moisture and holds weeds back. Established plants take light frost, but spells below about 7 degrees C can stop heads forming properly. Check for aphids, caterpillars, flea beetles and powdery mildew; hose pests off, cover plants with netting or row covers, and water the soil rather than the leaves. Rotate so cabbage-family crops return to the same ground only every three to four years.
text.harvest: Cut the main head while the buds are still tight and compact, before any yellow flowers appear, taking about 10 to 15 cm of stem with it. Leave the plant growing, because smaller side shoots keep forming for later cuttings. A head whose buds loosen or turn yellow is past its best. Expect the first head roughly 55 to 100 days after transplanting. Keep heads unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the fridge for around 3 to 5 days, and rinse them just before use.
common_mistakes: Leaving transplants in their trays too long, which can lead to small early heads.
Letting seedlings sit for weeks in cold conditions, which can bring on small early flower heads.
Feeding heavily with nitrogen, which can hollow the stems.
Cutting the head late, after the buds have loosened or turned yellow.
Growing the crop through very hot weather, which gives loose, bitter heads.

problems.name: Cabbage worms and loopers

problems.name: Flea beetles

problems.name: Loose or bitter sprouts in hot weather

prevention: Time the crop so the sprouts form in cool weather
In warm climates, grow it over winter to avoid extreme heat
Keep the soil moist

problems.signs: The tissue inside the sprout, close to its centre, breaks down and turns dry, brown or black.

problems.name: Alternaria leaf spot
problems.signs: Spots with a black, sooty look form in concentric circles on the leaves.

problems.name: Clubroot
problems.signs: A severe disease that makes the roots swell, and the cause can persist in the ground for over a decade.

text.summary: Brussels sprouts are a cool-weather crop grown for the small cabbage-like buds that form along the stem. They suit a sunny bed with fertile, well-drained soil and steady moisture, they tolerate frost, and the buds are picked from the bottom of the stem upward over a long period.
text.how_to_plant: Raise seed indoors for about 4 to 8 weeks, or sow it where it will grow, covering it with 0.6 to 1.3 cm of soil; seed usually comes up within one to two weeks. Choose a sunny spot with fertile, well-drained soil and a pH of roughly 5.5 to 7. Set plants 30 to 90 cm apart, in rows 61 to 100 cm apart. Plan the planting so the sprouts form in cool weather, since heat leaves them loose and bitter. From transplanting, allow roughly 70 to 140 days before the first picking.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil steadily moist, because letting it dry out spoils the flavour; a drip line or soaker hose keeps the leaves dry. Grow them in soil rich in organic matter, work a balanced fertiliser in before planting, and add nitrogen side dressings as the plants grow. Spread straw or compost around them once hot weather arrives, to hold moisture and keep the soil cool. Cover plants with a floating row cover against caterpillars, and rotate with crops from other families, because clubroot lasts in soil for many years.
text.harvest: Start picking when the lowest sprouts are firm, compact and deep green, about 2.5 to 3.8 cm across. They mature from the bottom of the stem upward, so work your way up over a long period, twisting, breaking or cutting each one off. Pick before the leaves turn yellow. Sprouts taste better after a light frost. In the fridge they keep for some weeks, though the flavour is best when they are fresh; blanch and freeze any surplus.
common_mistakes: Letting the sprouts mature in hot weather, which leaves them loose and bitter.
Letting the soil dry out completely, which gives stronger, unpleasant flavours and, in one guide's words, makes the crop fail.
Letting seedlings become stunted in their trays before they are planted out.
Leaving the picking until the leaves have yellowed.

text.summary: Cabbage is grown for its firm head. It does best in a sunny spot with fertile, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and it needs generous, steady moisture. You can sow it in the ground, raise seedlings indoors, or buy young plants, and it will grow in a pot, one plant per container. Watch for caterpillars, aphids and slugs.
text.how_to_plant: Start seed indoors and set the seedlings out after about 4 to 7 weeks, sow straight into the ground, or buy young plants. Sow seed about 0.5 to 1.3 cm deep; it usually comes up within 3 to 42 days, and one guide puts the lowest soil temperature for germination at about 7 degrees C. Space plants 23 to 61 cm apart in rows 40 to 91 cm apart; closer spacing gives smaller heads. Choose a sunny site, or part shade, with fertile, well-drained soil rich in organic matter and a pH of about 6 to 7.5. Avoid oversized, woody-stemmed bought plants.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly and generously moist through the season, watering the ground rather than the leaves and doing it early in the day so foliage dries. Mulch around the plants to hold moisture and hold weeds back. A nitrogen-rich feed suits established plants, but do not feed late once heads are forming, because that can split them. Cover plants with netting against butterflies and moths, pick off caterpillars, rinse aphids off with water, and keep slug hiding places cleared. Move cabbage-family crops to fresh ground, waiting three to four years before they return.
text.harvest: Cut a head once it has reached its full size and feels firm and compact; a soft head is not ready. Cut the whole head with a short piece of stem. Guides differ on where to cut, from just under the head with a few outer leaves left on, to a few centimetres above the ground, to ground level. Expect roughly 60 to 90 days after planting out. If heads split after rain follows a dry spell, cut them promptly. Cabbage keeps in the fridge for about two weeks.
common_mistakes: Letting soil moisture swing between wet and dry while heads are forming, which splits them.
Feeding late in the season, which can split heads.
Setting out large, woody-stemmed bought plants, which can flower without forming a head.
Planting cabbage-family crops in the same ground year after year.

problems.name: Ricey heads

text.summary: Cauliflower is a brassica grown for its edible head, which is cut once it has filled out. It does best in full sun and fertile, free-draining ground with plenty of organic matter, with steady moisture through growth. Interrupted growth or a cold or hot spell can leave small button heads, so keep plants growing and watch for caterpillars and aphids.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where it will grow or raise seedlings in trays and set them out when they are about 4 to 7 weeks old. Seed needs soil of at least about 7 degrees C and goes in roughly 0.5 to 1.3 cm deep; seedlings usually show in about 4 to 14 days. Space plants 30 to 70 cm apart in rows 30 to 100 cm apart. Choose a sunny site with fertile soil that drains well and is rich in organic matter, around pH 6.0 to 7.5. Count on about 50 to 80 days from planting out to a first head.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly and generously moist, and shield young plants from a run of cold days below about 13 degrees C and from heat above about 27 degrees C, because stalled growth can lead to small button heads. Mulch around the plants to hold moisture and keep the soil cool. While the head is still small, tie the outer leaves loosely over it to keep it pale, unless the type covers itself. Wash aphids off with a hose, net plants against moths and butterflies, and put cardboard collars around young seedlings. Keep brassicas away from the same ground for about four years.
text.harvest: Cut the head while it is fully formed, compact and firm, before the florets begin to separate or turn coarse and grainy. Cut through the main stem and leave a few green leaves around the head to protect it. Expect a first head about 50 to 80 days after planting out. Put heads in a perforated bag in the fridge soon after cutting.
common_mistakes: Letting growth stall through drought, heat or cold, which can leave small button heads.
Leaving the head uncovered in strong sun, so it discolours.
Cutting late, after the florets have started to separate and quality drops.
Tying leaves over a wet head, which can encourage disease.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Small sap-sucking insects gather on new shoots and under the leaves; leaves wilt, discolour, crinkle or curl, and honeydew can draw ants.
prevention: Knock them off with a strong jet of water from a hose
Encourage predatory insects into the garden

problems.name: Cabbage moth and white butterfly caterpillars
problems.signs: Caterpillars chew large holes in the leaves and can skeletonise them; the eggs are laid under the leaves.
prevention: Cover plants with netting to keep butterflies and moths off
Use decoys to deter them

problems.name: Whitefly
problems.signs: Many small insects under the leaves that swarm up in clouds when disturbed; leaves yellow or wilt and growth slows.
prevention: Wash them off with a hose
Encourage beneficial insects that prey on them
Remove and destroy badly affected plants

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: White spots on the leaves that can spread to cover the whole leaf; yields can fall.
prevention: Water at soil level, not over the leaves
Allow good air flow between plants
Remove affected leaves

problems.name: Tough or bitter leaves

prevention: Pick more often when it is warm, or choose younger leaves
Keep soil moisture even

text.summary: Kale is a leafy brassica grown for its tender leaves, which are picked a few at a time. It does best in a sunny spot with fertile, well-drained soil that is rich in organic matter, and it can be grown in pots as well as in the ground. Watch for aphids, whitefly and caterpillars.
text.how_to_plant: Kale can be sown where it will grow or raised in trays and planted out later. Sow when the soil is at least about 7 degrees C, putting seed roughly 0.6 to 2 cm deep. Seedlings usually appear within about 4 to 14 days. Trays need around 3 to 6 weeks before the young plants are ready to go out. Allow 20 to 60 cm between plants and 45 to 100 cm between rows. Pick a sunny or part-shaded site with fertile soil that drains well and is rich in organic matter, around pH 5.5 to 7.5. It also grows in pots.
text.how_to_care: Spread a layer of mulch, such as straw, about 5 to 8 cm deep around the plants to keep moisture in and hold weeds back. Give it plenty of water, and light shade can help in hot spells. Mature plants are very hardy. Check regularly for aphids, whitefly, caterpillars and powdery mildew; hose pests off, cover plants with netting, water at the base rather than over the leaves, and remove affected leaves. Pick often in warm weather, because older leaves turn tough and bitter. Keep cabbage-family crops from returning to the same ground for three to four years.
text.harvest: Begin picking once the plant has several leaves that have reached full size. Take the older outer leaves first and leave the growing centre alone, so new leaves keep forming; avoid taking more than about a third of the plant at once. A first picking usually comes roughly 40 to 80 days after sowing, and harvesting can carry on through the season. Keep unwashed leaves in a bag in the fridge for around 3 to 5 days.
common_mistakes: Letting leaves grow old before picking them, so they turn tough and bitter in warm weather.
Taking more than about a third of the plant in one picking.
Cutting out the growing centre when harvesting.
Letting soil moisture swing between wet and dry, which toughens the leaves.

text.summary: Kohlrabi is a cool-weather vegetable grown for its swollen, round stem, which is eaten raw or cooked; the young leaves are edible too. It suits a sunny bed with fertile, well-drained soil, grows from seed sown in place or started indoors, and is picked while still small and tender.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed 0.5 to 1.3 cm deep where it will grow, or start it indoors and move seedlings out after about 5 to 6 weeks. Seed usually comes up in 3 to 10 days, and soil of around 10 degrees C or more suits sowing. Thin or space plants 5 to 30 cm apart, in rows 30 to 61 cm apart. Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil rich in organic matter. One seed company advises at least 40 litres of pot space for a plant.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil steadily moist: uneven watering leaves the stems tough, woody or cracked, and one guide calls for plentiful water. Kohlrabi is described as a heavy feeder, so a balanced fertiliser worked in before planting suits it. Mulch with straw once the weather warms, to cool the soil and hold weeds back. Where you can, keep it away from other cabbage-family crops, which share its pests, and watch for maggot damage at the roots.
text.harvest: Pick the swollen stem while it is young and tender, about 5 to 7.5 cm across according to one guide, though others give smaller limits. Larger, older stems turn tough and woody. Pull or cut the stem at ground level, or just above it. The young leaves can be cooked like other greens. Kept in the fridge, kohlrabi lasts about two weeks.
common_mistakes: Letting soil moisture swing between dry and wet, which makes the stems tough and woody.
Leaving stems to grow large and old before picking, when they turn tough and woody.
Growing it through hot weather, which can make the stem woody and tough.

text.summary: Turnip is a root crop grown for its roots and its leafy tops. Sow seed straight into sunny, well-drained soil and thin the seedlings. Roots are usually ready about 35 to 90 days after sowing. Keep the plants growing steadily and pull the roots while they are still small and tender.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed straight into the ground where the plants will grow. Pick a sunny spot with soil that drains well; loam suits it, at a pH of roughly 6 to 7. Press seed in about 0.5 to 2 cm deep, with rows usually 20 to 61 cm apart. Seedlings come up in about 5 to 14 days. Thin the young plants so each has room: most guides land near 15 cm, though advice runs from about 5 to 20 cm. Sow a little more seed every two to four weeks if you want a steady supply.
text.how_to_care: Keep soil moisture even, because swings between wet and dry split the roots, and turnips are not drought tolerant. Use a balanced general fertiliser, and avoid too much nitrogen, which can reduce root formation. Mulch with straw to hold moisture. Netting or floating row cover keeps moths, butterflies and flea beetles off. Grow turnips where other cabbage-family crops have not grown for the last three to four years; rotating cabbage-family crops helps keep clubroot and other diseases down.
text.harvest: Pull the roots when they are about 5 to 7.6 cm across; bigger ones turn tough, pithy and stringy. Roots do not improve once past full size, so lift them promptly. The tops can be picked too, from a young stage or when they are about 10 to 15 cm tall. Roots keep for roughly two weeks in the fridge, and they can be frozen after blanching.
common_mistakes: Leaving roots in the ground past full size, so they turn tough, pithy and woody.
Letting the soil swing between dry and wet, which splits the roots.
Leaving seedlings crowded, so the roots stay small.
Growing roots through hot weather, which brings a strong flavour and pithy roots.

text.summary: Pot marigold, or calendula, is an annual grown for bright yellow and orange daisy-like flowers whose petals can be eaten. It tolerates a little shade, copes with light frost and is easy to raise from seed sown where it will grow. It suits beds and pots and flowers for a long season.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a spot in full sun, or part shade, with well-drained soil. Sow seed where it will grow once the soil has warmed to about 16 degrees C, or raise it in trays and plant the seedlings out. The seed needs darkness to germinate, so cover it with 5 to 15 millimetres of soil. Seedlings usually appear within 5 to 15 days. Thin or space plants anywhere from 15 to 60 centimetres apart, depending on the guide. For a pot, allow at least 10 litres for each plant.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy: overwatering can lead to root rot. Water the soil rather than the leaves. Plants need little extra feeding, so go easy on fertiliser. Remove faded flowers regularly to keep new blooms coming; plants left to set seed will self-sow. Watch for aphids, whiteflies and powdery mildew, and give plants room so air can move between them.
text.harvest: Pick whole flower heads once they are fully open, then pull off the petals for salads, desserts or as a colour garnish. Flowers keep appearing over a long season, and picking them regularly encourages more. Flower heads can be dried in an airy place out of the sun and stored in a sealed container somewhere cool and dark. Use the petals in the kitchen, and check with a vet or poison centre if unsure.
common_mistakes: Leaving the seed uncovered: it needs darkness to germinate, so cover it well.
Overwatering, which can lead to root rot.
Watering over the leaves.
Leaving faded flowers on the plant, which slows further blooming.

text.summary: Chilli is a warm-season fruiting plant grown as an annual for its hot pods. It needs full sun, warm soil and frost-free weather, and it grows well in a large pot. Cool nights or very hot days can make flowers drop. Pods are usually picked red-ripe, and gloves protect your skin.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a spot with at least six hours of direct sun and well-drained soil at a pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Sow seed 0.5 cm deep in trays and keep the mix warm, around 20 to 35 degrees Celsius; seed takes one to three weeks to sprout. Seedlings need roughly six to ten weeks before planting out. Harden them off over one to two weeks. Plant out only when frost danger has passed and soil and nights have warmed. Space plants 30 to 60 cm apart in rows 60 to 100 cm apart, or give each pot at least 20 litres. Avoid soil that held tomatoes, eggplant or potatoes recently.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, because uneven watering brings blossom end rot and dry spells cause flower drop. Mulch to hold moisture, but wait until the soil has warmed. Feed with a starter feed at planting, then follow the product label; chillies need a moderate amount. Support each plant with a stake, or a cage, as stems can snap. Give some shade in the late afternoon when days are hot. Water at soil level to keep leaves dry and lower the risk of mildew. Leave the leaves on in the hottest weather, since they shade the fruit.
text.harvest: Expect the first pods roughly 60 to 85 days after planting out, depending on the variety. Most hot chillies are picked red-ripe, when they are hottest, though green pods can be picked earlier. Cut pods with a knife or clippers, because most are firmly attached. Pick regularly so the plant keeps cropping. Wear gloves when picking or cleaning seeds, and keep hands away from your eyes.
common_mistakes: Planting out before frost danger has passed, since the plants cannot tolerate frost.
Planting into soil that is still cold, which leaves plants stalled.
Watering unevenly, which causes blossom end rot, or letting the soil dry out, which causes flower drop.
Stripping leaves in the hottest weather, which exposes fruit to sunscald.
Handling hot pods with bare hands.

text.summary: Sweet pepper, also called capsicum or bell pepper, is a warm-season fruiting plant grown as an annual. It wants full sun, warm soil and no frost, and it does well in a large pot. Fruit can be picked green or left to colour, and coloured fruit is sweeter.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil at about pH 6.0 to 6.8. Sow seed 0.5 cm deep in trays and keep the mix warm; seed sprouts in one to three weeks. Seedlings need roughly six to ten weeks before they go outside. Plant them out only once frost danger has passed and the nights are warm. Space plants 30 to 60 cm apart in rows about 36 to 107 cm apart, or give each pot at least 40 litres. Avoid soil that grew tomatoes, eggplant, potatoes or peppers within the last one to three years.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist, never soggy, and take special care while fruit is setting and swelling. Mulch to hold water, but wait until the soil has warmed. Give a starter feed at planting, then follow the product label. Support each plant with a cage, trellis or stake, because brittle stems break under a heavy crop. Late-afternoon shade helps in hot spells, and leaves left on the plant shade the fruit. Water at soil level and leave room for airflow to lower the risk of mildew.
text.harvest: Expect the first fruit roughly 60 to 85 days after planting out, depending on the variety. Pick when the fruit has reached full size and feels firm. Green fruit is fine to eat, but fruit left on the plant to turn red, yellow or orange is sweeter. Cut the fruit off instead of pulling, because the branches are brittle. Pick regularly so the plant keeps producing. Fresh fruit keeps about two to three weeks in a cool, moist fridge.
common_mistakes: Planting out before frost danger has passed, since the plants cannot tolerate frost.
Planting into soil that is still cold, which leaves plants stalled.
Watering unevenly or letting the soil dry out, which brings blossom end rot and flower drop.
Pulling fruit off instead of cutting it, which breaks brittle branches.
Stripping leaves in the hottest weather, which exposes fruit to sunscald.
