problems.name: Papaya ringspot virus
problems.signs: Leaves show yellow mottling and clearing of the veins, then become distorted and smaller. Dark green streaks can appear on the leaf stalks and trunk, and the fruit has dark rings or C-shaped marks.
prevention: Remove and destroy any plant showing the symptoms
Avoid saving seed from small, pear-shaped fruit, which are more susceptible
Replant papaya every 18 to 24 months

problems.name: Root rot
problems.signs: The plant loses vigour and can die quickly; stems and fruit can rot as well.
prevention: Set new plants where drainage is better, or use raised beds
Start new plants in clean potting mix that has not been used before
Water with care

problems.name: Papaya fruit fly
problems.signs: Infested fruit shows yellow areas and can drop early.
prevention: Cover small fruit with a paper bag or fine cloth until harvest

problems.name: Nematodes
problems.signs: Plants lose vigour, and because roots are lost they topple more easily.
prevention: Plant in clean soil, away from areas with known nematode problems

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: White growth on the leaf surface, small light yellow spots underneath, then pale yellow spots on top, and finally dead patches that fall out and leave holes.
prevention: Remove infested leaves and keep them away from the plants

problems.name: Whitefly
problems.signs: Leaves drop, fruit production falls, and sooty mould can grow on leaves and fruit.
prevention: Remove infested leaves

problems.name: Two-spotted mite
problems.signs: The leaf surface browns, then the upper surface, and the leaf is eventually skeletonised; leaves may fall early.

problems.name: Anthracnose
problems.signs: Small water-soaked spots on ripening fruit enlarge, turn brown or black and sink into the skin.

problems.name: Leaf tip burn from salty soil or water
problems.signs: Leaf tips and edges brown.

text.summary: Papaya is a tropical fruit plant with a single trunk topped by lobed leaves. It wants full sun, a wind-sheltered position and well-drained soil, and freezing weather damages or kills it. Fruit comes only from female and bisexual plants, so start more than one seedling. It can be grown in a deep, wide pot.
text.how_to_plant: Papaya is grown from seed or from a young potted plant. For seed, take it from a ripe fruit, rub off the jelly-like coating, rinse the seeds and dry them out of direct sun. Sow a few seeds in each pot of clean, unused mix, keep the pots warm and sunny, then cut off all but the strongest seedling. Seedlings can turn out male, female or bisexual, so raise two or three. Choose a sunny, wind-sheltered, well-drained spot, with roughly 2.1 to 3.7 metres between plants. For a container, use a pot at least 60 cm deep.
text.how_to_care: Full sun and shelter from strong wind matter most, because plants carrying a lot of fruit can topple in gusts. Papaya will not tolerate wet or waterlogged soil, which causes root rot, so keep the mix or soil well drained and water the soil rather than wetting the fruit and leaves. Mulch the root area with bark or wood chips about 5 to 15 cm deep, but keep it 20 to 30 cm back from the trunk. Do not prune routinely; if the top is damaged, keep one or two vigorous side shoots. Remove dead leaves and pull out plants showing ringspot virus markings.
text.harvest: Fruit can be picked green and cooked as a vegetable, or left to ripen. For eating ripe, pick once some yellow shows on the peel; more colour on the tree gives sweeter fruit, but fruit left hanging can be damaged by fruit flies and birds. Finish ripening picked fruit indoors at room temperature, then keep ripe fruit in the fridge. Paper bags placed over small fruit help keep fruit flies out.
common_mistakes: Letting the soil stay wet or waterlogged, which leads to root rot.
Planting in a windy spot, where plants heavy with fruit can topple.
Keeping a plant that shows ringspot virus signs instead of removing it.
Piling mulch against the trunk.
Letting the plant dry out, which can make it drop flowers, leaves and young fruit.

problems.signs: Small sap-sucking insects cluster on new shoots and the undersides of leaves; leaves may wilt or lose colour, and sticky honeydew can attract ants.

text.summary: Madagascar periwinkle, often sold as vinca, is a flowering plant with glossy leaves and pinwheel blooms in pink, red, white or lavender. It is mostly grown as an annual in beds, borders, pots and hanging baskets, tolerates heat and dry spells once established, and needs well-drained soil. All parts are poisonous.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a spot in full sun or light shade with soil that drains freely, because soggy roots invite rot. Seed needs darkness to sprout, so cover it with about 2 to 4 millimetres of mix and keep the tray out of the light until seedlings show, which usually takes one to three weeks. Seed can be started indoors in a flat. Set plants roughly 20 to 50 centimetres apart. In a pot, allow at least 10 litres for each plant and use a free-draining mix.
text.how_to_care: Overwatering is a main danger because it brings on root rot, so let the soil drain and water the soil rather than the leaves. Established plants cope well with dry spells and heat. Give plants room so air moves between them, since crowding leads to leaf blight. Modern hybrids need no pinching or deadheading. Disease-resistant series are available. Check under the leaves for aphids and whiteflies.
text.harvest: This plant is grown for show, not for the kitchen. Every part contains vinca alkaloids, and eating a large amount can cause vomiting, low blood pressure and more serious effects, so keep it away from children and pets. The long flowering season is the main reward. If a person or a pet eats some, check with a vet or poison centre.
common_mistakes: Overwatering, which causes root rot.
Crowding plants, which brings on leaf blight.
Watering over the leaves instead of at the soil.
Leaving seed uncovered, when it needs darkness to sprout.

text.summary: Endive and escarole are two leaf types of one cool-season salad green. Endive has finely cut, curled leaves; escarole has wide, flat ones. Both grow upright, tolerate light frost and suit beds and containers. The pale heart is often blanched for a couple of weeks to soften its bitterness.
text.how_to_plant: Pick a sunny spot with well-drained, loamy soil. Sow seed very shallowly, about 5 to 7 mm deep, either where it will grow or in trays to plant out after about 6 weeks. Seed usually comes up in 4 to 7 days, best in soil around 15 to 20 degrees C. Thin or space plants to about 30 cm, with rows about 45 to 60 cm apart.
text.how_to_care: These are cool-season crops, so grow them through the cooler part of the year. They take a light frost once established. Keep the soil moist and give an even supply of water. About two to three weeks before cutting, blanch the heart: when the leaves are dry, tie the outer ones together over the centre, or cover each plant with a pot. Tying damp leaves can rot the inner ones. Check leaf undersides for whitefly and watch for slugs and snails at night.
text.harvest: Allow about 60 to 80 days from sowing. Cut the whole head at ground level; blanched heads are cut once their hearts have developed. Cut before plants grow old, since slow growth and late cutting make the leaves bitter. For short-term storage, drain the heads, bag them and keep them in the fridge, and discard the tough outer leaves.
common_mistakes: Leaving the spreading plants unblanched, which leaves them bitter.
Tying the outer leaves while they are damp, which can rot the inner leaves.
Cutting late or letting growth stall, which makes the leaves bitter.
Sowing in very hot weather, which can lead to bolting.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: White fungal patches that start on older leaves.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties
Water in the morning or at soil level so leaves dry
Rotate crops

problems.name: Cucumber beetles
problems.signs: Striped or spotted adult beetles feed on leaves and vines and weaken the plant; the pest matters most on seedlings and young plants.
prevention: Pick beetles off by hand
Cover young plants with row covers and remove the covers when flowers open so bees can reach them
Keep weeds down
Use a trap crop

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Green or black soft-bodied insects feed on the undersides of leaves; they can spread virus, which shows as light green, mottled, curled or stunted leaves.
prevention: Knock them off with a strong stream of water
Cover young plants with row covers
Remove badly infected plants

problems.name: Wilt diseases
problems.signs: Leaves wilt on one or more vines while others stay healthy.
prevention: Keep cucurbits out of the same ground for several years
Clear dead foliage at the end of the season
Avoid working among wet plants

problems.name: Blossom-end rot
problems.signs: Fruit starts to decay at its blossom end.
prevention: Keep soil evenly moist but not saturated
Avoid over-fertilising
Black plastic mulch helps in dry weather

problems.name: Seed rot in cold soil
problems.signs: Seed sown too early in cold soil rots or the seedlings fall to disease.
prevention: Sow only after the soil is warm and frost danger has passed

text.summary: Watermelon wants full sun, fertile, well-drained soil and plenty of room. Bees must carry pollen between separate male and female flowers before fruit forms. Sow seed once the soil is warm, or raise seedlings indoors for a few weeks, and expect the first ripe fruit about three months after transplanting.
text.how_to_plant: Wait until frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed to at least 18.3 C (65 F), because seed sown in cold soil can rot. Pick a site with six or more hours of direct sun and fertile, well-drained soil, ideally a sandy loam. Sow seed about 2 to 5 cm deep, or raise seedlings indoors for three to six weeks and then set them out. Allow each plant roughly 60 to 180 cm along the row and keep rows about 1.2 to 3 m apart. Seed usually sprouts within 4 to 14 days when the soil is warm.
text.how_to_care: Water so that the leaves dry quickly, and avoid sprinkling from above, which encourages disease. Mulch to hold moisture and to keep ripening fruit off bare soil; black plastic warms cool soil early on. Let the vines sprawl, or train them up a sturdy trellis and support heavy fruit in slings. Bees must reach the flowers, so take row covers off once plants bloom, and plant a seeded variety beside any seedless type.
text.harvest: Expect the first ripe fruit about 85 to 90 days after transplanting, though varieties differ. Judge ripeness from several signs together: the curly tendril nearest the fruit turns brown and dry, the skin looks dull rather than glossy, and the spot where the fruit rested changes from white to yellow or cream. Cut the fruit from the vine and leave a short piece of stem. Whole fruit keeps roughly one to two weeks at room temperature.
common_mistakes: Planting out or sowing before frost danger has passed and the soil is warm; cold soil can rot seed.
Watering from above, which encourages leaf diseases.
Over-feeding with nitrogen, which grows vines instead of fruit.
Growing seedless types without a seeded variety nearby to supply pollen.
Picking by tendril colour alone; one source says the tendril can brown a week or more before the fruit is ripe.

problems.name: Citrus canker
problems.signs: Pinpoint spots on leaves and fruit, then raised brown spots of round or uneven shape, each with a yellow halo, on leaves, stems and fruit. Heavy infection can strip the leaves and weaken the tree.
prevention: Give the tree full sun and good air movement
Avoid wetting the foliage when watering, which may help reduce the severity

problems.name: Citrus greening (yellow shoot disease)
problems.signs: Parts of the tree show yellow blotching, yellow veins and smaller leaves, much like nutrient shortage, along with hard corky main veins and dieback of stems and limbs. The tree can decline and die.
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free trees
Remove infected trees, which can infect nearby citrus

problems.name: Foot rot
problems.signs: Bark peels at the crown roots and the base of the trunk, with gum oozing from the wound, yellowing leaves, dieback and tree decline.
prevention: Avoid trunk damage
Avoid wetting the trunk when watering
Keep mulch back from the trunk

problems.name: Root rot and collar rot
problems.signs: Branches lose leaves and die back; the tree can quickly wilt, shed leaves and die. Fruit bearing declines.
prevention: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun
Avoid overwatering
Keep mulch back from the trunk

problems.name: Citrus leaf miner
problems.signs: Meandering mines and squiggly lines appear on the leaves, which become distorted. Young newly planted trees can be weakened.

problems.name: Citrus red mite
problems.signs: Brown, dead patches on the upper leaf surface, and leaf drop when the infestation is severe.

problems.name: Aphids and soft scale insects
problems.signs: Sap-sucking insects leave a sticky honeydew on the tree, and ants may be seen running up and down it.

problems.name: Sooty mould
problems.signs: A black powdery film appears over leaves and stems, growing on honeydew.

problems.name: Melanose
problems.signs: Small brown sunken spots appear on young leaves and later turn raised and sandpaper-rough. On fruit, raised irregular brown spots appear with pale halos.

problems.name: Postbloom fruit drop
problems.signs: Water-soaked lesions on the petals, which turn orange and dry out; the young fruit drops, leaving the button of the flower attached.
prevention: Plant in full sun in a spot with good air movement
Do not water the foliage during bloom

problems.name: Stylar-end breakdown
problems.signs: Tissue at the end of the fruit breaks down and the whole fruit can decay, mostly in large mature fruit.
prevention: Handle fruit gently when harvesting
Harvest in the afternoon

problems.name: Trunk injury from mowers and trimmers
problems.signs: Damage to the trunk where mowing or trimming equipment has struck it weakens the tree and in severe cases leads to dieback or death.
prevention: Keep a grass-free area 60 to 150 cm or more around the trunk
Never hit the trunk with mowing equipment or use a trimmer near it

text.summary: Tahiti lime, also called Persian lime, is a small evergreen citrus tree with white, fragrant flowers and sour green fruit. It wants full sun, soil that drains well and shelter from all but light frost. It can be grown in a container with drainage holes that is moved under cover when cold weather is expected.
text.how_to_plant: Buy a healthy nursery tree certified free of disease, and avoid a large tree squeezed into a small pot, because its roots may be bound. Choose a full-sun site with soil that drains well, roughly 4 to 6 metres from buildings and other trees. Where water tends to pool, plant on a raised mound of free-draining soil. Dig a wide hole, several times the width of the container, and set the tree so the soil in the pot sits level with or just above the ground. Water straight away. For a pot, use a container with good drainage holes in full sun, and consider a dwarf form.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moderately moist but never waterlogged; wet ground and overwatering, even from lawn sprinklers on a timer, bring root and collar rot. Avoid letting the tree dry out from flowering through fruit development. Limes are hungry trees that need plenty of nutrients. Mulch with a layer of bark about 5 to 15 cm deep, kept 20 to 30 cm from the trunk. Keep mowers and trimmers away from the trunk. Shelter the tree from frost, and wheel a potted tree inside or to a protected spot when cold weather is expected.
text.harvest: Limes are picked green. One guide picks at about 4.5 cm across when dark to medium-dark green, because smaller fruit may have little juice; another prefers a paler, smooth fruit that gives a little under a gentle squeeze. Ripe fruit does turn yellow, but green limes are what is commonly sold and used. Handle fruit gently and pick in the afternoon to avoid damage to the rind. Fresh limes keep about 10 days in a bag in the fridge. Some people can get a skin rash from handling the plant.
common_mistakes: Planting in poorly drained soil or overwatering, which invites root and collar rot.
Piling mulch against the trunk.
Letting mowers or trimmers strike the trunk.
Leaving the tree exposed to hard frost.
Buying a tree that is not certified disease-free.

problems.name: Aphids and scale insects
problems.signs: Leaves turn sticky with a clear, sugary coating (honeydew), black sooty mould may grow on it, and ants may gather.
prevention: Knock aphids off with a jet of plain water
Check the tree often so scale insects are caught while numbers are small

problems.name: Spider mites

problems.name: Cold damage
problems.signs: Cold-damaged wood may show nothing until growth restarts. In severe winters an outdoor tree can be killed back to the graft, and the rootstock then regrows with seedy, sour fruit that cannot be eaten.

problems.name: Fruit drop and poor fruit set from drought
problems.signs: Fruit fails to set if the tree runs short of water while it flowers, and fruit drops and yields fall if water runs short at other times.

text.summary: Lemon is an evergreen citrus tree that grows large in the ground but can also be grown in a large pot. It needs full sun, soil that drains well and shelter from cold, so in cool climates keep it in a container that can come indoors. One tree is enough for fruit. Contact with the plant can irritate skin.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot, sheltered from wind, where the soil drains well. Lemons resent having their roots disturbed, so put a young tree in its permanent place rather than moving it later. When planting into a container, set the tree no deeper than it grew in its nursery pot. Where the climate is cool, use a container that is large enough for the full-grown tree, filled with a commercial potting mix, so that you can move it indoors when it turns cold. Citrus trees are often grafted onto a seedling rootstock.
text.how_to_care: Drainage matters: citrus cannot tolerate wet roots, and standing water can kill the tree. Take care in dry spells, especially while it flowers, because drought then stops fruit setting. Feed with a nitrogen-rich fertiliser. Prune lightly, only to remove dead, diseased, damaged or rubbing limbs and keep the shape; never cut below the graft. Cold can kill a tree back to the graft, so protect it and bring potted trees indoors to a well-lit spot, hand-pollinating the flowers with a small brush while it is inside. Some branches carry thorns, and contact with the plant can irritate skin; check with a vet or poison centre if a pet or child chews it.
text.harvest: Because lemons are grown for their sharp, acid flavour, pick them once the fruit has reached a usable size and the juice is good enough. Rind colour is not the test, and lemons can be picked while still green. Flowers, young fruit and ripe fruit often hang on the tree together. Most citrus will keep in the refrigerator for several weeks.
common_mistakes: Setting a potted tree deeper than it grew in its nursery pot.
Letting water stand around the roots, which citrus cannot tolerate.
Pruning below the graft union when removing cold-damaged wood.
Moving a lemon to a new spot after it has grown, since it dislikes root disturbance.

text.summary: Coleus is a foliage plant grown for its brightly coloured, patterned leaves, on upright plants roughly 15 to 90 centimetres tall. It does best in part shade and in moist, well-drained soil, and frost kills it. It suits pots and beds, and is easy to multiply from cuttings.
text.how_to_plant: Coleus can be started from stem cuttings or from seed. Cuttings root easily, though cultivars sold as patented should not be multiplied this way, and sterile cutting-grown types cannot be raised from seed. Seed needs light to germinate and sprouts in roughly 1 to 2 weeks when kept warm, around 18 to 24 degrees C. Seedlings need about 6 to 8 weeks indoors before they are ready to move out. Set plants about 30 to 50 centimetres apart in part shade, in well-drained soil rich in organic matter. In a pot, allow at least 20 litres for each plant.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil lightly moist but never soggy, since poor drainage and overwatering damage coleus. Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves. Avoid feeds made for flowering plants, which can leave coleus leggy. Mulch helps hold soil moisture. Pinch back growing tips to keep plants branching and compact, and pinch off the flower spikes. Frost kills coleus, so before cold weather take cuttings or lift plants to overwinter indoors.
text.harvest: Coleus is grown for its colourful leaves, so there is no harvest to plan around. The small flower spikes are not showy; removing them helps keep the plant full and appears to slow decline. The flowers draw pollinating insects. Prized plants can be multiplied from cuttings, which root in water or moist potting mix. The leaves may cause skin irritation in some people; check with a vet or poison centre if unsure.
common_mistakes: Leaving the soil waterlogged or poorly drained, which damages coleus.
Planting cultivars that are not sun-tolerant in full sun, where the leaves bleach and fade.
Using a fertiliser made for flowering plants, which leaves coleus leggy and pushes it to bloom.

text.summary: Coriander, also called cilantro, is an annual herb grown for its fresh leaves and its seeds. It likes sun to part shade, well-drained soil and cool conditions, and it runs to seed quickly in heat. It suits beds and pots and is best sown where it will grow.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where the plants will grow, because the taproot dislikes disturbance. Choose a spot with sun to part shade and well-drained soil. Cover seed with about 6 to 13 mm of soil. If you can, keep it near 18 to 21 C; it usually sprouts in one to three weeks. Space plants 5 to 25 cm apart, closer for leaves and wider for seed, in rows 20 to 38 cm apart. In a pot, allow at least 10 litres and a depth of 20 cm.
text.how_to_care: Keep seedlings from drying out; soggy, humid conditions do plants no good. Spread mulch around seedlings once they emerge to hold the soil cool and hold back weeds. Heat is the main threat: plants bolt quickly once temperatures pass about 27 C. Sow again every two to four weeks, or weekly, for a steady supply, give some shade in hot spells, and pinch off flower stems to prolong leaf picking.
text.harvest: Start picking leaves when plants stand about 10 to 15 cm tall, which can be as soon as 30 days after sowing but may take up to 70. Take outer leaves, or snip stems a few centimetres above the soil so they regrow; whole plants can also be cut. For coriander seed, let the flower heads turn brown, then cut the plant and finish drying it in a paper bag. Fresh leaves keep about a week in the fridge; freezing keeps them much longer. Dried seed lasts several years in a sealed container.
common_mistakes: Letting plants dry out, which stresses them into bolting.
Disturbing the roots when transplanting; the taproot dislikes it.
Overwatering in damp, humid conditions.

text.summary: Cosmos (garden cosmos) is a fast-growing tender annual with upright stems and daisy-like flowers in pink, white, purple and other shades. It likes full sun and well-drained soil, copes with dry spells, and is sown straight where it will flower. It also suits large pots and draws bees and butterflies.
text.how_to_plant: Pick a spot with full sun, at least 6 hours a day, and soil that drains well. Sow seed straight where the plants will flower, once the soil has warmed to about 18 degrees C or more. Barely cover the seed, about 3 to 6 millimetres deep, because deep seed germinates poorly. Seedlings usually appear in 3 to 21 days, and warm soil of 21 to 26 degrees C suits germination best. Leave 20 to 45 centimetres between plants, or thin to about 25 centimetres. In a pot, allow at least 20 litres for each plant.
text.how_to_care: Established plants cope with dry spells, so avoid overwatering, which can reduce flowering. Heavy feeding also tends to cut down on flowers, so hold back on fertiliser. Remove faded flowers regularly to keep new blooms coming. Cosmos attracts bees and butterflies. Watch for aphids, thrips and powdery mildew; water the soil rather than the leaves and give plants room for air to move.
text.harvest: Cosmos is grown for its flowers rather than as a harvest crop, so there is no harvest window to plan around. Stems can be cut for indoor vases, since it is described as a good cut flower. Removing faded blooms regularly encourages more flowers over a long blooming season. The plants reseed readily, so leaving a few seed heads at the end of the season gives you new seedlings.
common_mistakes: Sowing the seed too deep, which hinders germination.
Overfertilising, which can mean fewer flowers.
Overwatering, which can also mean fewer flowers.

Not counted: s2's and s7's full-sun sentences (word for word on their tomato pages, template) and s3's sun line (names no crop, rules 66 and 77).

65 F = 18.3 C. s1 says to plant when soil is at least 60 to 65 F (a range counts at the safer end, 65 F, rule 14); s2 says plant when soils are 65 F or after all frost danger has passed; s4 says to seed once the soil is very warm, at least 18 C (within 0.5 C). s6 says sow when temperatures are over 24 C, ideally approaching 30 C, and that soil temperature should be well above 20 C for best results; the tool reads it as soil from the clause before it. s6 gives four figures: seed germinates in soil as low as 18 C; soil temperature should be well above 20 C; seed should be sown when temperatures are over 24 C, ideally approaching 30 C; and the sowing temperature should be at least as warm as the one suggested for pumpkins (over 15 C, per the verifier). By rule 25, read within one source (rule 85e), s6's own sowing figure is the highest of its four, 24 C. s7's 20 C is a germination range (see germ_soil_temp_opt_c). FLAG: stated figures spread from 18 to 24 C (6.0 C). Across sources rule 85e sends the choice to the majority and flag rules (13, 16): the higher figure rests on s6 alone, so the majority value 18.3 (three sources) is stored. s4's sentence is the direct-seeding one ('can be seeded directly into the garden once the soil is very warm'); its separate 18 C line for transplanting out is not used (rule 26).

Seed companies' germination temperatures count as the optimum (rule 27). s7: soil 20 to 32 C. s6 gives a wide band (Germination Temperature 24 to 35 C) and an ideal (sow when over 24 C, 'ideally approaching 30 C'); under rule 43 the ideal is s6's figure, 30 C, and the wider band is not counted. Rule 85a: a single ideal figure ('ideally approaching 30') is s6's figure and its wider band is not counted, so 20 to 32 stands. Range spans every counted figure: 20 to 32. Two independent sources inside it (s6 30, s7 20 to 32); both ends are s7's. This changes the earlier 20 to 35, whose top end came from s6's wider band. The coordinator's brief called 30 'the 30 C end'; I did not store 30 as the top, because s7 states 32 and rule 15 spans every stated figure. FLAG: the 20 C end rests on s7 alone and is 10 C below the next figure (30, s6). The 32 end is 2 C from 30.

50 F = 10.0 C. s16 (Texas AgriLife Extension, Masabni, a commercial guide; a crop-biology line, not a scale figure, rules 6 and 128d) says night temperature below 50 F stunts growth, a stall temperature under rule 28. One source, flagged for the horticulturist. Not counted: the Utah State (Knott's) table's 60 F = 15.6 C, row 'Cucumber, Muskmelon' (rule 140: the table fills a field only where no other allowed source states it). s4 gives no figure. s16 also says low soil and air temperatures can stunt growth (no figure) and that fruit maturing below 70 F is usually poor quality (a quality line, not used).

Rule 140, the only source: Utah State Extension, Temperature Management in High Tunnels, Table 3 (credited to Knott's Handbook), row 'Cucumber, Muskmelon', maximum 90 F = 32.2 C (rounded to the nearest tenth, rule 100b; rule 209). No other allowed source states this field. Flagged.

s1: these melons are very tender and should be planted after the last chance of frost; s6: melons are frost tender annuals. Not counted: s7's tender-crop sentence (word for word on its tomato and cucumber pages; the tomato page is a different family, so template) and s3's frost sentence (page-level).

s2: cantaloupes prefer organic, rich, well-drained, sandy soils for best growth (the same sentence is on USU's watermelon, pumpkin and cucumber pages, all cucurbits, and not on its tomato or pepper pages, so not template under rule 75); s6: excellent crops of melons are produced in sandy soils (per the verifier). s2 also says most soils will grow cantaloupe if well-drained; 'most soils' is weaker than 'any well-drained garden soil' (rule 62), so it is not read as all textures. s4 and s7 give no texture.

s5 (Georgia commercial cantaloupe bulletin; pH is not a scale-specific figure): pH 6.0 to 6.5 is important for cantaloupe production. s6: pH must exceed 6.0 (a floor, inside the range; melons are less tolerant of acidic soils than pumpkins). Top end rests on s5 alone. FLAG: second source gives a floor only (same reading as the cucumber file).

s2 'Most soils will grow cantaloupe provided they are well-drained'; s4 'Melons grow best in rich, well-draining, moist soil' (frame on USask cucumber, pumpkin and zucchini pages only, so counted under rule 75); s8 'Well drained' (growing trait). s7's well-drained sentence is template (its tomato page) and is not counted. s3's 'well-drained area' is under a general heading and not counted. s6 suggests a mounded bed to improve drainage.

s2: can be trained to a fence or trellis or grown in a large pot; s4: gives a container size and says to choose a bush type melon for containers; s6: can be grown in pots if the roots have enough space and there is room for the long vine.

Direct: s1 (plant seed or transplants), s2 (plant seeds directly in the garden), s4 (direct seeding works), s6 (best direct sown once soil has warmed), s7 (grow best sown directly). Indoors: s2 (allow 6 weeks to grow transplants), s4 (seedlings 10-14 days old), s6 (in pots in a short growing season), s8 (starter trays, transplant after 3-4 weeks). s3 (direct sow; start seeds indoors 3 weeks before transplanting) is under a general heading and not counted. No source says to buy transplants, so transplant_bought is not listed.

Seedling age at planting out, widest span of stated figures, weeks at 7 days (rule 48). s2 6 weeks; s4 10 to 14 days = 1.4 to 2.0 weeks (10 / 7 = 1.43, rounded to 1.4; the sentence is on USask's cucumber, pumpkin and zucchini pages with the same figure, all cucurbits, so not template under rule 75); s8 3 to 4 weeks (group page that names rockmelon, general line). FLAG: 1.4 rests on s4 alone and is 29% below the next figure, s4's own 2.0 (rule 60); 6 rests on s2 alone and is 50% above s8's 4. s4 adds that melons dislike root disturbance, so seedlings should not be started too early. s4 also says: 'Start seedlings about 2 weeks prior to transplanting out.' (2.0 weeks, inside the range). Rule 85f: 10 days = 1.43 weeks is rounded outward to 1.4 as the minimum. Left out: s3's 3 weeks (general heading, see header) and s2's none counted back from frost.

s6 6 to 10 days, and 'up to two weeks' at the lower temperatures of its range (14 days); s7 8 to 16 days (at soil 20 to 32 C). Two sources, each end stated (6 by s6, 16 by s7). No flag: the next figure to 16 is s6's 14 (rule 60), 14% away; 6 is 25% below 8.

Days from transplanting to first ripe fruit (rule 32), counted from transplanting under rules 47 and 131b. Figures: s16 (Texas AgriLife, commercial guide, crop biology, rule 128d) 'Transplanted - 70-80' days after planting = 70 to 80; s19 (Oregon State) approx. 70 days from transplanting in the lower Columbia Basin and 75 in the Willamette Valley; s20 (Penn State, a transplant-only page, rule 33) Table 1 'Days to Maturity' for 16 recommended cultivars, lowest 68 (Goddess) and highest 85 (Strike); those are cultivar figures counted under rule 127a and flagged. Both ends (68 and 85) rest on s20's cultivar table alone: 68 is 2.9 percent below 70 and 85 is 2.4 percent above the next figure below it, s20's 83 (Tirreno), so no end exceeds 25 percent. If the horticulturist prefers crop-wide figures only, the range without the cultivar table is 70 to 80 (s16, s19). FLAGGED: ends rest on one source's cultivar table; s20's days have no stated start of their own (start from page context). Other start points, kept out under rule 47: sowing 80 to 100 (Alabama ANR-2876-H, a direct-sowing-only page) and 85 to 95 (s16 'Direct seeded'); s3's 80 to 100 days from transplanting stays out under the header ruling on s3 (rules 66, 77). Left out as measuring something else (rules 19, 32): s1 30 to 35 days and s2 35 to 45 days from pollination or flowering. Tie broken 2026-11-24 by s20 (rule 215b).

Rules 128a and 131b: transplant has three votes (s16 states 'Transplanted - 70-80'; s19 states 'from transplanting'; s20 by page context, rules 33 and 135b: the page never mentions seeding or sowing in the field. Its sentence that cantaloupes are generally started as transplants matches Penn State's tomato page apart from a word-order swap, so it is template and gives no context (rules 229b, 68). The page's context comes from its non-template lines: the line setting 24 to 30 inches between plants in the row, and the line on early feeding by cucumber beetles on young transplants). Sowing has two (s16 'Direct seeded - 85-95'; Alabama ANR-2876-H, by page context). Alabama is not cited here because its figures are counted under sowing. Flagged: s20 supplies its vote by context only.

Seed depth, converted: 1/2 to 3/4 in = 1.27 to 1.91 cm (s1); 1 to 2 in = 2.54 to 5.08 cm (s2); 2 cm (1 in) (s4, as printed); 10 to 15 mm = 1.0 to 1.5 cm (s7); s4 also gives 1 cm per Jiffy-7 pot for indoor sowing (per the verifier; the sentence is only on USask cucurbit pages, so counted under rule 75), so 1.0 is stated by s7 and s4. FLAG: 5.08 rests on s2 alone, 100% above the next figure (2.54). 1.0 is 21% below 1.27, not flagged.

s4 adds two figures the first draft left out: 'Sow 3-4 seeds 2 cm deep and 25 cm apart within the row' followed by 'Thin to the strongest seedling' (plant spacing of 25 cm, rules 42 and 61), and 'For vine varieties of melon, space 1.8 m (8') apart within the row and between rows' (180 cm; the printed 8 ft would be 243.84, the metric figure counts and the mismatch is noted, rule 70). FLAG: both ends rest on s4 alone; 25 is 45% below 45.7 and 180 is 50% above 120. Other figures: between plants in the row, converted: 18 to 24 in = 45.7 to 61.0 (s1); transplants 2 ft = 61.0 (s2); 24 in = 61.0 (s3, bullet that names muskmelon (cantaloupe)); seedlings 90 cm (s4, bush varieties); seeds 90 to 120 cm apart (s7). Left out: s7's 'If growing on the ground, allow at least 2 square metres per plant.' (an area, not a spacing; rule 85b); mound or hill spacing (s2 mounds 4 ft apart, s8 mounds 1 m apart, s3 hills 6 to 8 ft; rule 23); s5's 2 to 3 ft in the row (commercial bulletin, field-scale). s6 'Spacing: 1 metre' sits next to mound sowing so it is not counted, but 1 m is inside the range. 120 rests on s7 alone, 33% above 90 (inside the range, no end flag). 45.7 is exactly 25% below 61.0.

Converted: 6 to 8 ft = 182.88 to 243.84 (s1; exact, stored exact under rule 85f); 4 to 6 ft = 121.9 to 182.9 (s2); 60 to 72 in = 152.4 to 182.9 (s3, bullet naming muskmelon); 90 cm between rows for bush varieties (s4, general line of a page that names cantaloupes); 130 to 160 cm (s7). Left out: s5's 4 to 6 ft (commercial bulletin; same as s2). s4 also gives vine varieties 1.8 m (8') between rows = 180 cm (rule 70), inside the range. FLAG: 90 rests on s4 alone, 26% below 121.9; 243.84 on s1 alone, 33% above 182.9.

s1 (watering section): melons need a lot of water, which states high (rule 86a). One source, no rival; flag for the horticulturist. s8's quick-facts 'Regular watering' is not a rating and is not counted. s2 and s4 give amounts, not a rating.

s1: melons need extra water during fruit set and development; s3: keep plants well-watered during establishment and fruit expansion (under the heading 'Growing and caring of cantaloupe, muskmelons, and watermelons'; establishment rests on s3 alone). s1, s2, s3 and s8 say to reduce watering as fruit ripens.

s8: keep leaves dry by watering at the base of the plant or early in the day; s1: drip irrigation instead of overhead keeps foliage dry. s7's two watering sentences are on its tomato page (template) and are not counted here; they still support the powdery mildew prevention (rule 12).

s4 names a soluble fertiliser with three equal N-P-K numbers before fruit set, which counts as balanced (rule 82). One source; flag for the horticulturist. Not mapped: s4's one-time transplant drench, s1's pre-planting and side-dressing grades, and s2's nitrogen side dressing (unequal formulas; a side dressing is a supplement and gives no vote, rule 86b). s7's balanced-fertiliser sentence is template (word for word on its tomato page) and gives no vote. s6 names only water-soluble plant food and complete organic fertilisers, no value.

s2: vines can be trained to a fence or trellis; s6: tie to a trellis once the vine is 1 m long; s7: vines can sprawl on the ground or be grown up a strong trellis. Fruit slings: s6 (stocking cradle), s7 (netting sling).

s4: a thick layer of mulch conserves moisture and reduces weeding (USask cucurbit pages only, counted); s6: mulch plants after the soil has warmed to keep moisture even and suppress weeds. Not counted: s2's two mulch sentences (word for word on USU's tomato page, a different family, so template; fourth review W1) and s3's thick organic mulch sentence (names no crop).

fields.value: Black plastic warms the soil early. Mulch holds water and cuts weeds, and mulch under ripening fruit helps against rot. Lay mulch once the soil has warmed. Black plastic can overheat soil in hot weather.
fields.note: Black plastic warms soil: s1 (one source; s2's sentence is template, W1). Too hot in summer: s1. Mulch holds water and cuts weeds: s4 and s6. Mulch after the soil has warmed: s6. Mulch under ripening fruit against rot: s7 (straw or sugar cane; not on its tomato or cucumber pages, so not template). s2's plastic-or-organic sentences are not used (template, USU tomato page).

Insect: s1 and s2 (bees pollinate the flowers), s6 (insect pollinated). Hand helps: s4 (use a small brush or q-tip to dab a male flower and transfer the pollen to the female flowers, per the verifier) and s7 (use a paintbrush to move pollen from male to female flowers; the same sentence is on The Seed Collection's watermelon, zucchini and cucumber pages, all cucurbits, so not template under rule 75). s4's brush sentence is on USask cucumber, pumpkin and zucchini pages only, so it counts too.
s2 starts the crop from seed. s3 also does, but is not counted for general lines.

s1: do not plant after other melons or similar crops (watermelon, cucumber, squash, pumpkin) for at least three years. 'At least', stored as 3. One source. Left out: s6's 'Always rotate your rockmelon crops from year to year to prevent disease and improve yields.' (states no gap figure; rule 85c).

fields.value: Netted melons are ready at full slip: the stem parts easily from the vine, the netting turns coarse and the skin beneath turns from green toward yellow.
fields.note: s1 full slip; s2 stem slips, netting coarse, background colour green to yellow; s8 stem begins to break away (its line names rockmelon). s3 gives the same slip sign under 'Harvesting muskmelon and watermelon'. s7's different sign (tough, woody stems, dry leaves) is the minority view and is not used (rule 20); dissenter s7.

s7: store in the fridge, best eaten within a few days (not template: the tomato page words it differently). One source. s2 and s4 describe cool storage (45-50 F, 5-10 C, 'a cool room'), which is not named as a fridge and is not mapped to cool_dark (rule 22).

Melon, cantaloupe, muskmelon, rockmelon, Cucumis, gourd, squash and cucumber are absent from the UGA C1245 toxic lists (s13, not a complete list) and from the Illinois Plants and Pet Safety list (s14, not all inclusive; read from text the coordinator extracted). Illinois mentions 'prickles on cucumbers' only as a plant defence, not a classification. NC State Toolbox skipped (pending O-19). Absence is not evidence of safety.

Melon, cantaloupe, muskmelon, rockmelon, Cucumis, gourd, squash and cucumber are absent from the Utah Poison Control web list (s11, 35 entries) and from both the toxic and non-toxic lists of the Utah brochure (s12, read from text the coordinator extracted). That melons are grown as food is not a toxicity finding.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: White spots start on older leaves and can spread over the whole leaf surface, which cuts yield.
prevention: Water at soil level or at the base and keep leaves dry
Space plants and choose a sunny, ventilated position so air moves through
Remove affected leaves
Choose resistant varieties

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Small green or black soft-bodied insects on the underside of leaves and new shoots, with crinkled or curled leaves.
prevention: Wash them off with a strong jet of water
Encourage predatory insects such as ladybirds

problems.name: Poor fruit set
problems.signs: Female flowers fall or fail to set fruit. Rainy, cold or cloudy weather keeps bees away, and extreme heat can drop flowers.
prevention: Keep row covers and tunnels off once flowers open so bees can reach them
Avoid pesticides while plants are in flower
Do not pinch out leaders until enough female flowers have set fruit
Hand pollinate early in the day

problems.name: Sunscald
problems.signs: White marks or blisters on the fruit that often turn mouldy; young unripe fruit are most at risk.
prevention: Leave the leaves on so they shade the fruit
Cover plants with light fabric on very hot days

problems.name: Too much vine, little fruit
problems.signs: Plants produce lots of vine and very little fruit when fed too much nitrogen or planted too close.
prevention: Avoid heavy nitrogen feeding
Give plants the spacing the guides advise

problems.name: Possums, birds and other animals
problems.signs: A large share of the crop can be lost overnight.
prevention: Exclude animals with netting or cages

text.summary: Melon, covered here as the netted cantaloupe, rockmelon and muskmelon group of Cucumis melo, is a frost-tender, trailing vine grown for its fruit. It wants full sun, warm soil and plenty of moisture while it establishes and sets fruit. Honeydew and other melon groups are not covered by this file.
text.how_to_plant: Sow only when frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed to about 18 degrees C or more; seed germinates best at roughly 20 to 32 degrees C. Choose a sunny spot with well-drained, sandy soil. Sow seed about 1 to 5 cm deep and thin to the strongest plants, leaving roughly 25 to 180 cm between plants (the widest for vine types) and 90 to 244 cm between rows. In cooler places, raise seedlings indoors first; guides give anywhere from about 1.4 to 6 weeks before planting out. Bush types can also be grown in a large pot.
text.how_to_care: Water at the base of the plant and keep the leaves dry. Give extra water while fruit sets and swells, then ease off as it ripens. Avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which grows vines at the expense of fruit. Mulch to hold moisture and cut weeds, using black plastic where the soil needs warming. Train vines up a fence or trellis and cradle heavy fruit. Bees do the pollinating, so take covers off once flowers open and avoid sprays during bloom; a small paintbrush can move pollen from male to female flowers.
text.harvest: Judge ripeness by the fruit rather than the calendar. A ripe netted melon parts easily from the vine at the stem, the netting turns coarse and the skin underneath shifts from green toward yellow. Pick it at that stage. The fruit can be kept in the fridge.
common_mistakes: Planting out before frost has passed or into cool soil.
Feeding heavily with nitrogen or crowding plants, which grows vine rather than fruit.
Wetting the leaves when watering, which encourages leaf diseases.
Keeping watering heavy as fruit ripens, which dulls the sweetness.
Using pesticides while plants are in flower.

s7 lists full sun; s6 says full sun and, for pots, to position in full sun. s8 says to choose a site with full sun, and s2 says cucumbers thrive in an abundance of sunlight; neither is counted (s8 possibly template, s2 gives no hours). s4 and s5 repeat template sun sentences and are not cited (D-030).

65 F = 18.3 C. s8 says to plant when soils are 65 F or after frost danger has passed (its planting section covers sowing seed); s9 says the soil should be at least 65 F for optimal germination. Other figures, not counted for the stored value: s1 says plant seed or transplants once soil reaches 70 F (21.1 C) and that seed will not germinate below 50 F (10 C), so by the D-023 rule s1 counts at 21.1 C; s7 says sow when soil exceeds 15 C and preferably 20 C, counted at its safer end, 20 C. s5's 18 to 35 C is a germination range (the optimum, see germ_soil_temp_opt_c), not a sowing minimum. The three stated figures (18.3, 20, 21.1) span 2.8 C, under the 3 C flag.

s7 gives germination temperature 15 to 35 C; s5 gives germination in 4 to 10 days at 18 to 35 C; s8 gives germination in 5 to 10 days at 65 to 85 F (18.3 to 29.4 C). Seed companies' stated germination temperatures count as the optimum (D-028); s8 is a university figure, also inside the range. The low end, 15 C, rests on s7 alone, 3 C below s5's 18 C (not more than the 3 C threshold).

s9: plant stress below 60 F (15.6 C) makes the fruit bitter; cold stress with crop damage counts like heat stress (D-027 symmetric clarification). One source, so HORTICULTURIST FLAG; it narrows planting windows noticeably. Not counted: s9's 10 C bee-activity figure (pollinators) and s2's -0.6 C (frost, in frost_tolerance).

s9: plant stress above 90 F (32.2 C) makes the fruit bitter; stress with fruit damage counts as harm (D-027, coordinator ruling). One source, so HORTICULTURIST FLAG. s8's 80 F (26.7 C) is a row-cover ventilation cue, not a limit.

s1 says cucumbers are very tender and can be killed by light frosts; s2 says outdoor plants are very sensitive to temperatures below 31 F (-0.6 C). s4's frost sentence is the same word for word on its eggplant page (template, not cited). s5's tender-crop sentence is template and is not cited.

s1 says 'well-drained sandy loam to clay loam soil enriched with up to 20% organic matter'; soil descriptions such as sandy loam and clay loam map to loam (D-031 clarification), wording kept here. s8 says sandy soils (its sentence reads like its eggplant page, so it is not counted). s2 says gravelly soils for South Florida and raised beds in low-lying gardens; s9 says most soils suit if fertile and rich in compost.
s1 gives 6.0 to 6.5; s9 gives 6.0 to 6.8; s7 says a pH above 6.5 (a floor with no upper end, inside the range). The top end, 6.8, rests on s9 alone and is within 25% of s1's 6.5.

s1 says well-drained sandy loam to clay loam; s6 says warm, well drained soil; s2 suggests raised beds and well-drained soil for low-lying gardens. s8 and s5 also say well-drained but their sentences are possible template text and are not counted.
s6 gives a pot or trough size; s7 says to select a large pot for 3 to 4 plants; s9 suggests large hanging baskets or other containers for compact (dwarf) types.

s6 says a pot or trough at least 400 mm wide and deep (40 cm). One source; extended field. s7 says a pot at least 30 cm in diameter for 3 to 4 plants, a width for several plants, not a depth. Not converted to litres.

Direct: s2 says direct seeding is best, s5 and s7 say to sow direct, s6 describes sowing in mounds, s3 gives a direct spacing. Indoors: s3 says to sow in peat pots or similar, s1 and s9 say to start seeds indoors, s8 says to allow 4 to 6 weeks to grow transplants. s2 says UF/IFAS does not recommend transplanting cucumbers. No source says to buy transplants, so transplant_bought is not listed.

Seedling age at planting out. s1 and s9 give 2 to 3 weeks before planting or transplanting; s4 says plants grown indoors 3 weeks before planting time; s8 allows 4 to 6 weeks to grow transplants. The top end, 6, rests on s8 alone and is over 25% beyond 3 (s4, s1, s9) and 4: HORTICULTURIST FLAG. Left out: s3's sow 3 to 4 weeks before the frost-free date (counted back from frost, not seedling age at planting out). s3 also says to transplant at two to four true leaves and not to let transplants get too large.
s8 gives 5 to 10 days at 65 to 85 F; s5 gives about 4 to 10 days at 18 to 35 C; s7 gives 7 to 10 days. The 4 rests on s5 alone, 20% below 5, so under the 25% threshold.

From sowing. s4 gives 50 to 65 from seed; s7 says harvest in around 60 to 70 days from sowing, and its table line reads 'Harvest: 52-90 days'; s2 says 'ready to harvest 40 to 65 days later' after describing sowing seed and recommends direct seeding only, so by the start-point clarification (page context describes one way of starting the crop) it counts from sowing. s7's 52-90 line counts under the same rule: the page gives only direct sowing ('Sow: Direct, sow after frost') and does not mention transplanting. The 90 end rests on s7 alone and is 29% beyond 70: HORTICULTURIST FLAG. The 40 end rests on s2 alone, 20% below 50. Left out: s1 (50 to 70) and s9 (as little as 50 days) because those pages describe both sowing and indoor starting; s5 (60 to 90) because its page mentions transplanting seedlings and gives no start point; s6 (7 to 12 weeks, an unlabelled quick-facts figure that does not say what it measures). If the coordinator rules s7's table line out, the range is 40 to 70. s8 gives harvest 5 to 7 days after flowering, a different measure, not counted.
s4 says 'from seed'; s7 says 'from sowing' and describes direct sowing only; s2 describes direct seeding only.

s7 says to pick regularly to encourage flowers and fruit for up to 2 months (2 x 30 days). prevention: Keep beetles off young plants

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: White fungal patches or spots, starting on older leaves.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties
Avoid overhead watering
Water at soil level
Improve air flow
Remove affected leaves

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects on the undersides of leaves; leaves wilt or lose colour.

problems.name: Cucumber mosaic virus
problems.signs: Stunted plants, mottled yellow leaves, and blotchy, bitter fruit.
prevention: Grow resistant varieties

problems.signs: Flowers drop, small fruit shrivel, or fruit is misshapen.

Hand-pollinate with a small brush
Wait for warm weather
Keep soil fertile and moist

problems.signs: White marks or blisters on fruit.

Cover plants with light fabric on very hot days

text.summary: Cucumber is a frost-tender vine that crops in warm weather. It wants full sun, rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture. Sow seed directly once the soil has warmed, or raise seedlings briefly indoors. Vines grown up a trellis save space and suit large pots, and frequent picking keeps the plants producing.
text.how_to_plant: Wait until frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed to at least about 18 C. Choose a sunny spot with rich, well-drained soil, ideally around pH 6.0 to 6.8, and mix in compost first. Sow seed 1 to 2.5 cm deep, or raise seedlings indoors for only two to six weeks, because oversized seedlings transplant poorly. Space plants about 15 to 60 cm apart, in rows roughly 0.6 to 1.8 m apart. Seed usually sprouts in 4 to 10 days. In a pot, use a container at least 40 cm wide and deep and add a trellis or frame.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist, since dryness can make the fruit bitter. Water at the base and keep the leaves dry to limit disease. Once the soil is warm, mulch to hold moisture; dark plastic warms cool soil early on. Train vines up a trellis, fence or cage to save space. Feed in moderate amounts, following the product label, and avoid too much nitrogen, which grows leaves instead of fruit. If bees are scarce or fruit fails to set, move pollen from a male flower to a female flower with a small brush.
text.harvest: Expect the first fruit roughly 40 to 90 days after sowing, depending on the type and the weather. Pick while the fruit is evenly green, firm and crisp, before it starts to yellow. Pickling types are cut smaller than slicing types, and sources differ on exact sizes. Cut the stem with a sharp knife or pruners, and check the vines every day or two, because regular picking keeps plants flowering and fruiting for up to about two months. Fruit keeps about 10 to 14 days in a cool store at around 13 C.
common_mistakes: Sowing or planting out while frost is still possible or the soil is cold, which can kill young plants or stop seed germinating.
Letting the soil dry out between waterings, which can make the fruit bitter.
Leaving fruit on the vine until it turns yellow.
Letting seedlings grow too large in their containers before planting out.
Wetting the leaves when watering, which encourages fungal disease.

problems.name: Powdery mildew and downy mildew
problems.signs: Powdery mildew shows as white, furry patches across the upper leaf surface; downy mildew as light-gold angular spots, with purple spots underneath. Warm days followed by heavy dew favour powdery mildew; long wet, humid spells favour downy mildew.
prevention: Water at soil level and avoid overhead irrigation
Space plants so air moves through them
Remove diseased or injured fruit promptly
Clear vines and plant debris after harvest
Rotate crops; one guide says not to follow cantaloupe, cucumber or watermelon with pumpkins for at least three years, another rotates every 3 to 4 years

problems.name: Cucumber beetles and squash bugs
problems.signs: Both attack seedlings, vines and fruit, young and mature. Squash bugs lay brown egg masses on the plants.
prevention: Hand pick the brown egg masses of squash bugs
Cover young plants with fabric row covers, and take the covers off during the day once flowers open so bees can reach them

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Small sap-sucking insects crowding on new shoots or under the leaves.
prevention: Wash them off with a strong spray of water from a hose
Encourage predatory insects

problems.name: Poor fruit set
problems.signs: Flowers drop, or small fruit forms and then shrivels and rots. Common in rainy weather when bees are inactive; heat and water stress when plants are young can also cause it.
prevention: Hand pollinate with a small brush, moving pollen from male to female flowers
Avoid insecticides while plants are in flower
Avoid water stress in young plants

problems.name: Damping off (seedlings dying after deep sowing)
problems.signs: Young seedlings look normal, then suddenly die back at a ring close to ground level. One guide blames seed sown too deep.
prevention: Sow seed shallowly, about 1.3 to 2.5 cm deep (depths given by several guides)

problems.name: Rats, possums and birds on fruit
problems.signs: Once fruit has set, rodents can leave holes and splits in it, and animal damage can ruin much of a crop overnight.
prevention: Exclude animals with netting or cages

text.summary: Pumpkin, covered here as Cucurbita maxima, is a sprawling, frost-tender vine grown for large hard-skinned fruit that keeps for months once cured. It wants full sun, warm soil, steady moisture and plenty of space, and it relies on bees, or a paintbrush, to set fruit. A very large pot can work too.
text.how_to_plant: Sow only once frost has passed and the soil has warmed; sow once the soil is above about 20 degrees C (one guide allows about 15.6), and seed germinates best at about 21 to 35. Put two or three seeds in each raised mound, about 1.3 to 2.5 cm deep, and thin to the strongest plant or two. Bush types need about 60 to 100 cm between plants in rows 90 to 185 cm apart; large-vined types about 90 to 200 cm between plants in rows 180 to 460 cm apart. Other guides, without naming a type, allow roughly 90 to 150 cm between plants and 100 to 370 cm between rows. Bush types can also grow in a large container of at least 40 litres. In a short season, raise seedlings indoors for about three weeks first and handle them gently. Pick a sunny spot with well-drained soil, dug over deeply with organic matter added.
text.how_to_care: Water deeply at the base of each plant and keep the leaves dry. Do not let the soil dry out while fruit is setting and swelling. Pumpkins are heavy feeders, but too much nitrogen builds vines at the expense of fruit. Mulch to hold back weeds. Bees must visit the flowers; if fruit fails to set, move pollen from male to female flowers with a small brush, and avoid spraying insecticides while plants bloom. A trellis can limit the spread. Lift ripening fruit off bare soil to reduce rot.
text.harvest: Allow roughly 70 to 140 days from sowing to the first ripe fruit, depending on type and weather. Pick when the colour is deep and solid, the rind is hard enough that a fingernail does not mark it, and the stem is dry and corky. Cut the fruit off with a few centimetres of stem left on. Cure it for a week or two somewhere warm and airy, then keep it cool, dry and dark. Frost kills the vines, so pick before hard frost. Well-cured fruit can last from weeks to many months.
common_mistakes: Sowing before frost has passed or into cold soil.
Sowing seed too deep, which can kill seedlings.
Wetting the leaves and fruit when watering, which favours mildew.
Feeding heavily with nitrogen, which grows vines and holds back fruit.
Spraying insecticides while plants are in flower, which harms the bees that pollinate them.

problems.name: Cucumber beetles and squash bugs

prevention: Cover plants with row covers, removing them at flowering so bees can reach the flowers

problems.name: Poor fruit set

Use insecticides as little as possible

text.summary: Zucchini, covered here with other summer squash, is a frost-tender, mostly bushy plant grown for young fruit picked while small. It likes full sun, warm soil and water at the base, and it needs bees or a paintbrush to set fruit. Plants crop quickly and keep producing if picked often.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where it will grow once frost has passed and the soil has warmed; one extension guide gives about 15.6 degrees C as the soil temperature to wait for, and seed sprouts best at 21 to 35. Sow about 1.3 to 2.5 cm deep and keep only the strongest seedlings. Give each plant roughly 30 to 90 cm, and leave about 80 to 180 cm between rows. For an early start, raise seedlings indoors for about three weeks and handle them gently. Pick a sunny spot with well-drained soil. For a pot, choose one at least 40 cm deep.
text.how_to_care: Water at the base of the plants and try to keep the leaves dry. Mulch round the base with straw to hold moisture. Bees carry pollen between flowers; if fruit fails to set, dab pollen from a male flower onto a female one with a small brush, ideally while the flowers are open. Use insecticides as little as possible. Row covers can keep out beetles and borers, but take them off once flowers open so bees can reach the plants. Zucchini has a medium need for nutrients.
text.harvest: Expect the first fruit roughly 42 to 56 days from sowing, depending on the guide. Pick while fruit is young and tender, about 15 to 30 cm long for zucchini; fruit whose rind resists a thumbnail is overmature. Check plants every day or two and take off old fruit so new fruit keeps forming, because large fruit left on the plant slows further fruit. Fresh fruit keeps about 5 to 14 days in cool, moist conditions.
common_mistakes: Planting before the last frost has passed.
Sowing seed into soil that has not warmed.
Wetting the foliage when watering.
Leaving large fruit on the plant, which slows new fruit.
Leaving row covers on once flowers open, so bees cannot pollinate.

text.summary: Lemongrass is a tender perennial grass grown for its lemon-flavoured stalks and fragrant leaves. It forms an upright clump, wants full sun, and is usually started from divisions of an existing clump or from bought starter plants rather than seed. It suits pots, which can be moved indoors to protect it from frost.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot with well-drained, moist, rich soil, or use a pot. Start from a division of an existing clump, which is a section of the bulbous stalk base with roots attached, or buy a starter plant. Divisions need plenty of room in the ground, about 90 centimetres apart. Seed is rarely used for this plant, so most growers skip it. Choose soil rich in organic matter, and avoid any spot where water stands, because waterlogged soil does the plant harm.
text.how_to_care: Lemongrass feeds heavily on nitrogen through the growing season. Keep the soil moist but never soggy, since overwatering invites root rot, and do not let a potted plant dry out. In dry air, mist the plant. Frost harms it, so move pots indoors when temperatures cool; indoors it makes fewer stalks in dim light. Cutting plants back hard to about 30 centimetres is one grower guide's routine, and dividing older clumps keeps them productive. Spider mites show up as pale speckling on the leaves, mostly on indoor plants.
text.harvest: Cut stems at ground level once they are about 1.3 centimetres thick, or push an outer stem aside, twist and pull it off. Leaf edges are sharp, so wear gloves. Strip away the tough outer layers and use the tender inner stalk. Leaves can be dried in the sun or an oven for use in soups and teas, and lemongrass can be frozen. Harvest can continue through the growing season.
common_mistakes: Leaving potted plants outdoors where frost can reach them.
Planting in waterlogged soil or overwatering, which leads to root rot.
Never dividing older clumps, which lowers productivity.

problems.name: Carrot fly
problems.signs: Small white maggots feed on the root and burrow into it as it grows.
prevention: Cover young seedlings with fabric row covers
Use insect netting over the crop to keep the flies off

problems.name: Forked roots
problems.signs: The carrot grows several roots or twists instead of one straight root, most often in heavy or stony soil.
prevention: Dig the bed deeply and add compost
Work the soil well before sowing

problems.name: Split roots
problems.signs: Roots crack open, usually after a dry spell followed by heavy watering or rain.
prevention: Water deeply and evenly so soil moisture stays steady
Ease off watering as harvest nears

problems.name: Green shoulders
problems.signs: The exposed tops of the roots turn green and bitter.
prevention: Draw soil up over the root tops
Mulch to keep the shoulders covered

problems.name: Bolting
problems.signs: The plant flowers early and goes to seed.
prevention: Water regularly and deeply in hot weather
Avoid sowing into very hot weather
Do not plant too early, while it is still cold

companions.reason: Radish sown in the same row germinates quickly, breaks the soil crust and marks the row.

text.summary: Carrot is a root crop sown straight into the ground in a sunny spot with loose, deep, well-drained soil. Expect a first harvest about 55 to 140 days after sowing. Short, round types suit pots. Steady moisture keeps roots from splitting, and deep, stone-free soil keeps them from forking.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where the carrots will grow, because they dislike root disturbance. Prepare deep, loose, well-drained soil free of stones and work in compost. Sow seed about 0.5 to 1.3 cm deep and keep the seedbed moist; it can take 7 to 21 days to come up, and one guide puts the lowest soil temperature for germination at about 10 degrees C. Thin seedlings while they are small so plants end up roughly 2.5 to 10 cm apart, in rows 25 to 61 cm apart. For pots, choose short, round or stubby types.
text.how_to_care: Give carrots plentiful moisture, and keep the seedbed from drying out while seed is germinating. Swings between dry and wet split the roots, so water deeply and evenly, and ease off as harvest nears. Mulch to hold moisture and cut weeds. Hill soil over any root tops showing above ground so they do not turn green and bitter. Cover seedlings with fabric or netting against carrot fly. Keep carrots out of the same spot for three years, and sow again every three weeks for a steady supply.
text.harvest: Pull carrots once the roots have reached a useful size; for fresh eating, pick them before they are much thicker than 2.5 cm across. Loosen the soil with a fork, pull by the tops and trim the leaves. Lift the biggest roots first and let the rest keep growing. Roots left too long turn tough and woody. Carrots can stay in the ground and be lifted as needed, under heavy mulch where it is cold. Cold, humid storage keeps them from a couple of weeks to several months.
common_mistakes: Letting soil swing between dry and wet, which splits the roots.
Growing carrots in heavy or stony soil, which gives forked roots.
Leaving root tops uncovered, so they turn green and bitter.
Leaving roots in the ground too long, so they turn tough and woody.
Replanting carrots in the same bed within three years.

problems.name: Fig rust
problems.signs: Leaves turn brown and carry orange growths on the lower part of the leaf. Badly affected leaves drop early, which weakens the tree and can leave the crop poorly ripened.
prevention: Rake up and destroy the infected leaves

problems.name: Root-knot nematodes
problems.signs: Roots swell or form galls, and the tree slowly loses vigour, wilts or yellows, crops less and may drop fruit early. The problem can go unnoticed for several years, and is worse in sandy soil.
prevention: Buy plants that are free of nematodes
Plant them in nematode-free soil
Keep tools and plant material clean so nematodes do not spread

problems.name: Winter cold injury
problems.signs: Stems and young trunks are injured or killed by hard cold, in the worst case down to the ground; the plant may then sprout again from the base, with a smaller or later crop.
prevention: Water the tree well a few days before a hard freeze
Plant on the side of a building that gives shelter from cold weather

problems.name: Birds
problems.signs: Birds peck ripening figs and damage the fruit.
prevention: Cover the tree with netting, row cover or shade cloth while the fruit ripens

problems.name: Fig mosaic virus
problems.signs: Leaves become mottled, and the tree bears fewer, smaller and misshapen fruit.
prevention: Inspect nursery plants carefully before buying

problems.name: Green fig beetle
problems.signs: Large, emerald-green beetles buzz around the tree and gather in groups to feed on single ripe fruits.
prevention: Clear garden waste and compost heaps away from the area where fruit trees grow
Cover the trees with a barrier such as shade cloth or a row cover before the fruit ripens
Use simple bottle traps baited with a sweet lure

text.summary: The fig is a deciduous fruit tree that grows large in the ground but can be kept in a big pot with a compact variety. It wants full sun, well-drained soil and steady moisture, is usually started from a cutting, and needs only light pruning. Its milky sap can irritate skin.
text.how_to_plant: Start from a rooted cutting, which is the usual way to begin a fig. Choose a spot in full sun with soil that drains well. In the ground, leave roughly 3 to 6 metres between trees. For a pot, pick a compact variety and a container of at least about 57 litres with a drainage hole in the base. Fill it with a light, porous mix and add compost if the mix is soilless. Move up to a larger pot as the roots fill the old one.
text.how_to_care: Keep a potted fig's mix consistently moist but never soaked, and do not let the pot dry out; water especially while fruit forms. Poor drainage invites root rot. Spread 5 to 8 cm of mulch out to the edge of the canopy, keeping it off the trunk. Prune lightly to remove dead wood and keep the centre open. The milky sap can irritate skin; check with a vet or poison centre if a pet chews the plant.
text.harvest: Pick figs when they feel soft and smell sweet. Fruit picked while still unripe will not ripen afterwards, so take only what you plan to use soon; ripe figs are quite perishable. Birds can peck ripe fruit, so cover the tree with netting, row cover or shade cloth while the figs ripen. Eat figs fresh, freeze them, or dry them. Do not refrigerate them.
common_mistakes: Letting a potted fig dry out, because figs are sensitive to water stress.
Keeping the potting mix constantly wet, which invites root rot.
Picking figs while still unripe, since unripe fruit will not ripen once picked.
Leaving a potted fig in the same pot after the roots have filled it.
Piling mulch directly against the trunk.

fields.value: name: Herb fennel (leaf, sweet, common and bronze types); note: Grown for feathery leaves and seed; does not form a bulb (s4, s7, s9). About 91 to 183 cm tall; the bronze types are non-bulbing (s11). Direct sow: it does not transplant well because of its taproot (s4, s9). Tolerates drought once established (s8)., name: Florence fennel (bulb fennel, finocchio; var. azoricum or var. dulce); note: Grown for the swollen, overlapping leaf bases (s3, s8, s11); only this type forms bulbs (s1). Shorter than herb fennel; fronds 30.5 to 76.2 cm before harvest (s7, 12 to 30 in). Needs steady moisture: if the soil dries it bolts and the bulb suffers (s4, s6, s8). Hot weather and long days speed bolting, so slow-bolting varieties are advised (s6). Sown so that it matures in cooler, shorter days (s9). Days to harvest: s6 and s7 60 to 90 days (s7 counts from transplanting), s3 14 to 20 weeks after planting (98 to 140 days), s9 cultivars 75 to 90 days, s11 cultivars 80 to 100 days, s8 cultivars 75 to 90 days (from this page no start point). Harvest when the base is about tennis-ball size (s4, s8, s9) or under 10.16 cm across and firm (s6, 4 in), or dig bulbs after 3 to 4 months (no start point given) at 5.08 to 7.62 cm across (s10, 2 to 3 in); some growers earth up the base to keep it pale (s6, s11); bulbs keep for several weeks cool (s4) or up to 5 days in the fridge (s9). Soil for this type: loamy soil rich in organic matter and pH 6.5 to 8 (s6). Succession: sow 3 to 4 ft of row every 3 to 4 weeks for a steady supply of bulbs (s6). Dogs and cats. Fennel, Foeniculum, finocchio, anise and dill are absent from the UGA C1245 list (s16, 26 entries, not complete) and from the Illinois pet list (s17, saved PDF text, not all inclusive). s2 (NC State Toolbox) tags the plant non-toxic for cats, dogs and horses: one positive source (rule 143g), and non_toxic needs two (Q7). Check with a vet or poison centre.

No allowed source classifies fennel as poisonous to people. Fennel, Foeniculum, finocchio, anise, dill, Apiaceae and parsley are absent from the Utah Poison Control web list (s14, 35 names; its Poison Hemlock and Water Hemlock entries are other plants, rule 38) and fennel, Foeniculum and anise from the Utah brochure (s15, saved PDF text, not necessarily comprehensive). s2 (NC State) shows no poison block. That fennel is eaten is not a safety finding (rule 36). s8 reports sap skin irritation, recorded under skin_irritant.
s8: the sap can cause skin irritation in sensitive people, especially in sunlight. One source.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Leaves wilt or turn a different colour; colonies build up on stalks and flower heads around flowering.
prevention: Wash them off with water from a garden hose.

problems.name: Cutworms
problems.signs: Seedlings are chewed through at the stem and fall over at ground level.
prevention: Pick the grubs off by hand at night.
Put a cardboard collar round the stem of each seedling.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.signs: Tender leaves and shoots are eaten, mostly at night.
prevention: Remove their hiding places.
Keep free-range poultry.

problems.name: Swallowtail caterpillars
problems.signs: Caterpillars eat the foliage; mature plants lose little, but young seedlings can be overwhelmed and a plant left alone can be stripped in days.
prevention: Pick them off by hand as needed.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.signs: The plant flowers early and goes to seed before it gives a good harvest.
prevention: Keep the soil well drained but moist.
Avoid sowing in very hot weather.

text.summary: Fennel is a tall, feathery herb grown for its leaves, stems, flowers and seeds. It wants full sun and well-drained soil, resents transplanting, and suits large pots. Left to flower it can self-seed and spread.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a spot in full sun with well-drained soil. Sow seed directly where it will grow, under no more than about a centimetre of soil, because the taproot dislikes being moved. Seed usually sprouts within one to four weeks. Thin seedlings to about 45 centimetres apart and leave the rows well apart. From sowing to a first harvest, allow roughly 80 to 100 days. In a pot, use a container of at least 40 litres, though a deep taproot means it usually does better planted in the ground.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moist but well drained, since waterlogged ground harms the roots and stems; established plants cope with dry spells. Mulch with straw, compost or bark to hold moisture and hold down weeds, and use a balanced feed. Tall plants may need a stake in windy spots. Remove spent flower heads if you do not want self-sown seedlings, because fennel can crowd out neighbours when it sets seed. Handle the sap with care: it can irritate sensitive skin, especially in sunlight.
text.harvest: Cut the feathery foliage as needed through the growing season, taking no more than a third of the plant at a time. Leaves can be dried or frozen for later, though dried leaves lose flavour, so use them fresh where you can. For seed, wait until the flower heads turn brown, cut them before the seed drops, and dry them in a paper bag. Fresh fennel can be kept briefly in the fridge.
common_mistakes: Trying to move seedlings, because the taproot does not transplant well.
Planting on poorly drained ground.
Letting flowers set seed, so fennel self-sows and crowds out its neighbours.

problems.name: Grey mould and fruit rots
problems.signs: Berries are covered in a fuzzy grey mould before they rot.
prevention: Remove infected fruit
Mulch so berries stay up off the soil
Avoid poorly drained soil and shade
Use drip irrigation, or water in the morning so fruit and leaves dry out

problems.name: Leaf spot
problems.signs: Reddish to purple spots with brown centres appear on the leaves.
prevention: Avoid poorly drained soil and shade

problems.name: Virus diseases
problems.signs: Plants lose vigour and yields drop, and infected plants cannot be cured.
prevention: Start with virus-free (virus-indexed) nursery plants
Choose runners that have sturdy roots and big crowns
Do not transplant from an existing bed, which may carry the viruses

problems.name: Birds taking fruit
problems.signs: Ripe berries are pecked or stolen from the plants.
prevention: Cover the plants with netting or wire cages

text.summary: Strawberry is a low perennial fruit grown for its red berries. It does best in a sunny spot with well-drained, organically rich soil, and it also grows well in pots and hanging baskets. Plants spread by runners and lose vigour with age, so beds are renewed every few years.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a place with full sun and soil that drains well, rich in organic matter and slightly acidic. Where drainage is poor, use a raised bed or a pot. Start with healthy nursery plants or dormant crowns from a source that offers virus-free stock. Spread the roots, bury them with just the lowest part of the crown, and leave the growing bud clear of the soil. Give each plant room: day-neutral types can sit closer together than types that crop once a year. Water in well. If you want the bed to fill out with runners, pick off the first flowers so the new plants put their effort into roots and runners.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moist but never soggy, and use drip or base watering so the leaves stay dry. Mulch with straw to keep berries clean off the soil. Feed with a balanced fertiliser, following the product label. Manage runners to suit your bed: remove them to push energy into fruit, or let a few root to fill gaps and make new plants. Protect open flowers on cold nights with a light cover. Where winters are cold, lay a thick mulch over the dormant plants and take it off when growth resumes. Replace tired plants after a few years.
text.harvest: Pick berries when they are fully red, tip included, because they do not ripen any further once picked. Check the plants every other day in the cool of the day, and keep the green cap on. Remove any diseased, overripe or damaged fruit from the bed. Berries keep in the refrigerator for several days if left unwashed; wash them just before eating. Freeze any surplus.
common_mistakes: Letting new plants flower and fruit heavily when you want them to spread by runners and fill the bed.
Keeping the same planting for too many years until yields fall.
Burying the whole crown, when it should sit partly above the soil with the growing bud clear.
Planting where tomatoes, potatoes or peppers grew recently.

text.summary: Sunflower is a fast-growing annual grown mainly for its big flower heads, and its seeds are edible. Types range from compact plants that suit pots to tall single-stemmed giants and branching forms. It needs full sun and well-drained soil, and the tall types need a sheltered spot.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where the plants will grow, in full sun and well-drained soil, once the soil has warmed. Plant seeds about 1 to 5 cm deep, going deeper in sandy soil. Space plants about 30 to 50 cm apart, and branching types about 45 to 60 cm, thinning seedlings to the final spacing. For a pot, pick a large, well-drained container and a compact type. Sunflowers dislike root disturbance, so if you raise seedlings first, do not start them too early and handle the roots gently. Sow again every one to three weeks for longer flowering.
text.how_to_care: Water the soil rather than the foliage; established plants cope well with dry spells. Feed with a balanced fertiliser, following the product label, and avoid heavy nitrogen. Stake tall types and grow them where strong wind cannot reach, because top-heavy heads can bend or snap. Cut off faded flowers to prolong blooming. Space plants so air can move between them, which helps against mildew. Bees visit the flowers.
text.harvest: For seed, let the head droop and dry on the plant. It is ready when the back turns yellow-brown and the seeds come away easily. Cut the whole head with a length of stem, then hang it somewhere dry for several weeks and tap the seeds out. Birds and squirrels go for ripening heads, so cover them with a paper bag or netting. For cut flowers, pick stems in the cool of the day just as the flowers begin to open, and stand them in cool water straight away.
common_mistakes: Starting seedlings indoors too early, so they become rootbound in pots.
Leaving seed heads uncovered where birds and squirrels can strip them.
Growing tall types in an exposed spot without support.
Saving seed from hybrid types, where many seeds may not be viable.
Watering over the leaves, which encourages leaf disease.
