text.summary: Roselle, also called rosella or Jamaica sorrel, is a frost-tender shrub grown as an annual for its calyces and its leaves. It wants full sun and well-drained soil. Flowering starts as the days shorten. One guide also uses the seeds and roots.
text.how_to_plant: Start seed in trays or pots, sow it where the plants will grow, or use cuttings, and plant out only once frost danger has passed. Seed germinates best at about 23.8 to 35 degrees C and usually shows in 5 to 21 days. Sow seed roughly 0.6 to 1.27 cm deep. Seedlings take about 4 to 6 weeks before they can move outside, and a week of gradual outdoor exposure helps. Space plants generously, from 45 up to 152.4 cm apart, with rows 100 to 152.4 cm apart. Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil, ideally pH 5.5 to 7.0, and avoid waterlogged ground.
text.how_to_care: Roselle handles dry spells, but water when rain is lacking and keep the soil from becoming waterlogged. Prune early to encourage branching and more flowering shoots. Do not follow other mallow-family plants in the same spot in later years. Protect developing fruit from caterpillars with netting or fruit bags, and watch for aphids. Flowering begins as the days shorten. It is damaged by frost, and temperatures under about 4.4 degrees C can harm it.
text.harvest: Pick calyces when they are plump, shiny and tender, about 7 to 10 days after the flower opens. Snip the whole fruit off the stem. Picking early and often encourages more flower buds. Leaves can be pinched or snipped from the outer part of the plant, leaving some behind. Calyx picking continues until cool weather arrives, so finish before temperatures fall under about 4.4 degrees C.
common_mistakes: Planting out before frost danger has passed.
Leaving the harvest so late that cold weather reaches the calyces.
Planting in the same spot after other mallow-family plants.
Growing it in shade or waterlogged soil.

text.summary: New Guinea impatiens is a frost-tender annual grown for bright flowers, usually started from cuttings. Plants reach about 15 to 50 centimetres tall and suit pots, hanging baskets and garden beds. They cope with more sun than ordinary bedding impatiens.
text.how_to_plant: This plant is usually grown from cuttings. Choose a spot in partial shade or partial sun; plants also manage in full sun if they never run short of water. Give them rich, loamy soil that drains well and holds plenty of organic matter. They suit hanging baskets and other containers as well as beds and borders. Expect plants roughly 15 to 50 centimetres tall and 45 to 90 centimetres across. Frost kills them.
text.how_to_care: The more sun a plant gets, the more water it uses, so check sunny spots often and never let the plants dry out. Keep the soil moist and well drained. Morning sun with afternoon shade also suits them. Group them with other plants that have similar watering needs, so one routine suits the whole planting. Frost kills these plants. Butterflies visit the flowers.
text.harvest: New Guinea impatiens is grown for its flowers and foliage, not as a crop, so there is no harvest window to plan around. Plants flower over a long part of the growing season rather than all at once. Place them where the blooms can be seen, such as hanging baskets, patio pots and borders, and where butterflies can visit. Treat it as an ornamental to look at rather than to pick.
common_mistakes: Letting plants dry out in a sunny spot.

text.summary: Sweet potato is a fast-spreading, frost-tender vine grown for its starchy roots, and its young leaves and shoots are eaten too. It is started from rooted shoots called slips rather than seed, and wants warm soil, plenty of sun and a long frost-free season. Compact bush types save space, and a large pot can work.
text.how_to_plant: Plant once frost has passed and the soil has warmed to about 18 degrees C. Start from slips, which are shoots sprouted from roots kept from an earlier crop; they are not sown like seed. Choose a sunny site with loose, well-drained soil. Plant each slip roughly 5 to 15 cm deep, depending on the guide, and water it in straight away. Space plants about 20 to 90 cm apart, with more room where the vines may roam, and set rows or ridges 75 to 180 cm apart. Where space is tight, try a compact bush type in a large pot.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist while the slips root and the plants settle in, since early drought does the most harm. Never leave the soil waterlogged, because that can rot roots. Go easy on fertiliser, especially nitrogen: rich soil grows leaves rather than roots, and a soil test shows what is needed. Vines grow fast, so give them room. Rotate beds to reduce nematodes and scurf, and avoid ground that was lawn or overgrown with perennial grass the year before, to reduce wireworm.
text.harvest: Expect roughly 85 to 150 days from planting, depending on variety and warmth. Dig when the leaves start to yellow or the vine tops die back, and before frost. Roots keep growing, so start checking their size from about 80 days. Cure freshly dug roots before storing them, to heal wounds and sweeten them. Then store them cool, dark and ventilated, never in the fridge and never colder than about 10 degrees C. Cured roots can last several months. Young leaves and shoots are edible too.
common_mistakes: Planting slips into cold soil or before frost has passed.
Feeding generously, especially with nitrogen, which gives leafy vines and few roots.
Letting newly planted slips dry out before they root.
Refrigerating roots or storing them below about 10 degrees C.
Storing roots without curing them first.

text.summary: Lettuce is a fast-growing, upright annual leaf crop that prefers cool weather and tolerates light frost. In heat it turns bitter and runs to seed, so shade, steady moisture and slow-bolting varieties help. It grows in beds and in containers, and leaf types can be picked a few leaves at a time.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny site with loamy soil at a pH of about 6.0 to 6.7. Sow seed very shallowly: pressed onto the surface or covered lightly, never deeper than about 2.5 cm. It usually comes up within one to two weeks, best in cool soil and poorly in hot soil, so do not sow when the ground is hot. You can also raise transplants indoors or buy them; head types in particular suit bought transplants. Space leaf types about 10 to 25 cm apart and heading types 25 to 38 cm, with rows 30 to 90 cm apart. Sow again every 10 to 14 days for a steady supply.
text.how_to_care: Water frequently enough to keep the soil evenly moist. Dry soil can push plants to bolt, but soggy soil invites rots. Mulch lightly to hold moisture. In hot weather give afternoon shade or shade cloth, and favour slow-bolting loose-leaf types over heading ones. Light frost is tolerated, but cover plants with a frost blanket in colder weather. A general feed can go in at planting, with one extra dose of nitrogen while the plants grow; follow the label.
text.harvest: Allow about 50 to 80 days from sowing, leaf types being quicker. Leaf types can be picked as baby leaves about 5 to 8 cm long or when plants reach about 13 to 15 cm tall. Take the outer leaves first and leave the centre growing, or cut the whole plant at ground level. Heading types are cut once, as a whole head. Harvest before a flower stalk forms, because bolted leaves turn bitter. Store in the fridge: crisphead keeps about two to three weeks, while leaf and butterhead types keep roughly one to two weeks, and up to four if bagged dry.
common_mistakes: Sowing into hot soil, where seed germinates poorly.
Letting the soil dry out or swing between wet and dry, which pushes plants to bolt and can cause tipburn.
Overwatering or poor drainage, which encourages rots and leaf disease.
Growing heading types through hot weather instead of loose-leaf or slow-bolting ones.
Planting seed too deeply; this tiny seed needs only a light cover or none.

text.summary: Sweet alyssum is a low annual that forms spreading mounds covered in tiny, honey-scented flowers, mostly white but also pink, purple or lavender. It suits borders, pots and hanging baskets, grows in sun or part shade in well-drained soil, and draws bees, butterflies and other helpful insects.
text.how_to_plant: Sow the seed where it will grow, or raise seedlings in trays and plant them out later, or buy young plants; 6 to 8 weeks of indoor growth is one guide's figure. The seed needs light, so cover it only lightly, or leave it uncovered. Keep the soil at about 18 degrees C or warmer; seedlings usually show in about two weeks. Pick a spot with full sun or part shade and well-drained soil. Allow roughly 7 to 10 centimetres between plants. It also grows well in pots and hanging baskets.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moist but not soggy. Plants left wet or crowded can rot, so give them room and very good drainage. Do not feed heavily: rich soil gives leaves at the expense of flowers. When plants turn leggy or the first flush of flowers fades, shear them back to prompt new blooms. It is a hardy annual. Shade in the hottest part of the day helps in hot climates.
common_mistakes: Feeding heavily, which gives more leaves and fewer flowers.
Letting plants stay too wet or crowded, which can lead to rot.
Burying the seed deeply; it needs light to germinate.

text.summary: Lemon balm is a lemon-scented perennial herb in the mint family, grown for its edible leaves. It does well in sun or part shade, in moist, well-drained soil, in beds or large pots. It spreads freely, so control the flower stalks or grow it in a container.
text.how_to_plant: Pick a spot with full sun or part shade and moist, well-drained soil. New plants can come from divisions, stem cuttings or layering, and seed also works. Leave roughly 30 to 60 centimetres between plants, since clumps widen quickly. Because lemon balm spreads, a large pot is a good home: allow at least 10 litres for each plant. Plants raised from seed are ready for a first cut about 60 to 70 days after planting out.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moist but never soggy, because the plants suffer in soggy soil. Prune flowering stalks before they set seed to stop seedlings appearing, and cut plants back by about half to bring on fresh, vigorous growth; thin crowded stems to let air move through. A compact, sterile form does not set viable seed, which makes it easier to control. Growing in a container also helps hold it in check.
text.harvest: Cut stems as you need them, ideally before the plant flowers, taking about a third of the foliage at one time. Established plants can give two or three cuttings in a season. Fresh leaves have the strongest flavour and fragrance. To keep some, hang stems in a warm, dark, airy place, then strip the leaves and store them in a sealed container, or freeze the leaves.
common_mistakes: Letting flowering stalks set seed, so the plant seeds itself around the garden.
Overwatering: the soil should stay moist but not wet.
Leaving it unchecked in a mixed herb bed, where it can crowd out other herbs.

text.summary: Mint, here spearmint, is a vigorous perennial herb grown for its leaves. It spreads fast by underground runners, so most guides advise a container or a confined bed. It copes with sun or part shade, likes evenly moist soil, and is sensitive to frost. Cuttings and divisions are the easiest way to get new plants.
text.how_to_plant: Most gardeners start mint from a rooted cutting, a division of an established clump, or a bought plant, because seedlings grown from seed often differ from the parent. Seed, if you use it, sprouts in 10 to 14 days. Choose sun or part shade and well-drained soil. Space plants roughly 30 to 45 cm apart. Grow them in a pot of at least 10 litres, or in a bed with the roots confined, so they cannot spread through the garden.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy, because too much water encourages root and leaf diseases. Water early in the day, or use drip irrigation, so leaves are not wet overnight, which invites rust. Pinch shoot tips and cut back often to keep growth bushy, and remove flower spikes to hold the leaf flavour. Divide crowded plants every three to four years. Watch for runners creeping over the pot rim and trim them. At the end of the season, cutting plants right back discourages pests and disease.
text.harvest: Start picking once plants stand about 8 to 10 cm tall, taking leaves or leafy stem tips whenever you need them. Frequent cutting encourages bushy new growth. Leaves taste strongest just before the plant flowers, which is the best time to cut for drying. Fresh mint keeps about a week in the fridge with the stems in water. Dry stems in a shaded, airy place, or freeze chopped leaves in water in an ice cube tray.
common_mistakes: Planting it loose in a bed, where it spreads and crowds out other plants.
Overwatering or leaving the soil soggy, which invites root and leaf disease.
Leaving the leaves wet overnight, which favours rust.
Letting plants flower, which dulls the leaf flavour.
Expecting seed-grown plants to match the parent; mints hybridise, so use cuttings or divisions to keep a type.

text.summary: Banana is a large, leafy tropical plant that grows best in warm conditions. It wants full sun, shelter from wind, moist well-drained soil and generous feeding. Each stem fruits once and then dies, while suckers at its base carry the clump on.
text.how_to_plant: Bananas are usually started from suckers, the young shoots that rise beside an established plant. Take one once its stem is about 5 to 15 cm across and plant it at the same depth it was growing before. Pick a warm, frost-free spot with full sun, shelter from wind and well-drained soil. For fruit, leave roughly 2.4 to 3 metres between plants, since each mat will hold several stems of different ages. Mulch around the base to keep weeds down.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moist but never waterlogged, since banana will not tolerate standing water or poor drainage. Feed generously, because it is a hungry plant. Strong wind tatters the big leaves and can flatten a plant heavy with fruit, so keep the clump sheltered. Thin the suckers so a few stems of different ages stand in each mat, and cut each stem down once it has fruited, because it will not fruit again. Cut off torn leaves that droop down the trunk.
text.harvest: Cut the bunch when the fingers look full and rounded, rather than waiting for the fruit to ripen on the plant; it is green but mature at that point. Hands can also be picked one at a time, which spreads out the harvest. Finish ripening off the plant, in a cool, shaded place or indoors. Once the bunch is cut, remove the stem that carried it so a sucker can take over. If birds are a problem, a large open-ended bag over the bunch helps.
common_mistakes: Planting where strong wind reaches the clump, which tatters the leaves.
Letting water stand around the plant.
Leaving every sucker to grow instead of keeping a few stems of different ages.
Leaving a stem in place after it has fruited.
Letting the plant go short of water, which can make it slow to fruit.

text.summary: Sweet basil is a tender annual herb grown for its fragrant leaves. It needs warm soil and sun, is damaged by frost, and does well in beds and in pots. Pinching out the tips makes plants branch.
text.how_to_plant: Wait until the soil is warm; nights should stay above about 10 C. Pick a sunny spot with well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Sow seed only 3 to 6 mm deep; it usually sprouts in about 5 to 10 days, sometimes up to two weeks. Seed can also be started indoors three to six weeks before planting out. Space plants roughly 25 to 60 cm apart, with rows 45 to 90 cm apart. Compact types are well suited to pots.
text.how_to_care: Water at the base, with drip or by hand, so the leaves stay dry. This lowers the risk of downy mildew, as do sun, airflow and uncrowded plants. Pinch growing tips to make plants branch, and remove flower buds as they appear. Go easy on nitrogen feed, which can affect flavour. In hot spells a little afternoon shade helps. Protect plants on cold nights, since leaves blacken in the cold.
text.harvest: Start picking once a plant has six to eight leaves. Cut stems with clean scissors, leaving a few leaves on each stem, or pinch off tips or single leaves. Flavour is strongest when flower buds have formed but not opened. Removing tips makes plants branch. Fresh sprigs do not keep well, and sources disagree about the fridge. Drying or freezing keeps the surplus.
common_mistakes: Planting out too early, while frost or cold nights can still blacken the leaves.
Watering over the leaves or crowding plants, which favours downy mildew.
Heavy nitrogen feeding, which one source says affects flavour.

text.summary: Sweet marjoram is a mild, aromatic kitchen herb grown for its leaves and small flowers. It wants full sun and soil that drains freely, copes with dry spells once established, and suits pots as well as beds. Frost harms it, and it is usually grown as an annual.
text.how_to_plant: Sow the tiny seed indoors, scattered on top of the mix with only a thin dusting over it, since it needs light to sprout; a soak in water overnight beforehand is said to help. Seedlings usually show within one to two weeks. Raise them for about six to eight weeks before planting out. Pick a sunny spot with light, free-draining soil, such as a sandy loam, and set plants or thin seedlings about 20 centimetres apart. Marjoram also grows well in a container.
text.how_to_care: Give moderate water and make sure the soil drains freely, since the plant rots in wet, poorly drained ground. Once established it copes well with drought. Spread mulch around the plants to hold moisture. Trim plants as needed once they stand about 15 to 20 centimetres tall, and cut them back close to the ground when flowers begin to open to bring on fresh growth. Frost harms the plant, so lift garden plants and bring them indoors before frost arrives.
text.harvest: Pick leaves and stem tips as you need them, clipping stems cleanly; regular picking of tips encourages bushier growth. Aim to harvest when ball-like knots form at the stem ends and before the flowers open, when flavour is best. A second flush after a hard cut-back is often the better crop. Harvest can carry on until frost damages the plants. Use fresh, refrigerate wrapped in damp paper, freeze, or dry the stems and keep the dry leaves in sealed containers.
common_mistakes: Planting in soil that stays wet; marjoram rots in poorly drained ground.
Overwatering, which brings root rot and fungal disease.
Burying the seed, when it needs light to germinate.
Leaving plants out in frost.

text.summary: Oregano is an aromatic herb grown for its leaves and flowers. It likes full sun and soil that drains well, tolerates drought, and does well in pots. Start it from seed, or take cuttings from a plant with good flavour.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot with soil that drains freely; oregano needs good drainage, and wet ground does it no favours. Press seed onto the surface and leave it uncovered, since it needs light to sprout. Seedlings can appear in about four days in warm soil. Space or thin plants 20 to 50 centimetres apart. Seed-grown plants can differ from the parent, so cuttings from a plant with good flavour are the surer route. In a pot, allow about 30 centimetres of depth.
text.how_to_care: Oregano tolerates drought, but it needs good drainage, so avoid soil that stays wet. Spread organic mulch around the base of plants to hold moisture. Pinch back growing tips to encourage branching, snip off flowers to keep growth leafy, and cut out old, leggy wood to refresh growth. Replace plants that turn woody, roughly every three to four years.
text.harvest: Pick leaves and stems as you need them. Cut stem tips just above a few pairs of leaves so side shoots form. Flavour is best just before flowering, and letting plants flower slows growth, so harvest before the blooms open. To dry, cut whole stems, hang them in a cool, dry, dark, airy place, then strip the dry leaves and keep them in a sealed container. The flowers are edible too, with a milder taste than the leaves.
common_mistakes: Planting in wet or poorly drained soil, when the plant needs good drainage.
Letting plants flower freely, which slows leaf growth.
Relying on seed-raised plants when strong flavour matters, because they often differ from the parent.
Letting plants turn woody and leggy instead of cutting them back.

problems.name: Caterpillars
problems.signs: Small holes appear in the leaves and growth slows as the foliage is eaten; some caterpillars burrow into soft fruit and leave a small hole in the skin.
prevention: Scout the vines regularly
Remove eggs and caterpillars by hand
Protect fruit with exclusion netting or fruit bags

problems.name: Fruit flies
problems.signs: Small holes and woody lumps on the fruit, fruit that drops early or shrivels, and fruit that rots from the inside.
prevention: Remove overripe and fallen fruit promptly
Cover fruit with insect exclusion netting
Plant vines well away from other plants that host the flies

problems.name: Brown spot
problems.signs: Tiny grey spots on fruit that turn light brown, then dark brown with wrinkled centres; reddish-brown spots on leaves that drop after a few spots; dark stem lesions. It is worse in humid, wet weather.
prevention: Space and prune vines so air can move through them
Control weeds and keep the planting clean

problems.name: Fusarium wilt
problems.signs: Young plants show pale-green leaves, mild dieback, dropping lower leaves and general wilting; adult plants show yellowing young leaves, then wilting and death. Cut stems show brown tissue near the roots and collar.
prevention: Avoid planting where the disease has already struck
Plant disease-free seedlings
Avoid injuring stems and roots
Use resistant rootstock or purple-by-yellow hybrids where available

problems.name: Nematodes
problems.signs: Wilting, slower growth and malformed roots.
prevention: Choose yellow-fruited vines where nematodes are a problem
Avoid overwatering, and trellis and prune the vines

text.summary: Passion fruit is a fast-growing, evergreen climbing vine grown for its juicy fruit. It needs full sun, free-draining soil, a strong support to climb and a spot the frost cannot reach. Purple and yellow forms differ in how they pollinate and how they cope with disease.
text.how_to_plant: Pick a sunny, frost-free site with free-draining soil, sheltered from strong wind, and put up a sturdy trellis, fence or pergola first. Give each vine room to spread, roughly 0.9 to 2 metres from its neighbour. Set the plant with its roots only just below the surface rather than deep. Seed germinates slowly: rub the coat with fine sandpaper, soak it for a day, then sow about 1 cm deep in warm, moist seed mix and keep it out of direct sun. One-year-old stem cuttings with two to four nodes also root in a few months. A pot at least 50 cm wide can work, though the vine stays smaller.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil moist but never waterlogged, and keep water off the leaves. Mulch to hold moisture and hold back weeds. Go easy on nitrogen feeds, which push leaves at the expense of flowers; a feed boosted with potassium suits flowering and fruiting. Each year cut back up to a third of the previous year's growth, keep the main branches, and remove dead, diseased or damaged stems. Clear fallen leaves and fruit. Yellow-fruited vines need pollen from another vine to set fruit; if few bees visit, move pollen between flowers with a soft brush.
text.harvest: Let fruit ripen fully on the vine, then pick it when the skin has turned deep purple or yellow and looks plump; earlier fruit is more acidic and less aromatic. Ripe fruit also drops by itself, so gather fallen fruit regularly, since overripe fruit on the ground breeds fruit flies and picked-up fruit may be bruised. If you pick from the vine, clip each fruit with a short piece of stem attached.
common_mistakes: Planting with no strong support for the vine to climb.
Overwatering or letting the soil stay waterlogged.
Planting where frost can reach the vine.
Feeding heavily with nitrogen, which gives leaves instead of flowers.
Replanting in a spot where wilt has already killed a vine.

text.summary: Pentas is a fast-growing, frost-tender shrub grown for dense clusters of star-shaped flowers in red, pink, white, lavender and purple. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit the blooms. It likes full sun and well-drained soil, suits pots and garden beds, and can be started from seed or softwood cuttings.
text.how_to_plant: Pentas can be raised from seed or from softwood cuttings, which root readily in either soil or water. The seed needs light to germinate, so press it onto the surface of moist seed-starting mix and leave it uncovered. Keep the mix at about 21 to 24 degrees Celsius; seedlings usually show within one to three weeks. Plant out into a sunny spot with well-drained soil, or into a pot. Allow about 20 to 60 centimetres between plants; the wider end is the figure given for mass plantings in beds.
text.how_to_care: Grow pentas in full sun and feed it with a balanced fertilizer, avoiding heavy nitrogen. Keep watering at a moderate level, since soggy soil risks rot, and established plants cope with moderate dryness. Avoid shearing the plant into a tidy hedge, because heavy clipping cuts flower production; flowers form on new growth. Pentas is frost tender, and a freeze can cut the top growth back. Caterpillars occasionally chew the leaves, but pests are rarely a serious worry.
text.harvest: Pentas is grown for its blooms, so there is no crop to pick on a schedule. The dense, star-shaped flower clusters come in red, pink, white, lavender and purple, and butterflies and hummingbirds visit them. Stems can be cut and brought indoors for arrangements, where the flowers last roughly three to five days. Leave the plants unclipped, since flowers develop on new growth.
common_mistakes: Shearing pentas into a hedge, which cuts flower production.
Burying the seed, which needs light to germinate.
Treating pentas as hardy: it is frost tender and a freeze cuts the top growth back.

text.summary: Parsley is a leafy herb grown for its fresh leaves and usually treated as an annual, though it is really a biennial. Curled and flat-leaf types both suit full sun or part shade, fertile well-drained soil and a steady supply of moisture. The seed is slow to sprout, so patience at the start pays off.
text.how_to_plant: Soak the seed overnight to help it germinate, because parsley is slow to sprout. Sow it 5 to 12 mm deep, either where it will grow or in trays about nine weeks before planting out, and expect seedlings in two to four weeks. Choose fertile, well-drained soil in full sun or part shade. Thin the seedlings to roughly 15 to 40 cm apart, in rows 30 to 45 cm apart. Handle seedlings gently, since the taproot dislikes being disturbed. In a pot, use quality potting mix and a container of at least 40 litres.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy, as waterlogged ground can rot the roots. A layer of straw mulch helps hold moisture. A balanced fertiliser suits it. Leave room between plants so air can move and mildew is less likely. Pinch out flower stalks as soon as they show, to keep leaves coming. The plant is hardy in the cold, but long spells above about 32 degrees Celsius slow growth sharply, so give some afternoon shade in hot climates. It can also be grown indoors.
text.harvest: Snip stems and leaves as you need them, taking no more than a third of the plant at once so it keeps growing. Stems are ready when they carry about three leaf segments and the leaves are dark green. For a larger amount, cut the whole plant. Fresh sprigs stay good standing in a container of water out of direct sun, or wrapped in a bag in the refrigerator. Leaves can also be dried and kept in an airtight container. Handling the plant and then standing in strong sun can irritate skin.
common_mistakes: Letting the soil stay waterlogged, which can rot the roots.
Planting too thickly, which cuts airflow and invites mildew.
Leaving flower stalks on the plant, which shortens the harvest.
Sowing too early in cold weather, which can push first-year plants to flower.
Moving seedlings roughly, when the taproot should be disturbed as little as possible.

text.summary: Petunia is a fast-growing garden annual grown for a long show of funnel-shaped, fragrant flowers in many colours. It wants full sun and free-draining soil and suits beds, pots and hanging baskets. Types range from compact to widely spreading. The seed is very fine and needs light to sprout.
text.how_to_plant: Raise petunias from seed in trays or pots, or buy short, compact young plants. The seed is very fine and needs light to sprout, so leave it on the surface or cover it by 3 millimetres at most. Keep the mix at about 21 to 28 degrees C; seedlings usually appear within 5 to 15 days. Start seed about 8 to 10 weeks before planting out. Choose full sun and free-draining, light soil. Space plants roughly 15 to 45 centimetres apart; spreading types need much more room. One plant in a container needs a pot of at least 10 litres.
text.how_to_care: Petunias flower best in full sun. Water so the soil stays moist while draining well; established plants cope with some dry spells, yet too much water makes them leggy. Keep leaves and flowers dry when watering, which helps prevent disease. Feed with a balanced fertiliser. Pinch back young plants to encourage branching. Watch for aphids, grey mould and, on seedlings, damping off; throw out plants badly infested with cyclamen mites. Mature plants survive a light frost.
common_mistakes: Covering the very fine seed deeply; it needs light, so leave it on the surface or under no more than 3 mm.
Giving too much water, which makes plants leggy.
Wetting leaves and flowers when watering, which invites disease.

Bean, green bean, snap bean, string bean, kidney bean, Phaseolus and legume are absent from the UGA C1245 toxic lists (s13, not a complete list) and from the Illinois Plants and Pet Safety list (s14, not all inclusive). Both list 'Castor Bean(s)', which is Ricinus communis, a different species (rule 38). NC State Toolbox skipped (pending O-19). Absence is not evidence of safety.

Bean, green bean, snap bean, string bean, kidney bean, Phaseolus and legume are absent from the Utah Poison Control web list (s11) and from both the toxic and non-toxic lists of the Utah brochure (s12). Only 'Castor Bean' (Ricinus) and 'Sweet Pea' (Lathyrus) appear, both different species (rule 38). That beans are eaten as food is not a toxicity finding.

problems.name: Mexican bean beetle
problems.signs: Rounded coppery or tan beetles marked with black spots, plus yellow egg clusters under the leaves. Their larvae chew leaves and pods and harm small plants most.
prevention: Pick off beetles, larvae and egg clusters by hand
Cover early plantings with floating row cover to keep beetles off
Clear crop residue after harvest to stop numbers building up

problems.name: Aphids and mites
problems.signs: Leaves wilt, dry out or become discoloured where these pests feed. Aphids can also spread bean mosaic virus.
prevention: Wash them off with a strong jet of water
Encourage predatory insects

problems.name: Seed rot, root rot and damping off
problems.signs: Seeds rot in cold soil. Seedlings darken, wilt and die, usually in cool, wet conditions.
prevention: Sow only once the soil is warm
Let the soil dry between waterings
Keep the soil well drained
Rotate crops

problems.name: Bean blight
problems.signs: Small water-soaked spots that grow into large patches on stems, leaves and pods.
prevention: Water carefully and let the soil dry between waterings

problems.name: Bean mosaic virus
problems.signs: Yellow blotches and distorted leaves.
prevention: Choose varieties resistant to bean common mosaic virus
Keep aphids down, as they spread it
Pull out affected plants

problems.name: Blossom drop
problems.signs: Flowers fall without setting pods during hot or dry spells; pods usually set again as days cool.
prevention: Keep soil moisture even while plants flower

text.summary: Green or snap bean is a frost-tender annual grown for its young, tender pods. It comes as low bush types and taller climbing pole types, and it is sown straight into warm soil where it will grow. Both like full sun and well-drained soil, and the pods are picked while still young.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed directly in the garden once frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed to at least about 15.6 degrees C; seed germinates in roughly 6 to 15 days. Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil. Sow about 0.6 to 5 cm deep. Space bush types roughly 5 to 30 cm apart in rows about 60 to 90 cm apart, and climbing types roughly 10 to 20 cm apart in rows about 60 to 90 cm apart. Climbing types need a trellis, tripod or stakes; bush types usually stand alone. Transplants are not recommended, because the roots dislike disturbance. Sow again every 1.4 to 3 weeks for a steady supply.
text.how_to_care: Water with most care while plants flower and set pods. Avoid waterlogged soil, which invites root rot, and avoid splashing the leaves. Mulch around the plants to hold moisture and hold back weeds. Heavy nitrogen feeding delays flowering and cuts pod set, so go easy. Hot spells above about 32 degrees C can make blossoms drop. Pick pods often to keep plants producing.
text.harvest: Pick snap beans while the pods are young, firm and tender, before the seeds swell enough to bulge or show through. A ready pod snaps cleanly when bent. Guides give about 50 to 60 days from sowing to the first picking for bush types and about 55 to 110 days for climbing types. Picking lasts about 2 to 3 weeks on bush types and about 5 to 6 weeks on climbing types. Picking often keeps plants cropping, while pods left to mature slow later production. Fresh pods keep in the fridge for about a week and can be frozen for longer.
common_mistakes: Sowing before frost has passed or into cold soil, where seed rots or germinates poorly.
Letting pods grow too large before picking, so they turn tough and the seeds bulge.
Overwatering or leaving the soil waterlogged, which encourages root rot.
Feeding too much nitrogen, which delays flowering and reduces pod set.
Transplanting seedlings, because beans dislike root disturbance.

fields.value: Shelling peas: pick when the pods are plump and well filled but still crisp, before the seeds turn starchy or hard. Snow peas: pick while the pods are large and flat, before the seeds begin to swell. Snap peas: pick once the pods have sized up and are good to eat.
fields.note: s3 plump pods before the seed becomes starchy, and flat pods before the seed enlarges; s5 snow and snap peas ready when pods are large enough to eat, shelling peas when pods are full and plump but crisp; s8 garden peas before the seed fills the pod and hardens, snow peas picked before the seeds develop, while pods are flat; s6 harvest once peas are plump.

fields.value: Pick snow and snap pods every day or two, before they turn fibrous.
fields.note: s8 pick sugar or snow peas daily before they become fibrous; s6 you may be picking every 2 to 3 days. s4 says check plants often and you may have to pick every day.

Fridge: s3 vented plastic bag, s4 perforated bag in the crisper, s5 whole pods or shelled peas short term, s8 coldest part of the fridge. Freeze: s4, s5 blanched shelled peas, s8 shell and freeze surplus. Dry: s4 lists dehydrating (drying) among long-term preservation methods for garden peas (rule 125c), one source, no rival. Not mapped: s4's fermenting (not pickling, rule 125c) and canning (not in the enum). s1's 'sealed containers in a cool dry place' is for dry peas, outside this file.

Pea, garden pea, snow pea, sugar snap, English pea, Pisum and legume are absent from the UGA C1245 toxic lists (s14, not a complete list) and from the Illinois Plants and Pet Safety list (s15, not all inclusive). Sweet pea (Lathyrus) is not listed either. NC State Toolbox skipped (pending O-19). Absence is not evidence of safety.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: White, powdery patches show on the older leaves and spread upwards, and in bad cases cover the whole plant.
prevention: Water early in the day so the leaves dry before evening
Avoid overcrowding and stake tall types so air moves through the plants
Mulch around the plants
Grow early-maturing or resistant varieties

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Green to pinkish insects cluster on the underside of leaves near new growth.
prevention: Wash them off with a strong jet of water
Grow virus-resistant varieties
Avoid over-feeding, which increases their numbers

problems.name: Pea weevil
problems.signs: A small brownish or greyish beetle with light markings on its back. Its larvae feed inside the peas and leave circular chambers, with an opaque window visible on dry seed.
prevention: Start from clean, uninfested seed, which is the main way the pest spreads
Sow and pick early, which reduces exposure

problems.name: Black spot and foot rot
problems.signs: Small purple spots form on the leaves and may enlarge and blacken, and affected leaves often die. Stems, flowers and pods can be spotted, and young plants may die from damage at the soil line.
prevention: Grow in well-drained soil in a sunny spot
Support the plants on a trellis
Use clean seed
Remove and destroy infected crop remains
Avoid planting peas in the same spot the following season

problems.name: Fusarium wilt
problems.signs: Plants yellow from the bottom upwards, wilt and may be stunted, and leaves curl downward while stems turn brittle. Inside the root and lower stem the tissue is discoloured, brick red in one guide and yellow-orange in another.
prevention: Start from healthy seed
Keep peas out of the same bed for as long as you can
Grow resistant varieties and sow early, so the crop develops before the soil warms up

problems.name: Seed rot and root rot
problems.signs: Seeds rot in cold soil, and seedlings are stunted with yellowing lower leaves.
prevention: Improve soil drainage
Avoid compacted or wet soil

text.summary: Pea is a cool-season annual grown for its seeds, or for the whole pod in snow and snap types. It likes full sun and well-drained soil, tolerates light frost and is sown straight into the garden. Tall types climb a trellis, while dwarf types stay low. Hot weather makes the flowers drop.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where it will grow, in a sunny spot with well-drained soil, once the soil has reached 4.4 degrees C. Seed sprouts in roughly 7 to 35 days, slowest in cold soil. Sow about 1.3 to 5 cm deep and 2.5 to 20 cm apart in the row, with rows from 20 cm to well over a metre apart, wider where a trellis will stand. Put the trellis up at sowing for tall types. Transplants are usually not advised. Sow again every 2 to 5 weeks to spread the harvest.
text.how_to_care: Hold moisture steady, with no heavy soaking while the plants are in flower, and water at the base or early in the day so the leaves dry before evening. Mulch to save moisture and hold back weeds. Go easy on nitrogen, which pushes leaf growth at the cost of pods. Tall types need a trellis, a cage or a fence, while dwarf types may manage alone. Hot spells above about 27 degrees C can make flowers fall. Leave one to four years before peas return to the same bed.
text.harvest: Pick shelling peas when the pods are plump and full but still crisp, before the seeds turn starchy. Snow peas are picked while the pods are flat and the seeds tiny, and snap peas once the pods have sized up; check these every day or two. Guides give roughly 50 to 112 days from sowing to the first picking, with cropping that runs for about 3 to 10 weeks. Fresh pods keep in the fridge, and shelled peas freeze well.
common_mistakes: Letting plants flower in hot weather, when the flowers drop and pods fail to set; sow early so pods form while it is still cool.
Feeding too much nitrogen, which gives lush leaves but poor flowering and few pods.
Picking snow and snap peas late, after the pods have gone fibrous.
Soaking the plants heavily while they flower, which can interfere with pollination.
Crowding plants or wetting the leaves late in the day.

text.summary: Moss rose is a low-growing annual grown for bright, many-coloured flowers that open in strong sun. It likes full sun and free-draining soil, copes well with heat and dry spells, and suits pots and hanging baskets as well as beds. It is damaged by frost.
text.how_to_plant: Pick a spot in full sun with light, free-draining soil. Pots and hanging baskets suit it too. Cover the tiny seed with only about 3 millimetres of fine soil. Sow once the soil has warmed to about 23 degrees C. Seedlings usually appear in about 10 to 14 days. They do not like being moved, so handle them with care. Thin seedlings to about 8 centimetres apart or more; for a solid ground cover, space plants up to about 30 centimetres apart.
text.how_to_care: Give it the sunniest spot you have. Established plants cope well with heat and dry spells. Wet soil can rot stems and roots, so grow it where water drains away freely. The flowers open in bright sun and close on cloudy days and toward evening. Watch for aphids and mealybugs: wash aphids off with a strong spray of water, and rinse mealybugs under running water, rubbing them off by hand. Frost ends the season for these plants.
common_mistakes: Planting in poorly drained soil, which can rot stems and roots.

problems.name: Fruit flies
problems.signs: Fly larvae feed inside the fruit, leaving spots on the skin, and infested fruit is usually unfit to eat.
prevention: Cover developing fruit with a paper bag once it is about 2.5 cm across
Wrap developing fruit in netting, ideally after all the petals have dropped

problems.name: Anthracnose
problems.signs: Young leaves show large, irregular dead spots, and fruit develops round brown to black spots that grow bigger over time. Stems may die back and leaves may drop.
prevention: Prune to open the tree to light and air movement
Choose a sunny, well-drained position with good airflow
Water the soil at the base rather than the leaves
Thin crowded stems so light and air reach the middle of the plant

problems.name: Red alga spot
problems.signs: Circular reddish to purplish-brown spots appear on leaves, and young fruit and stems can be marked too. A severe attack causes leaf and fruit drop and a loss of vigour.
prevention: Prune to open the tree to light and air movement

problems.name: Cold damage
problems.signs: Cold can damage or kill stems, limbs and the trunk, and young trees can be killed. Leaves may drop in cold weather.
prevention: Plant in the warmest part of the landscape

problems.name: Heat stress
problems.signs: Leaves wilt during hot weather.
prevention: Water more often in hot weather
Mulch the base of the plant to cut water loss

problems.name: Nematodes
problems.signs: Roots are attacked, and the tree loses vigour, is stunted, wilts and yellows, with stem dieback and, in bad cases, death.
prevention: Avoid planting guava where severe nematode problems are known

text.summary: Guava is an evergreen fruit tree. It needs full sun and well-drained soil and is frost tender. It grows large but can be kept smaller by pruning or a big pot. Seedlings do not come true, so buy a container-grown tree. It can escape and spread in some regions, so check local rules.
text.how_to_plant: Buy a healthy container-grown tree. Raising one from seed gives fruit unlike the parent. Avoid a large tree in a small pot, as its roots are likely to be tightly bound. Choose the warmest, sunniest spot, where soil drains well and does not stay wet, and keep clear of other trees, buildings and power lines, allowing roughly 4.6 to 7.6 m. Dig a hole about three to four times as wide as the container and set the tree so the top of its root ball sits at or just above the soil around it. In a pot, one source says at least 600 mm wide, another at least 1 m deep; use a loamy mix.
text.how_to_care: Guava has a medium water need and tolerates short dry spells once established, but water in dry periods around flowering and fruit development. Do not let water stand around the roots, which can cause rot. Prune lightly each year to hold the size and open the canopy to light and air. Spread mulch 5 to 15 cm deep, keeping it 20 to 30 cm from the trunk. Keep mowers and trimmers away from the trunk. Bag young fruit to keep fruit flies out.
text.harvest: Harvest by type. Pink and red types are picked when the peel turns from light green to yellow, then left at room temperature to soften. White types are usually eaten while still green to light green and crisp. Ripe fruit gives slightly under a gentle press and smells strongly sweet. Ripe and green fruit can both be kept in the fridge for 5 to 7 days.
common_mistakes: Buying a large tree in a small pot, whose roots are likely to be bound.
Growing guava from seed and expecting fruit like the parent tree.
Hitting the trunk with a mower or trimmer.
Planting where the ground floods or stays wet.
Heavy lawn feeding or timed sprinklers near the tree, which can reduce fruiting or cause decline.

text.summary: Radish is a root crop sown straight into the ground. It likes a sunny spot with loose, well-drained soil and little feeding, and it also suits containers. Roots are ready roughly 20 to 60 days after sowing, and repeat sowings every week or two keep them coming. Avoid hot weather and swings between wet and dry soil.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed straight into the ground where the plants will grow. Seed can go in once the soil reaches about 4 degrees C, and it comes up best between roughly 7 and 30 degrees C, usually within 3 to 14 days. Sow about 0.5 to 1.3 cm deep, in rows 20 to 61 cm apart, and thin the seedlings; guides give final gaps from a few centimetres up to about 20 cm. Pick a sunny spot with loose, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil, rich in organic matter, at a pH of about 6 to 6.8. Radishes also grow well in containers. Sow a little more seed every week or two for a steady supply.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist: swings between dry and wet split the roots, and slow growth makes them woody and hot-tasting. Radishes need little feeding, and extra nitrogen grows leaves at the expense of roots. Mulch around the plants to hold moisture. A floating row cover keeps flea beetles and root maggots off, netting keeps caterpillars away, and a collar around each seedling stops cutworms. Grow radishes in a different spot each year. Hot weather pushes plants to flower and makes roots woody, so avoid sowing in very hot weather.
text.harvest: Pull the whole plant while the roots are still small, about 2.5 cm across or less, then trim off the tops. Expect the first roots roughly 20 to 60 days after sowing, depending on the type and the weather. Left too long, roots turn pithy, woody and hot-tasting, and they may crack. Refrigerate them in a bag; guides give anywhere from about 5 days to 4 weeks. The leaves and young seed pods can be eaten too.
common_mistakes: Letting the soil swing between dry and wet, which cracks and splits the roots.
Leaving radishes in the ground too long, so the roots turn pithy, hot and woody.
Sowing in hot weather, which brings flower stalks and woody roots.
Feeding with too much nitrogen, which grows leaves instead of roots.
Sowing too thickly and not thinning, which gives small roots.

text.summary: Rosemary is an evergreen, fragrant herb that grows as a perennial shrub. It wants full sun and light, well-drained soil, copes with dry spells once settled, and does well in pots or in the ground. It is best started from cuttings, as seed is slow and unreliable.
text.how_to_plant: Start from a rooted cutting, which succeeds more often than seed. Seed is slow and uneven, usually sprouting within two to four weeks if you do try it. Pick a spot with at least six hours of sun and light, sandy or loamy, well-drained soil with a pH of about 6 to 7. A raised or slightly mounded bed drains best. Sources suggest anywhere from 20 to 150 centimetres between plants. In a pot, give each plant at least 20 litres.
text.how_to_care: Rosemary is easy to overwater, so allow the soil to dry between waterings and never leave a pot standing in water. Once established it copes well with dry spells. It seldom needs feeding, and too much fertiliser cuts flowering and fragrance. Prune after flowering to keep it neat, and pinch the tips of young plants to shape them. Leave space between plants so air can move and mildew stays away. A healthy plant tolerates a light freeze; where winters are harsher, grow it in a pot and bring it to a sunny indoor spot before the first frost.
text.harvest: Cut sprigs or leafy tips as you need them once the plant has grown large enough, taking no more than about a fifth of the growth at a time and letting it recover between pickings. Use the leaves fresh, keep cut stems in the fridge, hang bundles to dry, or slice and freeze them. Dried leaves keep well in an airtight container.
common_mistakes: Overwatering, which is the biggest cause of decline and death.
Planting in wet, poorly drained clay soil.
Crowding plants so air cannot move between them, which invites powdery mildew.
Counting on seed, which germinates slowly, unevenly and often poorly.
Over-fertilising, which reduces flowering and fragrance.

text.summary: Pineapple sage is a fast-growing, tender perennial with upright stems, leaves that smell of pineapple when crushed, and red flowers that draw hummingbirds. The leaves and flowers can both be eaten. It likes sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil, and grows well in a container.
text.how_to_plant: New pineapple sage plants can be raised from stem cuttings. Choose a sunny place with moist, well-drained soil, and leave room for a clump that can spread roughly 0.9 to 1.2 metres wide. Pick a spot sheltered from wind, because the tall stems can snap at the base. Avoid positions lit by street lights at night, which can stop it flowering. It also grows well in a pot, which is easy to move under cover when the weather turns cold.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist all season, because dry soil makes the plants wilt, the leaves curl, and then drop. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and a denser shape. Cut out old, woody shoots once new growth appears. Where winters are cold, grow it in a container and move it indoors before the cold arrives. It flowers as the days shorten, so keep it away from lights that stay on at night.
text.harvest: Both the leaves and the flowers can be eaten. Pick them fresh and use them whole as garnishes, or add them to salads, desserts and herbal teas, or to jams and jellies. The flowers have a fruity sweetness with a minty, spicy edge, and crushing a leaf releases a pineapple scent. Blooms keep coming until frost, so flowers stay available for picking over a long stretch.
common_mistakes: Letting the soil dry out, which makes the plant wilt and drop its leaves.
Growing it under street lights or other night lighting, which can stop it flowering.
Leaving tall stems exposed to strong wind, where they can break at the base.

The brochure's 'Latana Camara (Red Sage)' is Lantana camara, a different plant, and is not counted (rule 38). The NC State Toolbox page (s4) has no poison fields; it says the edible flowers should not be eaten in large amounts, which is a caution, not a classification (reading question Q5). text.summary: Sage is a woody, evergreen perennial herb with aromatic, edible leaves. It likes full sun and very well-drained soil, and grows in the ground or in pots. Start it from seed, cuttings or divisions, or buy young plants, and replace plants every few years as they turn woody.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot with loamy or sandy soil that is very well-drained, because sage should not sit wet over winter. Sow seed about 5 millimetres deep, either in place or in trays to move later; seedlings usually appear within one to three weeks at a soil temperature of 18 to 21 degrees Celsius. Space plants about 45 to 60 centimetres apart. Cuttings, divisions and young nursery plants are alternatives to seed. In a pot, allow at least 10 litres for each plant.
text.how_to_care: Water only when the soil has dried out. Prune lightly during the growing season and trim after flowering to keep plants tidy and stop them becoming leggy, but do not cut into old woody stems, which seldom shoot again. Plants turn sparse and woody with age, so replace them every three to four years. Space plants so air moves between them, and water at soil level rather than over the leaves.
text.harvest: Pick leaves as you need them, or cut stems about 15 to 20 centimetres long, and never take more than half the plant at a time. Leaves are best picked before the plant flowers. Harvest lightly from a new plant until it has settled in. Dry leaves keep in the fridge, loosely packed in plastic. For longer storage, dry the leaves or freeze them.
common_mistakes: Planting in soil that does not drain freely, especially where it stays wet over winter.
Cutting back into old woody stems, which seldom shoot again.
Taking more than half the plant in one cut.
Keeping an old, woody plant instead of replacing it every few years.

text.summary: Dragon fruit is a fast-growing climbing cactus with fragrant white flowers and scaly-skinned fruit. It needs full sun, very free-draining soil and a sturdy frame or trellis to climb, and it does best where frost never comes. You can start it from stem cuttings or from seed.
text.how_to_plant: Pick a roomy, sunny site with free-draining soil, 3 to 6 m or more from other plants, trees and buildings, and put up a strong post with a frame on top first. For a cutting, take a stem segment about 12 to 50 cm long from a healthy plant, let the cut end dry and callus, then root it 2 to 3 cm deep in a small pot before moving it out. Seed sprouts within about two weeks on damp paper in a warm, shaded spot. For a large pot, use cactus mix and a container of at least 75 litres.
text.how_to_care: Water periodically, more steadily from flowering through harvest, but never let the soil stay soggy, because too much moisture causes rot. Feed with a fruit fertiliser that is rich in potassium. Mulch with bark or wood chips 5 to 15 cm deep, kept 20 to 30 cm from the stem. Tie the main stems to the support, remove side shoots until the plant reaches the height you want, then cut the tips so it branches. As needed, take out dead, damaged or crowded stems and any that reach the soil. Keep mowers and trimmers away from the base.
text.harvest: Pick a fruit when the scales or wings on its skin look slightly withered, about four weeks after the flower opened, and only when it is well coloured and full size. Cut it from the plant with clippers, trimming the stalk flush with the fruit. The fruit does not ripen further once picked, so do not pick early. Whole fruit keeps for several days at room temperature, or for weeks in a bag in the fridge. Too much moisture while fruit forms can split it.
common_mistakes: Planting in poorly draining soil.
Overwatering, which leads to stem and root rot.
Picking fruit early, because it does not ripen after picking.
Using a weak trellis or bare wire, which cannot carry the plant or can cut the stems.
Letting a mower or line trimmer hit the stem base.

text.summary: Tomato is a warm-season fruiting vegetable that needs plenty of sun and frost-free weather. Bush types stay compact and ripen most fruit together, while vine types keep growing and need support. Small types suit large pots. Even watering protects the fruit, and very hot nights can stop large types from setting it.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil rich in organic matter, at a pH of about 6.0 to 6.8. Sow seed 5 to 8 mm deep. Sow where it will grow only in warm regions, where soil and nights stay warm; otherwise raise seedlings in pots first. Plant out only once frost danger has passed. Set each plant deeper than it sat in its pot, so only the top few leaf sets show. Allow 30 to 120 cm between plants, closer for dwarf types and wider for vigorous or caged vines, and at least 60 cm between rows. Avoid soil where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant or potatoes grew in the last three years.
text.how_to_care: Water thoroughly and evenly, and avoid swings between drought and soaking. Uneven watering causes cracked fruit and blossom end rot, so spread a mulch of straw, chopped leaves or compost to hold moisture. Support vine types with stakes, cages or a trellis; bush types also do best staked or caged. On staked plants, remove side shoots so only a few main stems remain. Begin feeding when you plant out, then keep topping up during the growing season as the product label directs.
text.harvest: Expect the first fruit roughly 55 to 90 days after planting out, depending on the variety. Start picking as soon as colour begins to change; this cuts cracking, splitting and insect damage and gives more usable fruit. You can instead leave fruit on the vine until fully coloured but still firm, which gives the best flavour. Vine types keep cropping until the first frost, while bush types give most of their crop in one burst, so plan for a glut.
common_mistakes: Planting out before frost danger has passed, which injures the top growth.
Watering unevenly, which brings blossom end rot and split fruit.
Planting shallow instead of burying the stem so only a few leaf sets show.
Growing tomatoes again in soil that held tomatoes, peppers, eggplant or potatoes within three years.

text.summary: Eggplant is a warm-season fruiting vegetable that wants full sun, fertile well-drained soil and a long stretch of warm weather. It is tender to frost and sets fruit poorly when nights are cool. Most gardeners start with transplants. Small and dwarf types suit pots, and most plants need a stake or cage.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny site with fertile, well-drained soil, ideally sandy loam enriched with compost, at about pH 5.5 to 7.2. Germinate seed indoors at a soil temperature near 21 to 32 C, covering it with only about half a centimetre of mix, then grow the seedlings on for 6 to 10 weeks in all. Seedlings usually show in one to two weeks. Plant out only when frost danger has passed and the soil and nights are warm, since cool conditions stunt the plants. Space plants about 46 to 91 cm apart in rows 60 to 120 cm apart, and set a stake or cage in at planting. In pots, pick a large one and a compact type.
text.how_to_care: Water steadily and deeply rather than often, and keep the soil moist through flowering and fruit development, because dry spells then cut flowering and fruit set. A drip line or soaker keeps the leaves dry. Once the soil is warm, mulch to hold moisture. Set plants against their support as they grow, and pinch out the growing tip when young plants are about 30 cm tall so they branch. Give a starter feed at planting and a second feed once fruit appears, following the product label. Rotate crops to limit wilt.
text.harvest: Expect the first fruit about 50 to 80 days after planting out, depending on the variety; plants grown from seed all the way take longer. Pick while the skin is glossy and the fruit is firm, before it dulls or yellows. For the usual large type that is roughly 15 to 20 cm long. Cut the stem with pruners or a knife, and wear gloves because the stem can be spiny. Picking often encourages more fruit.
common_mistakes: Planting out before frost has passed or while the soil is still cold, which kills or stunts young plants.
Watering little and often instead of soaking deeply, which keeps roots shallow.
Leaving fruit on until the skin turns dull or yellow.
Laying organic mulch on cold soil before it has warmed.

text.summary: Potato is grown from seed potatoes, which are tubers, not from seed. It wants full sun, well-drained soil and a few months to crop, and frost can harm it. Soil is drawn up around the stems as the plants grow, so the new tubers stay covered and do not turn green.
text.how_to_plant: Start with certified disease-free seed potatoes rather than tubers saved from your own crop. Cut large tubers so each piece keeps at least one eye, and let the cut surfaces dry. Plant once the soil has warmed to about 15 C, 2.5 to 15 cm deep and roughly 13 to 51 cm apart, in rows at least 50 cm apart. Choose a sunny spot with well-drained soil. Whole tubers hold up better than cut pieces in hot soil. A large pot about 50 cm deep, with good drainage holes, can also work.
text.how_to_care: Draw soil up around the stems as they grow, so light cannot reach the tubers and turn them green and bitter. A thick straw mulch helps keep the soil cool and moist. Potatoes are hungry plants, but too much fertiliser grows leaves at the expense of tubers. Keep water off the leaves, which can spread fungal disease. Pick off beetles by hand. Keep potatoes, tomatoes and other family members out of the same bed for three to four years.
text.harvest: Full-size potatoes are usually ready about 80 to 120 days after planting, once the foliage has yellowed and died back. If you plan to store them, leave the tubers in the ground for a couple of weeks after the tops die, then dig gently with a fork when the soil is dry, taking care not to skin them. Cure them for two to three weeks, then keep them in a cool, dark place. Cut away small green patches and discard very green tubers.
common_mistakes: Saving your own tubers as seed potatoes, which builds up viruses and diseases.
Leaving tubers exposed to light, which turns them green and bitter.
Planting cut pieces into hot soil, where they decay more readily than whole tubers.
Fertilising heavily, which grows leaves rather than tubers.
Digging the crop while the soil is wet.

text.summary: Spinach is a frost-hardy leaf crop that forms a low rosette of dark green leaves, about 20 to 30 cm tall. It bolts, running up flower stalks, as days lengthen and temperatures rise. Sow it where it will grow in fertile, well-drained soil, keep it moist and pick the leaves while they are young.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed straight into the ground or a roomy pot, 0.8 to 1.3 cm deep, in fertile, well-drained soil that holds plenty of organic matter. Wait until the soil is at least about 7.2 degrees C, and use seed packed for the current year. Seedlings usually show in 5 to 10 days. Thin them once they stand about 2.5 cm tall, leaving plants roughly 5 to 35 cm apart. Rows can sit 30 to 91 cm apart. Sow again about every 2 weeks to keep leaves coming. A pot needs at least 20 litres.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist, watering deeply and regularly, because spinach grows best with plenty of water. It is a hungry crop, so dig in compost or fertiliser before sowing and feed again partway through the crop. Mulch holds moisture, keeps leaves clean and holds back weeds. Established plants shrug off frost. When days lengthen and the weather warms, plants send up flower stalks, so slow-bolting varieties are the better choice for warmer-weather crops. Give plants room, water at soil level and remove spotted leaves to limit downy mildew, and use row covers against leaf miners.
text.harvest: Pick individual leaves once a plant has about six true leaves, choosing tender dark green ones roughly 8 to 15 cm long. Cutting full-size leaves lets new ones grow from the centre. You can also cut whole plants at soil level, and late thinnings can be eaten. One guide gives about 28 to 55 days from sowing to a first picking. Once flower stalks appear, harvest what remains of the crop. Keep the leaves in a bag in the fridge.
common_mistakes: Growing the crop into warm weather and long days, which makes it bolt.
Letting the soil dry out; spinach wants steady moisture.
Leaving plants to run to seed instead of taking the rest of the crop once flower stalks form.
Crowding plants, which cuts air flow and invites downy mildew.
Sowing old seed, which loses viability quickly.

text.summary: African marigold is a tender annual grown for bold flowers in yellow, orange, cream and red on plants about 30 to 120 centimetres tall. It likes full sun and soil that drains well, and it suits pots. French and signet marigolds are smaller, separate species.
text.how_to_plant: Pick a spot that gets at least 6 hours of direct sun, with soil that drains well and is slightly acidic to neutral. Start seed indoors, sowing it about half a centimetre deep, and plant out seedlings about 8 weeks old. Seed sprouts in roughly 4 to 10 days when the soil is warm, around 24 to 28 degrees C. Space plants 20 to 40 centimetres apart. In a pot, allow at least 20 litres for each plant and use a free-draining mix.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged. Tall types may need a stake or a spot sheltered from strong wind and heavy rain. The sap and flowers can irritate skin, especially in sunlight, so handle them with care. Watch young growth for slugs and snails, and watch leaves for powdery mildew. Water at soil level and keep air moving between plants.
text.harvest: African marigold is grown for its flowers rather than as a harvest crop, so there is no single picking window. Blooms keep opening over a long season. Handle the flowers and sap with care: they can cause a skin rash, particularly where skin is broken and then exposed to sun.

Thyme, Thymus, Thymus vulgaris and Lamiaceae are absent from the UGA C1245 list (s11, 27 names; it says it is not a complete list) and from the Illinois Plants and Pet Safety list (s12, read as PDF; it says it is not all inclusive). The NC State Toolbox page (s5) has no poison fields; its tags say non-toxic for cats and dogs, which is one positive source and non_toxic needs two (rules 36, 143g). Absence is not evidence of safety.

Thyme, Thymus, Thymus vulgaris and Lamiaceae are absent from the Utah Poison Control web list (s9, 35 names) and from both the toxic and the non-toxic lists of the Utah brochure (s10, read as PDF; its toxic list is not necessarily comprehensive). The NC State Toolbox page (s5) has no poison fields and no people tag. That thyme is eaten as a herb is not a safety finding (rule 36).

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.signs: Yellow to grey-brown patches appear on the leaves, most often on the undersides.
prevention: Water the soil, not the leaves
Remove and destroy affected leaves
Do not overcrowd plants, so air can move between them

problems.name: Fusarium and verticillium wilt
problems.signs: Leaves and branches wilt and dry out, the plant can die, and leaves may turn yellow. Soil-borne fungi enter the roots and block water and nutrients.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties
Dispose of affected plants and the soil around them
Keep the garden clean and rotate crops

text.summary: Thyme is a small perennial herb with aromatic leaves. It likes full sun and light, well-drained soil, copes with dry spells once settled, and grows in pots or in the ground. Start it from seed, or divide or take cuttings from an established plant.
text.how_to_plant: Pick a sunny spot, with at least six hours of sun a day, and light, sandy or loamy soil that drains well. Poorly drained soil, especially over winter, shortens a plant's life. Sow seed very shallowly, about 3 to 13 millimetres deep, and expect seedlings in two to three weeks at a soil temperature of 18 to 21 degrees Celsius. Space or thin plants about 20 to 30 centimetres apart. Seed can germinate unevenly, so dividing an established clump or taking cuttings is easier. In a pot, allow at least 10 litres for each plant.
text.how_to_care: Once established, thyme needs little watering and no feeding, and the soil can stay on the dry side. Trim plants after flowering to keep them neat, and cut back leggy or woody growth so fresh shoots form. Every few years, cut older plants back hard to renew them. Give plants room, and water the soil rather than the leaves, so air can move through and downy mildew is less likely. Established plants tolerate frost.
text.harvest: Cut stems or leafy sprigs as you need them; pinching off outer growth and leaving some on the plant lets it keep producing. Cutting just before the plant flowers is the usual advice, and stems can be cut through the growing season. One seed company's figure is a first picking about 70 to 90 days after planting out. To store thyme, dry it until the leaves are crisp, strip them from the stems and keep them in a sealed container. Sprigs can also be frozen.
common_mistakes: Planting in poorly drained soil, especially where it stays wet over winter.
Overcrowding plants or watering the leaves, which invites downy mildew.
Never trimming or renewing the plant, so it turns woody and leggy.
Relying only on seed, which germinates unevenly.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Small sap-sucking insects crowd on new shoots or under the leaves, and plants wilt or discolour.
prevention: Hose insects off.
Encourage predatory insects.

problems.name: Caterpillars (cabbage white butterfly)
problems.signs: Holes chewed in the leaves.
prevention: Cover plants with netting.
Pick caterpillars off by hand.

problems.name: Thrips
problems.signs: Small white or clear marks on leaves and petals.
prevention: Hose insects off.
Welcome predatory mites and lacewings into the garden.

problems.name: Whitefly
problems.signs: Leaves turn yellow or wilt.
prevention: Hose insects off.
Remove badly affected plants.

text.summary: Nasturtium is a fast-growing annual grown for bright flowers and peppery edible leaves and blooms. Compact types stay low, while trailing and climbing types sprawl or scramble up supports. It likes sun and well-drained soil that is not too rich, and it suits pots.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot with soil that drains well and is not too rich. Sow the seeds where they will grow, about 1 to 1.5 centimetres deep, and cover them lightly. Seedlings usually appear in one to two weeks when the soil is about 16 to 20 degrees C. Space plants roughly 30 to 45 centimetres apart. For a pot, allow at least 20 litres. Tall types will need a stake or trellis, while dwarf forms stand on their own. Climbing types can be trained up a support or left to sprawl along the ground.
text.how_to_care: Nasturtium does best in soil that is not too fertile, so avoid enriching it heavily. Give it a sunny position, and stake the tall types. Aphids gather on new shoots and under the leaves; also watch for caterpillars, thrips and whitefly. Hosing insects off and covering plants with netting are simple, non-chemical ways to protect the leaves.
text.harvest: Pick leaves and flowers fresh for salads; both taste peppery, and young leaves and flowers are best. Harvesting can continue through the whole growing season. Flower buds and seed pods are edible too, and the pods can be pickled and used like capers.
common_mistakes: Planting in rich soil when the plant prefers well-drained soil that is not too fertile.

problems.name: Birds taking fruit
problems.signs: Birds strip the ripening berries, sometimes the whole crop from a small planting.
prevention: Cover the plants with netting, such as a light small-mesh plastic net over a frame, before the berries ripen

problems.name: Mummy berry
problems.signs: Berries shrivel, turn hard and tan, and drop early. Infected flowers turn brown and die.
prevention: Remove all mummified fruit from the planting every year

problems.name: Grey mould
problems.signs: Flowers and fruit rot, and green fruit can rot where hail has wounded it.
prevention: Avoid overhead watering during the growing season

problems.name: Root rot
problems.signs: Sections of the plant die, and whole plants die over time.
prevention: Plant in well-drained soil at least 45 cm deep
Plant on raised beds or mounded rows where drainage is poor

problems.name: Spotted wing drosophila
problems.signs: Larvae feed inside ripening berries, with little damage showing on the outside.
prevention: Cover the plants with fine-mesh netting before any fruit begins to colour

text.summary: Blueberry is a long-lived fruiting plant grown for sweet blue berries. It wants a sunny site and acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Types differ in size, chilling need and cold hardiness, so pick one that suits your climate. Most types fruit better with a second variety planted nearby.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a sunny spot with loose, well-drained, acidic soil that is rich in organic matter, and test the pH before you plant. Where drainage is poor, grow in a raised bed or mounded row. Buy nursery plants of a type suited to your climate and set at least two varieties close together. Plant each at the depth it grew in the nursery, soaking bare-root plants first, and cut the top back after planting. Leave generous room between plants, more for the larger types. In a pot, use an acidic mix and a wide, deep container. In the planting year, pick off the flowers so the plant puts its energy into growth.
text.how_to_care: Spread bark or a similar mulch in a ring around each plant or along the row, and keep the layer topped up. Water so the soil stays moist and never dries out, but avoid waterlogging, and water the soil rather than the leaves. Feed with a nitrogen fertiliser, following the product label, because heavy doses can harm the plants. Prune every year, cutting out the oldest canes to encourage new growth. Shelter plants from strong wind and cover them with netting to keep birds off the fruit.
text.harvest: Berries ripen a few at a time, so pick regularly, anywhere from every few days to every two weeks depending on the weather. Wait until each berry is blue all over with no green near the stem; they take a few days after colouring to sweeten and do not sweeten once picked. Ripe berries come away from the stem easily. Net the plants before the fruit colours. Berries keep in the refrigerator for a few weeks, depending on the variety, or freeze them in a single layer first.
common_mistakes: Letting young plants fruit in the planting year.
Planting where the soil is not acidic enough.
Giving heavy doses of fertiliser, which blueberries are easily damaged by.
Planting too deep, which can smother the roots.
Picking as soon as the berries first turn blue, before they have sweetened.

text.summary: Yardlong bean, also called snake bean or asparagus bean, is an annual climbing vine grown for its very long pods. It needs a strong trellis, a sunny spot and free-draining soil. Insects pollinate the flowers, and the young pods are picked often while the seeds inside are still small.
text.how_to_plant: Put up a strong, tall trellis first, because the vines can reach about 2.7 to 3.7 metres. Sow seed in the spot where it will grow, about 2.5 to 5 cm deep, with vines roughly 10 to 30 cm apart along the support (spacing given for the 'Black Seeded' type). Choose a sunny site with free-draining loam or clay and a soil pH of about 5.5 to 6.5, and make a raised bed if drainage is poor. Seedlings usually appear in about 6 to 14 days. Seedlings raised elsewhere can be set out once they have two true leaves.
text.how_to_care: Keep the vines on a sturdy trellis. Avoid soggy ground and frost, since both hold growth back and wet roots can rot. The crop copes with drought, but very humid weather can bring powdery mildew. Thin crowded vines so air moves through them, keep water off the leaves and cut away leaves that are badly infected. Do not overfeed once plants are growing. Bees and other insects pollinate the flowers. Yellowing, wilting plants in wet soil point to root rot, so improve drainage.
text.harvest: From sowing, first pods are ready after roughly 40 to 90 days, depending on location. Pick the pods young, while the seeds inside are still immature, when they are about 25 to 30 cm long; young pods are the most tender. Pick by hand often, even daily. For dried beans, leave some pods on the vine until the seeds are fully developed and mature.
common_mistakes: Letting the soil stay waterlogged, which slows growth and can rot roots.
Growing it where frost can reach it.
Skipping a strong, tall trellis.
Over-fertilising once plants are growing.
Leaving pods until the seeds are fully mature when tender pods are wanted.

text.summary: Southern pea, also called cowpea or black-eyed pea, is a frost-tender annual grown from seed sown straight into warm soil. It likes full sun, copes well with dry spells and has a low feeding need. Plants come as bush or vining types, and the peas are picked fresh for shelling or left to dry.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed where the plants will grow, once frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed to at least 18.3 degrees C; cold, wet ground can rot seed. Place seeds about 1.3 to 5.1 cm deep and roughly 5.1 to 7.6 cm apart, in rows 51 to 122 cm apart. Choose a sunny spot with well-draining loam or light clay, and avoid waterlogged ground. Guides accept a soil pH from about 5.5 to 7.5. Expect seedlings within about 4 to 14 days. One guide thins to about 30 cm. Sow again every 3 weeks for a steady supply of fresh peas.
text.how_to_care: Cowpeas tolerate dry spells, so water mainly around flowering and pod fill, and keep the soil from becoming waterlogged. Spread organic mulch to hold moisture. The crop has a low feeding need, and too much nitrogen gives leafy growth at the expense of pods. The flowers pollinate themselves. Rotate so the crop returns to the same soil only after about three years, to limit disease. Watering at the base of the plants suits hot, dry weather while they are in flower and podding.
text.harvest: From sowing, guides give a first harvest anywhere from about 50 to 125 days, depending on type. For fresh shelling, pick once the seeds have filled out and the pods open easily, before the pods start to dry. For dry peas, wait until the pods are tan, dry and brittle. Fresh pods keep in the fridge; shelled peas can be frozen after blanching, and fully dried peas store in a cool, dry place.
common_mistakes: Sowing into cold, wet soil, which rots seed and kills seedlings.
Planting before frost danger has passed.
Feeding with too much nitrogen, which grows leaves rather than pods.
Letting the soil become waterlogged.
Leaving fresh pods on the plant until they begin to dry when shelling peas are wanted.
