problems.name: Corn earworm
problems.signs: Caterpillars eat the silks and the ear tips: holes in the tips, silks gone and damp droppings near the silk.
prevention: Choose varieties whose husks close tightly over the ear tip
Remove the damaged part of the ear at harvest

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Small green or black insects on leaves, tassels and ears. Heavily infested young plants crinkle and stunt, and sticky honeydew coats leaves and ears.
prevention: Dislodge them with a strong jet of water

problems.name: Poor kernel fill
problems.signs: Ears with gaps or poorly filled tips and few kernels, after drought or hot spells while tassels and silks are active.
prevention: Keep soil moist in dry weather
Plant at the spacing advised
Plant in a block of several rows rather than one long row
Keep feeding up so plants do not run short

problems.name: Corn smut
problems.signs: Swollen white fungal galls on the ears, stems or tassels.
prevention: Remove infected ears promptly from stalks and garden
Clear plant debris after harvest

problems.name: Cutworms
problems.signs: Young plants cut off close to the soil surface.
prevention: Place a small collar, such as a paper cup with the base cut out, around each seedling

problems.name: Seedling rot
problems.signs: Seedlings darken, wilt and die, usually in cool, wet soil.
prevention: Let the soil dry out before watering again

problems.name: Lodging
problems.signs: Plants fall over, for example in thunderstorms.
prevention: Run one or two strands of heavy string round the planting to hold stalks up

text.summary: Sweet corn is an annual grown for its ears of sweet kernels. It likes full sun, fertile well-drained soil and plenty of water, above all while the tassels open and the ears fill. Wind does the pollinating, so plant it in a block. Sweeter types are fussier about cold soil than standard types.
text.how_to_plant: Sow seed straight into the ground once frost danger has passed and the soil is warm, about 18 degrees C or more; standard types tolerate slightly cooler soil than the sweeter types. Pick a sunny, well-drained, fertile spot out of strong wind. Place seeds about 2.5 to 5 cm deep and roughly 18 to 45 cm apart, with rows 60 to 90 cm apart, and plant several short rows side by side as a block. If two seeds go in each hole, thin to the stronger one. Sow again every 10 to 14 days for a longer supply. In a pot, use one at least 30 cm deep.
text.how_to_care: Keep the soil evenly moist, taking most care while tassels open and ears fill, because dry spells then leave ears gappy. Corn is hungry, so work in a fertiliser before sowing and add a nitrogen side dressing partway through growth. Spread organic mulch round the base, away from young plants, to hold water and hold weeds back; weed gently so roots are not damaged. On a dry morning, a gentle shake of the plants as pollen sheds can help. Grow one type, or keep sweeter types apart, so cross-pollination does not spoil the sugar.
text.harvest: Expect the first ears roughly 63 to 120 days after sowing, depending on variety and temperature, and each sowing ripens over only about a week, so stagger sowings. Pick when the husk is still green, the silks have dried brown and a kernel squeezes out milky juice instead of watery juice. Eat quickly: sweetness fades with every day of storage, and fridge storage buys only a short time. Expect about one ear per plant, sometimes a smaller second.
common_mistakes: Sowing into cold soil, where seed germinates poorly.
Growing corn in one or two long rows, which gives poorly filled ears.
Letting plants run dry while tassels open and ears fill.
Planting sweeter types close to standard corn, which loses their extra sweetness.
Storing picked ears for days, which costs sweetness.

text.summary: Ginger is a tropical perennial grown for its spicy underground stems, called rhizomes. It is planted from pieces of rhizome rather than seed, and it is slow: mature rhizomes take many months, although young ginger can be dug earlier. It likes warm soil, shelter from hot afternoon sun and steady moisture, and it suits large pots.
text.how_to_plant: Start from plump pieces of rhizome, each with at least two buds, often called eyes. If you cut a large piece apart, let the cut ends dry for a few days first so they do not rot. Plant in warm soil in a loose, well-drained bed rich in organic matter, or in a large pot. Set the pieces with the buds facing up, about 2.5 cm deep, although some guides go as deep as 15 cm. Space them roughly 15 to 38 cm apart. Keep the soil moist, not soggy, until shoots appear.
text.how_to_care: Ginger copes with partial shade as well as sun, but hot afternoon sun browns the leaf tips, so shelter it through the hottest hours. Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy, because cold, wet soil rots the rhizomes. Mound soil up around the base as the rhizome pushes upward. Grow it in a container where cold is likely, and bring it indoors before temperatures drop. The leaves die back and the plant rests, so hold off watering container plants until new shoots show.
text.harvest: Young ginger can be dug early, before the flower spikes appear; its skin is thin, so it needs no peeling, and the taste is milder. Mature rhizomes need many months, roughly 120 to 300 days from planting depending on the guide, and are ready when the leaves yellow and die back. Dig gently, and take only part of the crop if you want the plant to carry on. Let the rhizomes dry in shade briefly before keeping them in the fridge or freezer.
common_mistakes: Leaving plants in hot, intense sun, which browns the leaf tips.
Leaving the soil soggy or cold and wet, which rots the rhizomes.
Leaving container plants outside when cold arrives.
Refrigerating rhizomes that are saved for replanting.
Letting the plant dry out completely while it is growing.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.signs: Small sap-sucking insects, a few millimetres long, gather on new shoots and under the leaves.
prevention: Wash them off with a strong jet from a garden hose.

problems.name: Spider mites
problems.signs: Leaves turn dry, wilted or discoloured, and the underside of a leaf can feel rough like fine sandpaper.
prevention: Prune plants so air moves freely through them.
Wash them off with a strong jet from a garden hose.

problems.name: Downy mildew
problems.signs: Yellow to grey-brown patches appear on the leaves, especially on the undersides.
prevention: Do not overcrowd plants, so air can flow between them.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.signs: A greyish-white powdery coating forms on the leaves, sometimes on flowers and stems.
prevention: Space plants so air circulates and the leaves dry.
Grow disease-resistant types such as the Profusion series.

problems.name: Leaf spots
problems.signs: Small round or angular spots form on the leaves: dark reddish, purplish or reddish-purple, some with pale grey or white centres.
prevention: Water at the base so the foliage stays dry.
Choose resistant types such as the Profusion series.

text.summary: Zinnia is a fast-growing annual grown for bright flowers in many colours, on plants from about 15 to 120 centimetres tall. It needs full sun and soil that drains well, and it is usually grown from seed sown where it will flower. It also suits pots.
text.how_to_plant: Choose a spot with at least 6 hours of direct sun and soil that drains well and holds plenty of organic matter. Sow seed about 6 millimetres deep straight where the plants will grow, because zinnias dislike having their roots disturbed. Seed sprouts in about 5 to 24 days when the soil is warm, around 21 to 29 degrees C. Spacing depends on the cultivar: dwarf types need about 20 to 23 centimetres, tall types about 30, and some sources allow up to about 60. First flowers usually open 8 to 12 weeks after sowing. In a pot, allow at least 40 litres for each plant.
text.how_to_care: Water at the base of the plants and keep the leaves dry, because wet foliage encourages disease. Give plants room, since crowding encourages disease and cuts airflow. Add some mulch around the base to hold moisture in the soil, and avoid overwatering, which harms the roots. Watch for aphids, spider mites, powdery mildew, leaf spots and downy mildew, and wash pests off with a jet from a hose.
text.harvest: Zinnia is grown for its flowers rather than as a harvest crop, so there is no harvest window to plan around. Plants keep producing blooms over a long season. The flowers can also be cut and brought indoors for display, and they draw bees and butterflies to the garden.
common_mistakes: Planting zinnias too close together, which encourages disease.
Letting water sit on the foliage, which encourages disease on the leaves.
